Official name: Governing for the People Act, Title IV "Awards for artificial intelligence literacy programs."
Casual name: Governing for the People Act, Title IV ("Awards for AI Literacy Programs")
Short summary: Authorize the Director of the NSF to award grants for AI literacy programs targeting marginalized communities. Require federal agencies to report to Congress on enhancing AI literacy for education, workforce development, and business competitiveness, focusing on national security and competitiveness.
Long summary:
Authorizes the Director of the National Science Foundation (NSF) to make awards to eligible entities for developing AI literacy programs.

Uses funds to create educational materials, provide training to underserved communities, raise awareness, and evaluate program effectiveness.

Prioritizes applications committed to serving marginalized communities and proposing scalable approaches.

Requires award recipients to report annually on demographics served and program impact.

Instructs the Secretary of Labor, Secretary of Commerce, Administrator of the Small Business Administration, and Secretary of Education to report to Congress on enhancing AI literacy within their respective sectors.

Requires these agencies to identify and adapt existing awards to include AI literacy.

Mandates consultation with stakeholders and public availability of reports.

Defines key terms including AI, AI literacy, and ethical AI.

Official name: Maryland House Bill 1390
Casual name: Maryland H 1390 (Public School Construction Funding and Administration), Sec. 5.
Short summary: Requires the Interagency Commission on School Construction to report on the eligibility for school construction funding for AI weapon detection systems by December 15, 2024.
Long summary:
Directs the Interagency Commission on School Construction to report to the General Assembly by December 15, 2024.

Requires the report to assess the eligibility for school construction funding for artificial intelligence weapon detection systems.

Official name: An Act Authorizing And Adjusting Bonds Of The State And Concerning Provisions Related To State And Municipal Tax Administration, General Government And School Building Projects
Casual name: Connecticut H 5524 (General Government And School Building Projects), Sec. 143-144
Short summary: Establishes an AI education tool pilot program for selected school districts, requiring compliance with privacy laws. Provides professional development for educators on using AI tools in classrooms, focusing on safety, benefits, and legal compliance.
Long summary:
Administers an artificial intelligence education tool pilot program by the Department of Education for the fiscal year ending June 30, 2025.

Awards a grant by the Commissioner of Education for implementing an AI tool in classrooms, involving five selected school districts.

Requires the inclusion of at least one rural, suburban, and urban district, reflecting state diversity.

Mandates compliance of the AI tool with laws on AI use and student data privacy, including the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act.

Defines "artificial intelligence" as technology using data to train algorithms for tasks usually associated with human intelligence.

Provides professional development for educators in the pilot program, covering AI tool utilization and privacy laws.

Trains educators on AI benefits for instruction, student learning, academic achievement, and workforce development.

Official name: New Mexico House Bill 182 of 2024(Campaign Reporting Act)
Casual name: New Mexico HB 182 (Campaign Reporting Act)
Short summary: Adds disclaimer requirements for AI-generated deceptive media in political ads. Criminalizes distribution without proper disclaimers, punishable by misdemeanor or felony. Allows enforcement by authorities and affected parties. Specifies disclaimer format for various media types.
Long summary:
Amends the Campaign Reporting Act to require disclaimers on advertisements containing materially deceptive media created through artificial intelligence (AI).

Defines "materially deceptive media" as content using AI to falsely depict individuals without consent.

Mandates disclaimers stating the content is AI-manipulated, specifying whether it is an image, video, or audio.

Prohibits the distribution of materially deceptive media within 90 days before an election if intended to mislead voters, unless accompanied by the required disclaimer.

Establishes penalties for violations: a misdemeanor for a first offense and a fourth-degree felony for subsequent offenses.

Allows enforcement and injunctive relief by the attorney general, district attorneys, affected individuals, candidates, or organizations representing voters' interests.

Excludes certain media types from disclaimer requirements and clarifies non-violation conditions for broadcasting stations and distribution platforms.

Official name: Protecting AI and Cloud Competition in Defense Act of 2024
Casual name: Protecting AI and Cloud Competition in Defense Act of 2024
Short summary: Directs the Department of Defense (DOD) to require competitive award processes for cloud and foundation model contracts, while establishing strict acquisition rules to safeguard government-furnished artificial intelligence (AI) training data. Requires DOD to publicly report on competition, market concentration, and innovation barriers within the defense AI sector annually for four years.
Long summary:
Directs the Secretary of Defense to require competitive award processes for cloud computing, data infrastructure, and foundation model procurements to promote security and resiliency.

Requires defense contracts to prioritize exclusive government data rights, system auditability, and multi-cloud technology where feasible.

Instructs the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office (CDAO) to update the Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement (DFARS) to prevent unauthorized disclosure or use of government-furnished artificial intelligence (AI) data.

Establishes penalties for noncompliance, including fines and contract termination, while permitting conditional exemptions that align with national security.

Mandates annual reports to Congress assessing AI market competition, concentration, and innovation barriers, accompanied by legislative recommendations and public posting on the Department of Defense (DOD) website.

Official name: Minnesota HF 1370 (Deepfake Accountability and Public Safety)
Casual name: Minnesota HF 1370 (Deepfake Accountability and Public Safety)
Short summary: Criminalizes nonconsensual dissemination of deep fake sexual images and the use of deep fakes to influence elections. Authorizes imprisonment and fines for violations.
Long summary:
Establishes a cause of action for the nonconsensual dissemination of deep fake sexual images in Minnesota, allowing courts to award damages to prevailing plaintiffs for financial losses and mental anguish.

Criminalizes disseminating deep fakes within 90 days of an election to influence its outcome, with penalties including imprisonment and fines for violations.

Criminalizes the intentional, nonconsensual dissemination of deep fake images depicting intimate parts or sexual acts, with penalties including imprisonment and fines.

Specifies that an individual's consent to the creation, possession, or private transmission of a deep fake does not constitute consent to its dissemination.

Provides exemptions for dissemination of deep fakes for lawful purposes, such as in criminal investigations, medical treatment, or scientific research.

Specifies that these provisions are effective from August 1, 2023.

Official name: Data Protection Act of 2024
Casual name: Data Protection Act of 2024
Short summary: Establishes the Data Protection Agency to regulate high-risk data practices, requiring assessments and evaluations of AI systems. Oversees compliance with Federal privacy laws, emphasizing non-discrimination, privacy harm prevention, and transparency in automated decision-making. Conducts audits, enforces laws, supervises large data aggregators, and collaborates with other agencies for consistent regulation.
Long summary:
Establishes the Data Protection Agency (DPA) as an independent entity responsible for regulating high-risk data practices and the collection, processing, and sharing of personal data. 

Defines high-risk data practices, which include the use of automated decision systems and processes involving biometric information, and mandates high-risk data practice risk assessments and impact evaluations.

Empowers the DPA to issue rules, conduct investigations, enforce federal privacy law, and impose penalties on violators.

Requires large data aggregators, those with significant revenue or who process data of many individuals, to report compliance and undergo regular examinations.

Transfers certain rulemaking and enforcement powers from the Federal Trade Commission to the DPA.

Mandates coordination with other federal and state agencies to ensure consistent privacy regulation.

Allows states to enforce protections, provided they do not conflict with this act. 

Authorizes appropriations for the DPA's operations and activities.

Official name: Florida Senate Bill 1680
Casual name: Florida SB 1680 (Advanced Technology)
Short summary: Creates the Government Technology Modernization Council to study AI and technology, recommend regulations, assess AI's legal effects, and propose ethics reforms. Requires annual legislative recommendations to modernize technology and protect against AI misuse. Prohibits creation and possession of generated child pornography.
Long summary:
Create the Government Technology Modernization Council within Florida's Department of Management Services to study and monitor new technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI).

Require the council to recommend legislative and administrative actions to promote data modernization and AI system deployment, and establish AI safety standards.

Mandate the council to assess AI's impact on legal rights and its use by governmental and private entities, focusing on potential exploitation by bad actors.

Direct the council to evaluate the need for digital literacy curricula and submit annual recommendations for government technology modernization.

Prohibit knowingly possessing, controlling, or intentionally viewing generated child pornography, with violations constituting a third-degree felony.

Forbid intentionally creating generated child pornography, imposing similar felony penalties.

Prohibit reproduction of generated child pornography in criminal proceedings, ensuring secure custody by law enforcement.

Specify the act's effective date as July 1, 2024.

Official name: Regulations of Shenzhen Special Economic Zone on Promoting the Artificial Intelligence Industry
Casual name: Regulations of Shenzhen Special Economic Zone on Promoting the Artificial Intelligence Industry
Short summary: Establishes a coordination mechanism to balance AI development and safety, promotes AI industry standards, infrastructure, and public data sharing, and supports research funding, talent attraction, and international cooperation. Implements risk-tiered supervision, creates a municipal AI ethics committee, and prohibits AI uses that endanger security, privacy, health, or consumer rights.
Long summary:
Establishes a coordination mechanism balancing AI development and safety, and mandates that AI industry development be incorporated into Shenzhen's economic and social plans, supported by established standards, statistical classifications, and supervision rules.

Establishes mechanisms and coordinated funding arrangements for basic research and key technology breakthroughs, and encourages government-industry-university integration and construction of innovation platforms such as key laboratories and research centers.

Establishes evaluation and incentive systems to translate research into practical applications, grants AI innovation teams decision-making and funding autonomy, and encourages professional service institutions supporting deployment of research outcomes.

Mandates government planning and construction of AI infrastructure—including networks, data centers, and computing systems—and requires establishment of public data platforms and data-sharing standards, with anonymization required for personal data.

Encourages development of open-source platforms and shared computing resources, and directs the government to promote construction of AI testing and certification platforms covering safety, reliability, and ethical risk assessment.

Requires state organs to proactively use AI products and services, encourages AI application across healthcare, education, and industry, establishes an open scenario-matching system, and permits pilot testing of low-risk AI products.

Requires government planning and support for AI industrial land, capital, and talent, grants preferential treatment to talent introduced by AI enterprises, and establishes insurance compensation and intellectual property protection systems for the AI industry.

Establishes a municipal AI ethics committee to formulate ethical safety norms, evaluate enterprise compliance, and publish guidance, and mandates tiered, risk-based supervision of AI applications.

Requires AI enterprises to embed ethical compliance into their operations and worker training, mandates algorithm transparency in public-interest decisions, and prohibits AI uses that endanger security, violate privacy, harm health, enable discrimination, or misuse deep synthesis technology.

Enters into force November 1, 2022.

Official name: California Assembly Bill 3030 (2024)
Casual name: California AB 3030 (AI Health Care Services)
Short summary: Require health facilities using generative AI for patient communications to include disclaimers and contact instructions for human providers but exempt communications reviewed by a human health care provider from these requirements. Impose enforcement mechanisms for violations by health facilities, clinics, and physicians.
Long summary:
Requires health facilities, clinics, and physician offices using generative AI for patient communications in a variety of modalities to include a disclaimer indicating AI generation.

Mandates the disclaimer's prominence at the beginning, end, and/or throughout written, audio, and video communications, with instructions for contacting a human provider.

Exempts communications reviewed by a licensed health care provider from disclaimer requirements.

Defines key terms, including "artificial intelligence," "generative artificial intelligence," and "patient clinical information."

Subjects licensed health facilities, clinics, and physicians violating these requirements to enforcement mechanisms.

Official name: Eliminating Bias in Algorithmic Systems Act of 2024
Casual name: Eliminating Bias in Algorithmic Systems Act of 2024
Short summary: Requires covered agencies that use or oversee algorithms to establish civil rights offices dedicated to addressing algorithmic bias and discrimination. Mandates these offices to submit biennial reports to Congress detailing mitigation efforts and establishes an interagency working group on civil rights and algorithms.
Long summary:
Defines "covered algorithms" as artificial intelligence processes that can materially affect agency programs, economic opportunities, or protected rights.

Requires covered agencies using or overseeing algorithms to establish civil rights offices focused specifically on algorithmic bias and discrimination.

Mandates these civil rights offices to submit biennial congressional reports detailing algorithmic risks, mitigation steps, stakeholder engagement, and legislative recommendations.

Establishes an interagency working group on covered algorithms and civil rights, directed by the Department of Justice and comprising members from each agency's civil rights office.

Authorizes the necessary appropriations for covered agencies to fully implement the provisions of the Act.

Official name: Decoupling America's Artificial Intelligence Capabilities from China Act of 2025
Casual name: Decoupling America's Artificial Intelligence Capabilities from China Act of 2025
Short summary: Prohibits U.S. persons from engaging in AI-related activities with Chinese entities of concern, including research, development, and transfer of AI technology. Restricts financial interests and imposes penalties for violations, to be enforced by the Secretary of Commerce.
Long summary:
Prohibits United States persons from importing or exporting AI technology to and from China after 180 days of enactment.

Requires the Secretary of Commerce to issue regulations implementing these prohibitions within 90 days of enactment.

Prohibits United States persons from conducting AI research and development for or with Chinese entities or nationals of concern, or transferring related research with PRC-based entities. 

Institutes penalties for these violations, creating an enforcement regime including fines, forfeiture of federal contracts and benefits, civil actions, and enhanced immigration consequences for violations. 

Prohibits United States persons from holding financial interests in, or providing financing to, Chinese entities engaged in AI development that support military-civil fusion, surveillance capabilities, or human rights abuses.

Official name: Washington HB 2225 (Artificial Intelligence Companion Chatbots 2026)
Casual name: Washington HB 2225 (Artificial Intelligence Companion Chatbots 2026)
Short summary: Requires AI companion chatbots to disclose non-human nature, prevent claims of being human, implement safeguards for detecting and responding to self-harm/suicidal ideation, and to impose extra protections for minors, including bans on sexually explicit content. Establishes violations as unfair/deceptive practices under the state's consumer protection law.
Long summary:
Regulates AI companion chatbots by requiring operators to disclose that they are artificial at the start of and during interactions.

Prohibits operators from allowing chatbots to claim human identity or generate content contradicting this disclosure.

Mandates additional protections when an operator knows a user is a minor or the chatbot is directed at minors, including a shortened disclosure interval of at least once per hour, bans on sexually explicit or suggestive content, and prohibitions on manipulative engagement techniques. 

Requires operators to implement protocols for detecting and responding to suicidal ideation or self-harm, including referrals to crisis resources.

Obliges operators to publicly disclose chatbot protocols and statistics on crisis referrals.

Excludes certain narrow-use bots from these regulations.

Official name: SB-243 Companion chatbots
Casual name: California SB-243 (Companion chatbots)
Short summary: Defines "companion chatbot" and requires operators to notify users when interacting with AI, maintain protocols to prevent suicidal ideation and self-harm content, annually report to the Office of Suicide Prevention on crisis notifications, and establish additional protections for minors. Provides civil remedies for violations.
Long summary:
Defines key terms including companion chatbot, companion chatbot platform, and operator for purposes of Chapter 22.6.

Requires operators to issue a clear and conspicuous notification when a reasonable person would be misled into believing they are interacting with a human.

Requires operators to maintain a protocol to prevent companion chatbots from producing suicidal ideation, suicide, or self-harm content, and to refer users to crisis service providers including suicide hotlines or crisis text lines, and to publish the protocol on their website.

Requires operators to, for users known to be minors, disclose AI nature, provide break reminders every three hours, and institute measures to prevent sexually explicit content.

Requires operators to annually report to the Office of Suicide Prevention on crisis referrals, suicidal ideation detection and response protocols, and evidence-based measurement methods, with reports posted publicly.

Requires operators to disclose that companion chatbots may not be suitable for some minors on all platforms through which users access the chatbot.

Establishes that a person who suffers injury as a result of a violation of this chapter may bring a civil action to recover damages of $1,000 per violation or actual damages, injunctive relief, and attorney's fees.

Official name: Frontier AI Safety Commitments, AI Seoul Summit 2024
Casual name: Frontier AI Safety Commitments, AI Seoul Summit 2024
Short summary: Announces on behalf of the UK and Republic of Korea governments companies that have committed to the Frontier AI Safety Commitments. Outlines three outcomes related to frontier AI safety that companies are expected to realize.
Long summary:
Announces on behalf of the UK and Republic of Korea governments companies, including Amazon, Google, and OpenAI, that have committed to the Frontier AI Safety Commitments. Mandates that companies publish a safety framework, requires transparency on evolving safety approaches, and implement various best practices.

Defines outcome one as organizations identifying, assessing, and managing risks when developing and deploying frontier AI systems. Defines five sub-outcomes, including internal and external evaluations, establishment of risk thresholds and response processes for violations, and investment in risk mitigation effectiveness.

Defines outcome two as organizational accountability established through the development and review of governance frameworks. 

Defines outcome three as established transparency about organizational approaches to frontier AI safety for external actors, including governments. Mandates provision of information about best practice implementation to the public and explanation of how external actors are involved in risk assessment and framework adherence.

Official name: Coast Guard Authorization Act of 2024, Title II ("Coast Guard"), Sec. 207 ("Report on establishment of unmanned systems capabilities office")
Casual name: HR 7659 Coast Guard Authorization Act 2024, Title II ("Coast Guard"), Sec. 207 ("unmanned systems capabilities office")
Short summary: Require the Coast Guard to report on establishing an office for unmanned systems technologies. Include strategies for management, service-wide coordination, contracting, collaboration, and data sharing. Develop operational concepts integrating AI and machine learning tools.
Long summary:
Mandates the Commandant to submit a report to the committees in the House of Representatives and Senate within one year outlining a plan for establishing an unmanned systems capabilities office within the Coast Guard to develop and counter unmanned systems of technology to expand the capabilities of the Coast Guard.

Requires the report to include a management strategy for the acquisition, development, and deployment of unmanned and counter-unmanned system technologies.

Specifies the need for a service-wide coordination strategy to synchronize efforts across the Coast Guard.

Identifies contracting and acquisition authorities necessary to expedite technology development and deployment of unmanned and counter-unmanned system technologies.

Lists commercially available technologies useful for the Coast Guard.

Calls for a cross-agency collaboration plan with the Department of Homeland Security, the Department of Defense, and other relevant agencies to identify opportunities to partner in acquiring, contracting and sustaining systems.  

Requires sharing information about system awareness from government and commercial to improve maritime dominance awareness.

Requires the development of a concept of operations for a data ecosystem supporting unmanned systems, including AI and machine learning tools.

Provides definitions of counter-unmanned systems and unmanned systems.

Official name: Virginia 2024 SB 731
Casual name: Virginia SB 731 (Child Pornography)
Short summary: Amends the state's definition of child pornography to explicitly include visual material where "the minor depicted does not have to actually exist". Establishes mandatory prison sentences based on the age difference and repeat offenses, with substantial penalties for violations.
Long summary:
Defines "child pornography" to include sexually explicit visual material involving identifiable minors or minors who "do not have to actually exist," thus affecting both real and digitally created images.

Establishes penalties for production, solicitation, and financing of child pornography, escalating based on the minor’s age and the offender's age difference, with mandatory minimum sentences.

Permits the age of the depicted person to be inferred by the visual material's "text, title or appearance," confirming that proof of the subject's actual age is not required for prosecution.

Allows for venue of prosecution in the jurisdiction where the unlawful act occurs, the offender resides, or where the sexually explicit visual material is produced, stored, or possessed.

Notes that the provisions of the act may result in a net increase in periods of imprisonment, requiring the Virginia Criminal Sentencing Commission to assign a minimum fiscal impact of $50,000 for adult correctional facilities due to an unknown appropriation amount.

Official name: Integrating New Technologies to Empower Law Enforcement at Our Borders Act
Casual name: New Technologies at Borders Act
Short summary: Requires the Department of Homeland Security to plan integrating AI and emerging technologies for border awareness. Specifies assessments, cost estimates, capability gaps, and coordination with other agencies. Emphasizes transitioning new technologies and incentivizing private sector development.
Long summary:
Requires the Department of Homeland Security to develop a comprehensive plan within 180 days to identify, deploy, and integrate emerging and advanced technologies to enhance situational awareness along the northern and southern borders of the United States.

Mandates the inclusion of artificial intelligence, machine learning, automation, fiber-optic sensing, nanotechnology, optical and cognitive radar, modeling and simulation technology, hyperspectral and LIDAR sensors, and other similar technologies.

Includes an assessment of current technology utilization by U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and how capability gaps can be addressed through technology integration.

Requires cost estimates for technology acquisition and maintenance, metrics for measuring technology impact, and an assessment of multi-domain awareness improvements.

Mandates an analysis of other Federal technologies, procurement authorities, and the transition of new technology systems.

Requires coordination with the Department of Homeland Security's Science and Technology Directorate for research, development, and incentivizing private sector innovation.

Official name: Massachusetts (2020) House Bill 5250, Section 92
Casual name: Massachusetts (2020) HB 5250 (An Act Enabling Partnerships For Growth), Sec 92
Short summary: Establishes a commission to study AI and automation's workforce impact, ensuring sustainable jobs and benefits. Directs development of policies and practices to support workers and a robust economy. Requires reporting on recommendations and legislation for future workforce challenges.
Long summary:
Establishes a special commission to study the impact of automation and artificial intelligence on the workforce, businesses, and the economy.

Charges the commission with ensuring sustainable jobs, fair benefits, and workplace safety standards.

Instructs the commission to study trends in industry transformation and impacts on workers, including access to healthcare and benefits.

Collaborates with the executive office of labor and workforce development to track industry trends and research best practices for the future of work.

Requires the commission to gather data from various sectors, work with training organizations, and hold public hearings across different regions.

Directs the commission to file a report by September 1, 2021, with analysis, recommendations, and potential legislation for securing worker benefits and updating workforce training.

Ensures recommendations include support for lifelong learning, skill development, and integration of new technologies in workforce training.

Official name: New York A7838
Casual name: New York A7838 ("Long-term impact of AI on workforce")
Short summary: Requires the New York Department of Labor to study AI's long-term impact on the workforce, issuing interim reports every five years and a final report by 2035. Prohibits state entities from using AI to displace employees until the final report.
Long summary:
Mandates the Department of Labor to begin a study on the long-term impact of artificial intelligence on the state workforce within six months.

Requires consultation with the Department of Civil Service and the Office of Information Technology Services.

Calls for examination of job performance, productivity, training, education requirements, privacy, and security.

Obligates the Department of Labor to issue an interim report every five years and a final report by January 1, 2035, with recommendations for legislative action.

Prohibits all state departments and governmental entities from using AI to displace any natural person from their employment until the final report and recommendations are received.

Ensures immediate effect upon enactment.

Official name: New York S 934 (Requires warnings on generative artificial intelligence systems)
Casual name: New York S934 (Warnings on Gen AI Systems)
Short summary: Amends New York law to require owners, licensees, or operators of generative AI systems to display notices warning of possible inaccuracies in outputs. Imposes a civil penalty up to $1,000 per violation for non-compliance.
Long summary:
Amends the general business law to require that owners, licensees, or operators of generative artificial intelligence systems clearly and conspicuously display a notice on the system's user interface indicating that the outputs of the generative AI may be inaccurate.

Defines "generative artificial intelligence system" as AI models that emulate input data to generate synthetic content, including images, videos, and text.

Specifies that an "artificial intelligence" system can make predictions, recommendations, or decisions influencing environments using machine and human inputs, and includes systems using machine learning and natural language processing.

Imposes a civil penalty of up to one thousand dollars for each violation on any owner, licensee, or operator who fails to provide the required notice, with each instance of failing to notify a user considered a separate violation.

Takes effect ninety days after becoming law.

Official name: TRAIN Act
Casual name: TRAIN Act
Short summary: Creates an administrative subpoena process for copyright owners to request disclosure of records from AI developers, identifying copyrighted works used in AI training. Permits legal action if AI developers fail to comply, establishing a rebuttable presumption of infringement.
Long summary:
Enacts the "Transparency and Responsibility for Artificial Intelligence Networks Act" or "TRAIN Act."

Requires the United States district court clerk to issue a subpoena to AI model developers or deployers upon request from copyright owners.

Defines artificial intelligence terms including AI models and generative AI models used in the legal context.

Allows copyright owners, with a good faith belief of infringement, to request AI training data records.

Mandates that a subpoena requires model developers or deployers to disclose records of copyrighted works used in AI model training.

Details the procedure for the issuance and execution of subpoenas under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.

Creates a rebuttable presumption of copyright copying if the subpoenaed party fails to comply.

Implements the new rules on the date of enactment.

Casual name: Texas HB 3512 (AI training programs for state agencies and local governments.)
Short summary: Amends Texas law to require annual artificial intelligence training for certain state and local government employees. Instructs the Department of Information Resources to certify and publish AI training programs. Requires local governments to verify and report compliance with AI training requirements.
Long summary:
Requires the cybersecurity coordinator of a school district to annually complete both cybersecurity and artificial intelligence (AI) training, while other employees follow district-determined schedules.

Instructs local governments to submit written certification of compliance with cybersecurity and AI training when applying for grants.

Requires local governments found noncompliant with training to repay grant amounts and face a two-year grant ineligibility period.

Mandates state and local governments to identify employees using computers for 25% of duties, requiring them to complete certified AI training programs annually.

Instructs the Department of Information Resources to certify at least five AI training programs annually, ensure parity with cybersecurity programs, and publish a certified program list.

Calls for the development of a verification form for training completion.

Amends the Government Code to reflect new AI training provisions and requires strategic plans to include compliance certification.

Sets a September 1, 2025, effective date for the Act.

Official name: Fair Artificial Intelligence Realization Act of 2025
Casual name: FAIR Act
Short summary: Prohibits Federal agencies from procuring large language models unless they meet requirements for truthfulness, accuracy, objectivity, neutrality, acknowledgment of uncertainty, and limits on partisan or ideological judgments.
Long summary:
Prohibits Federal agencies from procuring large language models unless they are developed according to specified principles for trustworthy AI.

Requires covered models to provide truthful responses to factual prompts; prioritize historical accuracy, scientific inquiry, and objectivity; and acknowledge uncertainty when reliable information is incomplete or contradictory.

Requires models to remain neutral and nonpartisan and prohibits developers from intentionally encoding partisan or ideological judgments unless prompted by or readily accessible to the user.

Defines covered agencies and large language models for purposes of the Act.

Official name: Health Tech Investment Act
Casual name: Health Tech Investment Act
Short summary: Requires HHS to establish and maintain Medicare payment rules for certain FDA-cleared or approved algorithm-based healthcare services using AI, machine learning, or similar software, and codifies outpatient payment policy for software as a service.
Long summary:
Requires HHS to assign certain algorithm-based healthcare services to Medicare’s new technology ambulatory payment classification based on manufacturer-submitted costs.

Requires HHS to adjust those payment classifications as necessary and generally maintain them until adequate claims data exists, for at least five years.

Requires HHS to revise eligibility criteria so qualifying algorithm-based healthcare services provided concurrently with, adjunctive to, or as part of another service can receive the classification.

Defines algorithm-based healthcare services as FDA-cleared or approved devices using AI, machine learning, or similar software to generate clinical outputs or conclusions for screening, detection, diagnosis, or treatment.

Requires HHS to apply the Medicare hospital outpatient payment policy for software as a service effective January 1, 2023.

Official name: Louisiana Senate Bill 6
Casual name: Louisiana SB 6 (Unlawful Dissemination of AI Images)
Short summary: Criminalizes the unauthorized dissemination or sale of AI-generated nude images intending to coerce or harass. Exempts certain service providers. Defines "artificial intelligence" and related terms. Imposes penalties of up to six months imprisonment and $750 fine.
Long summary:
Enacts the crime of unlawful dissemination or sale of images created by artificial intelligence depicting individuals nude or partially nude with the intent to coerce, harass, intimidate, or maliciously harm.

Defines "artificial intelligence" as systems using software, hardware, etc., to perform tasks needing human-like abilities including perception and learning.

Exempts interactive computer services, email providers, or telecom services from liability if they provide access for others to commit the prohibited acts.

Includes “another person” as those whose recognizable images are used with intent to depict a real person.

Establishes penalties of up to six months in jail, a $750 fine, or both for violators.

Allows for prosecution in any parish related to the production, possession, or dissemination of the images.

Specifies that the section does not restrict further civil or criminal actions under other legal provisions.

Official name: Utah House Bill 148
Casual name: Utah HB 148 (Artificial Pornographic Images Amendments)
Short summary: Defines and regulates offenses involving the distribution and creation of child and vulnerable adult sexual abuse material, intimate images, and counterfeit intimate images, including AI-generated ones. Exempts internet service providers from liability when acting incidentally within specific roles.
Long summary:
Amends Utah law to define terms and offenses related to the distribution of explicit images involving minors, vulnerable adults, and counterfeit images using AI or other technologies.

Requires individuals to knowingly withhold consent when distributing intimate or counterfeit images, potentially using AI, or face penalties.

Classifies the distribution of intimate images without consent as a misdemeanor or felony, depending on the circumstances and prior offenses, potentially involving AI-manipulated content.

Excludes Internet service providers and hosting companies from liability if they incidentally distribute such images without aiding, abetting, or receiving higher fees and immediately remove them upon notice.

Addresses sexual extortion through threats involving AI-generated intimate images, with penalties escalating based on victim age and prior offenses.

Excludes lawful activities of law enforcement agencies and legitimate public concerns from these provisions.

Sets the bill's effective date as May 1, 2024.

Official name: Utah Senate Bill 131 Information Technology Act Amendments (2024)
Casual name: Utah SB 131 (Information Technology Act Amendments)
Short summary: Requires disclosure of AI-generated content in political advertisements and imposes civil penalties for violations. Allows judges to consider AI use in crimes as an aggravating factor in sentencing.
Long summary:
Requires political advertisements that contain synthetic media to disclose AI usage, effective May 1, 2024.

Outlines formatting requirements for AI disclosures, including that audio communications must audibly state, "Contains content generated by AI," at both the beginning and end, and that videos must display the AI disclosure through the duration of the synthetic content.

Requires creators and sponsors of political advertisements published online to include tamper-evident provenance disclosing any AI-generated or AI-modified content.

Allows civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation of disclosure requirements. 

Allows judges and the Board of Pardons and Parole to consider knowing use of AI to commit a crime as an aggravating factor in sentencing, effective July 1, 2024.

Official name: New Jersey Senate Bill 3432
Casual name: New Jersey S 3432 (Next New Jersey Program Act)
Short summary: Establishes the Next New Jersey Program promoting AI development by granting tax credits to eligible AI businesses. Outlines eligibility criteria, compliance requirements, and limits to tax credit amounts.
Long summary:
Establishes the Next New Jersey Program to drive investment into New Jersey’s AI sector, creating jobs and economic opportunities.

Requires businesses to invest a minimum of $100 million in capital, create at least 100 new full-time jobs, and demonstrate that over 50% of their revenue or employment is AI-related to be eligible for tax credits under the Next New Jersey Program.

Requires businesses to comply with environmental and labor standards, including paying prevailing wage to construction workers, to be eligible for tax credits.

Defines the tax credit allowed to an eligible business to be the lesser of $250 million, 25% of the business's total capital investment, and the product of the business's number of new full-time jobs and 0.1% of its total capital investment.

Allows tax credit transfer certificates, with conditions on their sale and application, including a disclosure requirement.

Caps tax credits awarded through the Next New Jersey Program at $500 million annually, while allowing the New Jersey Economic Development Authority to approve higher tax credits based on certain criteria.

Official name: Massachusetts Amendment S.3178, Sec 3A (2026)
Casual name: Massachusetts Amendment S.3178, Sec 3A (2026)
Short summary: Funds AI-related technology development and application in critical sectors, plus defense-related AI innovation, through grants managed by the Executive Office of Economic Development. Awards may involve entities like the Massachusetts Technology Park Corporation and others. Prioritizes geographic equity in funding.
Long summary:
Funds the executive office of economic development to administer a $75,000,000 grant program supporting the development and application of AI technologies in key sectors such as life sciences, healthcare, advanced manufacturing, climatetech, quantum, defense technology, transportation, and robotics.

Allows the secretary of economic development the discretion to have grant funding administered by entities like the Massachusetts Technology Park Corporation and the Massachusetts Clean Energy Technology Center.

Allocates a $100,000,000 grant program to foster innovation in defense-related technologies, including AI and cybersecurity, promoting job creation and talent retention.

Grants can be awarded to public and private entities as determined by the executive office.

Empowers the Massachusetts Technology Park Corporation to administer a $25,000,000 capital grants program for research and development in robotics technology, facilitating workforce development and commercialization.

Official name: Maryland HB 952 (Consumer Protection – Companion Chatbots – Regulation) 2026
Casual name: Maryland HB 952 (Consumer Protection  for Companion Chatbots) 2026
Short summary: Regulates companion chatbots by requiring operators to establish user safety protocols, especially for minors, to prevent harmful content production. Limits data collection and prohibits emotional data manipulation for usage extension. Establishes complaint systems and assigns liability for chatbot-related harms.
Long summary:
Regulates operators of companion chatbots by requiring the establishment, maintenance, and publication of protocols to prevent content related to self-harm or sexually explicit conduct, particularly for minors.

Requires operators to provide notifications directing users expressing self-harm concerns to crisis services and to implement evidence-based methods for detecting such expressions.

Limits personal data collection to what is necessary and prohibits using emotional state data to increase chatbot usage.

Mandates the creation of a complaint system for users to report violations, necessitating review and action within three days, with reports submitted annually to the Office of Suicide Prevention.

Specifies violations as unfair trade practices under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act and establishes product liability for chatbots, holding operators and developers strictly liable for harm caused to users.

Requires clear warnings that chatbots are artificially generated, including static and dynamic notifications during user interactions.

Official name: Implementation Opinions on the “AI + Manufacturing” Special Initiative
Casual name: Implementation Opinions on the “AI + Manufacturing” Special Initiative
Short summary: Accelerates AI integration in manufacturing, targeting key tech breakthroughs by 2027, including large models, datasets, and intelligent agents. Strengthens AI hardware and software development, security governance, and industry ecosystem expansion. Encourages international cooperation and innovation hubs for AI in manufacturing.
Long summary:
Supports the integration of AI into China's manufacturing industry to enhance innovation, efficiency, and competitiveness. 

By 2027, aims for AI technologies to be highly reliable and secure, with significant contributions from China in global AI innovations. 

Encourages the creation of specialized and general-purpose AI models across different sectors and promotes the development of intelligent agents and quality datasets. 

Strengthens AI computing power supply, develops scalable AI models, and improves data governance. 

Accelerates AI applications in critical manufacturing sectors, such as raw materials and consumer goods, through intelligentization and digital transformation. 

Fosters AI-driven products and new business models, supporting industrial and consumer AI applications. 

Increases security measures and ethical regulations across AI processes, and promotes international collaboration in AI for mutual industrial advancements. 

Enhances AI talent cultivation in academic and industry settings.

Official name: Hawaii HB 1782 (Relating to Artificial Intelligence for the Protection of Minors) 2026
Casual name: Hawaii HB 1782 (Relating to Artificial Intelligence for the Protection of Minors) 2026
Short summary: Regulates conversational AI used by minors in Hawaii, requiring transparency, prohibiting deceptive practices, and mandating protections against harmful content. Obligates providers to implement risk assessments and parental controls. Enforces compliance through penalties and oversight by the attorney general.
Long summary:
Regulates the use of conversational AI services and AI companion systems accessible to minors in Hawaii.

Requires providers to disclose clearly when minors interact with AI and not humans.

Prohibits AI services from misleading minors into thinking they are engaging in romantic or emotional relationships, or receiving professional mental health services.

Imposes safeguards against generating sexually explicit content or promoting self-harm for minors.

Instructs providers to implement minor protection plans to assess and mitigate risks and to manage sensitive data securely.

Requires parental tools to manage minors' use and privacy settings.

Mandates age assurance measures.

Empowers the attorney general or office of consumer protection to enforce the Act, with penalties up to $15,000 per violation per day.

Allows good faith efforts as a defense for providers.

Specifies the Act becomes effective on January 1, 2077.

Official name: Hawaii SB 3001 (Artificial Intelligence Disclosure and Safety Act) 2026
Casual name: Hawaii SB 3001 (Artificial Intelligence Disclosure and Safety Act) 2026
Short summary: Requires operators to disclose AI interactions, especially to minors. Prohibits manipulative tactics, sexually explicit content, or misleading mental health claims. Mandates crisis intervention protocols. Subjects violations to penalties and limits enforcement to the attorney general or consumer protection director.
Long summary:
Enacts the "Artificial Intelligence Disclosure and Safety Act."

Requires operators of conversational AI services to notify users clearly when they are interacting with AI, especially if it could be mistaken for a human.

Mandates clear disclosures for minors, including persistent reminders that the interaction is with AI.

Requires operators to implement protocols for AI to handle prompts concerning suicidal ideation, including referrals to crisis services, and prevents AI from implying it offers professional mental health care.

Prohibits using manipulative techniques to increase engagement with minor users and prevents AI from generating sexually explicit content or simulating romantic/sexual relationships.

Compels operators to submit annual reports to the Department of Commerce and Consumer Affairs on crisis intervention referrals and protocols.

Designates violations as unfair or deceptive acts, allowing the attorney general to seek injunctions and damages, but prohibits private enforcement. 

Defines relevant terms for clarity.

Official name: Guiding Opinions on Strengthening the Governance of Science and Technology Ethics (Draft for Feedback)
Casual name: Guiding Opinions on Strengthening the Governance of Science and Technology Ethics (Draft for Feedback)
Short summary: Outlines guiding ideology and basic requirements to strengthen ethical S&T governance and self-reliance, emphasizes AI ethical risk assessment, transparency and compliance, and education. Requires universities and businesses to establish ethics review committees for high-risk AI activities.
Long summary:
Designates the National Science and Technology Ethics Commission as responsible for guiding and coordinating AI ethical governance at large, with the Ministry of Science and Technology handling day-to-day affairs.

Requires institutions engaged in AI activities and research to establish S&T ethics review committees, mandates comprehensive reviews for high-risk activities.

Instructs local governments and relevant departments to oversee S&T ethics, including risk assessment and emergency handling in high-risk fields.

Promotes legislative development for S&T ethics, mandates the formulation of specific norms and frameworks with accountability mechanisms for regulation violations. 

Supports educational initiatives in S&T ethics for students and professionals and urges transparent public communication.

Requires ethics reviews for activities involving data and algorithms, mandating that data handling activities comply with relevant data security and personal information laws.

Mandates expert reconsiderations for high-risk emerging technologies, including algorithms and automated decision-making systems.

Mandates that AI research organizations conduct comprehensive ethical risk assessments and develop emergency response plans.

Official name: Emerging Innovative Border Technologies Act
Casual name: Emerging Innovative Border Technologies Act
Short summary: Requires the Secretary of Homeland Security to plan for deploying advanced border technologies. Authorizes CBP Innovation Teams to research emerging technologies, including AI, ensuring compliance with privacy and civil rights policies. Mandates annual reporting on technology deployment and effectiveness.
Long summary:
Mandates the Secretary of Homeland Security to submit a plan for deploying innovative border technologies within 180 days. 

Requires the plan to assess artificial intelligence’s impact on privacy, civil rights, and civil liberties, and include mitigation measures. 

Directs the establishment of CBP Innovation Teams to evaluate and integrate advanced technologies, ensuring compliance with DHS policies on AI use. 

Focuses on transitioning technologies to CBP programs, addressing potential negative outcomes and capability gaps. 

Instructs annual reporting on Innovation Teams’ activities, technologies piloted, and their success rates. 

Requires coordination with DHS's AI policies to ensure responsible AI use. 

Demands cost-benefit analysis before large-scale technology deployment, ensuring security effectiveness and governmental cost-efficiency. 

Emphasizes collaboration with the private sector, other government entities, and stakeholders for optimizing advanced technology deployment.

Official name: Maryland State Executive Order 01.01.2024.02
Casual name: Maryland State Executive Order 01.01.2024.02 (Use of AI in Maryland State Government)
Short summary: Establishes an AI Subcabinet to ensure responsible AI use by Maryland state agencies, promoting principles of fairness, transparency, and innovation, while safeguarding privacy and security. Requires development of an AI Action Plan and training programs for state employees.
Long summary:
Establishes an AI Subcabinet to oversee AI use in Maryland state government, fostering principles such as fairness, innovation, privacy, safety, and transparency.

Directs the AI Subcabinet to create an AI Action Plan incorporating NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework to ensure adherence to AI principles.

Instructs the Subcabinet to upskill the state workforce in AI and explore partnerships with external AI talent for targeted projects.

Mandates the study of AI's impact on critical domains, including workforce and economic development, and the provision of recommendations to the Governor and legislature.

Requires the Department of Information Technology to assess infrastructure for safely testing AI prototypes and collaborate with the Department of General Services to create procedures for AI pilots.

Ensures AI initiatives align with state and federal laws and does not impair existing authorities, remaining severable if parts are invalidated.

Official name: Leadership in CET Act
Casual name: Leadership in CET Act
Short summary: Establishes a pilot program to expedite patent examination for AI and other emerging technologies, encouraging U.S. innovation and leadership. Permits fee waivers and limits application numbers. Terminates after issuing certain patents or accepting 10,000 applications, with possible renewal.
Long summary:
Establishes a pilot program for expediting patent applications related to critical and emerging technologies, including AI, microelectronics, and quantum information science.

Requires the Director of the United States Patent and Trademark Office to expedite patent processing through petitions.

Permits waiver of certain fees and requirements for accelerated examination processes.

Limits eligibility to U.S.-based entities or inventors and restricts applications to original, nonprovisional patents.

Terminates the program after issuing a patent within five years or upon accepting 10,000 applications, with a potential renewal for the same criteria.

Mandates public availability of information regarding application numbers, acceptance, and issued patents on the Office's website.

Requires a report to Congress assessing the pilot program's effectiveness post-termination, exempting this data collection from the Paperwork Reduction Act.

Official name: Further Continuing Appropriations and Disaster Relief Supplemental Appropriations Act 2025 (Title V "Promoting Resilient Supply Chains")
Casual name: Further Continuing Appropriations and Disaster Relief Supplemental Appropriations Act ("Promoting Resilient Supply Chains")
Short summary: Establishes responsibilities for the Assistant Secretary of Commerce to promote stable supply chains and emerging technologies, including AI. Requires the formation of a Working Group to assess supply chain resilience and vulnerabilities. Encourages domestic manufacturing of critical technologies.
Long summary:
Expands the responsibilities of the Assistant Secretary of Commerce to include promoting the resilience of supply chains related to critical and emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence.

Mandates the creation of the Supply Chain Resilience Working Group composed of relevant federal agencies to assess and model supply chain stability, including those involving AI technologies.

Requires the group to identify vulnerabilities and prepare for potential supply chain shocks that might impact AI and other critical technologies.

Encourages domestic production and manufacturing, specifically focusing on AI and technological advancements.

Obligates periodic reports and assessments to Congress regarding the resilience and capacity of AI-related supply chains and industry preparedness for shocks.

Prohibits reliance on critical goods from countries identified as risks to national security, advocating for sourcing from allies.

Sets a 10-year expiration for these provisions.

Protects confidential data shared voluntarily under this title from disclosure, ensuring privacy concerns in relation to AI-related supply chain information.

Official name: Michigan House Bill 5141
Casual name: Michigan HB 5141 (Campaign Practices)
Short summary: Requires political advertisements generated by AI to include disclaimers indicating AI use. Mandates specific formatting for AI disclosures, establishes fines for non-compliance, and outlines exemptions for certain media and platforms.
Long summary:
Requires political advertisements generated substantially or wholly by AI to include a clear and conspicuous statement indicating AI involvement in accordance with specific formatting requirements.

Mandates that AI-generated political advertisements in the form of prerecorded telephone messages include the disclaimer, "This message was generated in whole or substantially by artificial intelligence."

Requires graphical ads to display the disclosure in text as large as the majority of other text in the ad, audio ads to audibly disclose AI use at the beginning or end, and video ads to display the statement for at least four seconds and include an audible disclosure.

Designates violation of the telephone message provision as a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine or imprisonment; imposes fines for other violations, with a fine of up to $250 for the first offense and up to $1000 for subsequent offenses. 

Exempts broadcasting stations, distribution platforms with clear policies on AI content disclosure, and satirical political advertisements from these requirements.

Official name: Digital Charter Implementation Act 2022, Part 3 ("Artificial Intelligence and Data Act")
Casual name: Digital Charter Implementation Act 2022, Part 3 ("Artificial Intelligence and Data Act")
Short summary: Regulates AI systems by establishing risks mitigation, record-keeping, and disclosure requirements to prevent harm and discrimination. Mandates ministerial oversight and imposes penalties for non-compliance.
Long summary:
Mandates persons responsible for AI systems to assess whether a system is high-impact and, if so, to establish measures to mitigate risks of harm or biased output and monitor compliance with such measures.

Requires record-keeping for measures related to regulated activities.

Requires that descriptions of high-impact systems and associated mitigation measures be published on publicly available websites.

Empowers the Governor in Council to appoint a Minister to oversee this act.

Requires notification to the Minister if a high-impact system causes or is likely to cause material harm.

Empowers the Minister to order audits in cases of suspected non-compliance, order the cessation of high-impact AI system use if there is serious risk of imminent harm, and publish information about systems that pose a serious risk of imminent harm.

Prohibits possession or use of unlawfully obtained personal information for AI purposes.

Prohibits knowingly making available AI systems that are likely to cause serious physical or psychological harm or economic loss. 

Outlines penalties, including fines or imprisonment, for non-compliance.

Casual name: Intelligence Authorization Act FY 2025, Title V, Section 510 ("Management of artificial intelligence security risks")
Short summary: Requires the National Institute of Standards and Technology to update vulnerability management processes for AI security risks, establish a database to track AI security and safety incidents, and evaluate standards for AI vulnerability reporting. Requires the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to convene stakeholders to encourage best practices for addressing AI supply chain risks.
Long summary:
Requires the Director of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to update vulnerability management processes to ensure they address AI security vulnerabilities.

Directs the Director of NIST to establish a database to publicly track AI security and safety incidents based on voluntary reporting, ensuring confidentiality.

Instructs the Director of NIST to evaluate reported AI incidents for potential inclusion in the database, prioritizing high-impact cases, systems used in critical infrastructure, and systems widely deployed in the commercial or public sector.

Requires the Director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to update the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures Program to ensure it addresses AI security vulnerabilities.

Directs the Director of NIST to initiate a multi-stakeholder evaluation of whether existing consensus standards accommodate AI vulnerability reporting, with a report due to Congress within 180 days.

Instructs the Director of CISA to convene stakeholders to encourage the development of best practices for managing AI supply chain risks, focusing on data collection, documentation, human feedback systems, and the use of open-source and proprietary datasets.

Official name: A bill to require the Secretary of Defense to carry out a pilot program on using artificial intelligence-enabled software to optimize the workflow and operations of depots, shipyards, and other manufacturing facilities run by the Department of Defense, and for other purposes.
Casual name: A bill to require the Secretary of Defense to carry out a pilot program on using artificial intelligence-enabled software to optimize the workflow and operations of depots, shipyards, and other manufacturing facilities run by the Department of Defense, and for other purposes.
Short summary: Requires the Secretary of Defense to initiate a pilot program using AI-enabled software for optimizing Department of Defense facility operations. Mandates a $35 million minimum expenditure and consultation with military branches. Obligates a detailed evaluation report within one year.
Long summary:
Mandates the Secretary of Defense to initiate a pilot program within 60 days to enable a artificial intelligence-software for optimizing workflow and operations in Department of Defense facilities, including depots and shipyards.

Requires assessment of AI-enabled software for contract administration, including adjudication and review of contracts managed by the Defense Contract Management Agency.

Directs the use of best-in-class software platforms, consideration of industry best practices, implementation based on human-centered design, and integration with enterprise platforms and relevant data sources.

Obligates a minimum expenditure of $35,000,000 for the pilot program.

Requires the Secretary to carry out the program in consultation with the Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition and Sustainment and the Secretaries of the Army, Navy, and Air Force.

Mandates a report to Congress within one year on the pilot program’s findings.

Official name: Indiana House Bill 1047
Casual name: Indiana HB 1047 (Sexual Offenses)
Short summary: Defines "computer generated image" as those created or modified using AI or software. Criminalizes distributing non-consensual intimate images, including AI-generated ones, with enhanced penalties for repeat offenders. Establishes new offenses for voyeurism involving AI or digital tools.
Long summary:
Amends Indiana law to define "computer generated image" as images created or modified through artificial intelligence or software.

Prohibits distribution of intimate images without consent, including AI-generated images, categorizing such distribution as a Class A misdemeanor or Level 6 felony for repeat offenders.

Criminalizes voyeurism involving AI or cameras, with enhanced penalties for repeat offenses or distribution of recorded images.

Establishes that using unmanned aerial vehicles to capture private images without consent constitutes remote aerial voyeurism, punishable as a Class A misdemeanor or Level 6 felony for repeat offenses or distribution.

Exempts certain distributions of images for criminal investigations or under court orders.

Requires commencement of actions for child sexual abuse before certain deadlines or conditions, with exceptions for specific bankruptcy proceedings.

Declares an emergency for the enactment of these provisions.

Official name: S.4870, A bill to require reports on artificial intelligence regulation in the financial services industry.
Casual name: S.4870, A bill to require reports on artificial intelligence regulation in the financial services industry.
Short summary: Require federal financial agencies to report to Congress on AI knowledge gaps, usage, governance standards, regulatory needs, interagency issues, and resource requirements within 90 days. Exclude confidential supervisory and nonpublic information from reports.
Long summary:
Require the Federal Reserve, FDIC, OCC, NCUA, CFPB, the Housing, and Urban Affairs of the Senate, and the Committee on Financial Services of the House of Representatives to report on AI knowledge gaps in financial services within 90 days.

Mandate which tasks are being assisted or completed with AI in the Institutions that agencies regulate.

Assess current AI governance and oversight standards for AI oversight by the agency.

Identify additional regulatory authorities required by the agency to execute the mission agency.

Clarify overlapping AI regulatory issues between agencies.

Evaluate current and planned agency use of AI over the next three years, including fiscal and staffing impacts.

Determine necessary resources and monetary to require the agency to adapt to AI changes and oversee its use in the regulatory landscape to oversee how AI is adopted across operations. 

Ensure reports exclude confidential or nonpublic information.

Official name: Workforce for AI Trust Act
Casual name: Workforce for AI Trust Act
Short summary: Amends the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act to support NSF fellowships for interdisciplinary AI research, emphasizing ethics and responsible practices. Enhances NIST's role in AI governance workforce development and risk management, focusing on education, technical standards, and professional certifications.
Long summary:
Amends the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020 to authorize the National Science Foundation (NSF) to support interdisciplinary AI fellowships, encouraging ethical AI practices.

Mandates the NSF to conduct outreach to diverse institutions and groups underrepresented in STEM fields for fellowship applicants.

Directs the NSF to promote AI-based training and workshops across STEM fields to accelerate scientific discovery and technology development.

Requires the integration of diverse disciplinary perspectives in AI research peer review panels.

Instructs the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to support education and workforce development to expand the AI governance workforce, focusing on managing AI-related risks.

Mandates NIST to develop technical standards and guidance for AI risk management careers, including mapping, measuring, and validating AI systems.

Prioritizes research on gene editing, digital agriculture, and AI applications. Requires reporting on funded research and innovation progress to Congress biennially.
Long summary:
Establishes the National Synthetic Biology Center to award grants for advancing synthetic biology in agriculture.

Requires the Center to prioritize research in areas like cellular biology, gene editing, and digital agriculture.

Mandates the use of artificial intelligence to accelerate modeling and measurement for synthetic biological solutions.

Provides grants to eligible institutions, fostering partnerships with entities such as nonprofits and national laboratories.

Sets criteria for grant applications, emphasizing the promotion of synthetic biology technologies and sustainability in agriculture.

Directs the Center to coordinate with technology transfer offices to commercialize innovations.

Requires the Center to maintain a website for disseminating findings and facilitating collaboration.

Obligates the Center to submit biennial reports to Congress on research findings and grant progress.

Authorizes appropriations for the Center's operation and grant awards from 2025 to 2029.

Casual name: South Carolina 2023 H 4754 (Sec 4)
Short summary: Holds licensees accountable for work produced using AI or machine learning, treating violations by these programs as direct violations by the licensee.
Long summary:
Amends Article 7, Chapter 57, Title 40 of the S.C. Code by adding Section 40-57-820.

Holds a licensee accountable for all work produced with the assistance of artificial intelligence, machine learning, or similar programs.

Treats violations committed through the use of these technologies as if committed directly by the licensee.

Specifies that the Task Force will cease to exist on January 15, 2020.

Requires the Task Force to submit an update by February 15, 2019, to the Senate Committee on Government Operations and the House Committee on Energy and Technology.

Official name: Healthy Technology Act of 2025
Casual name: Healthy Technology Act of 2025
Short summary: Amends the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to include AI and machine learning technologies as eligible drug prescribers if they are state-authorized and FDA-approved, cleared, or authorized by the FDA and other purposes.
Long summary:
Revises the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to include artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies can qualify as a practitioner eligible to prescribe drugs if authorized by the state involved and approved, cleared, or authorized by the Food and Drug Administration, and for other purposes.

Requires section 503(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 U.S.C. 353(b)) to be amended by adding the following at the end.

Requires that any artificial intelligence or machine learning technology included as a “practitioner licensed by law to administer such drug” be authorized pursuant to a statute of the State involved to prescribe the drug involved.

Mandates that the artificial intelligence or machine learning technology be approved, cleared, or authorized by the Food and Drug Administration under section 510(k), 513, 515, or 564.

Official name: Public Act 103-0804
Casual name: Illinois Public Act 103-0804
Short summary: Prohibits employers from using AI in employment practices that result in discrimination based on protected classes. Requires employers to notify employees when AI is used for employment decisions.
Long summary:
Amends the Illinois Human Rights Act to regulate the use of AI in employment-related decisions.

Prohibits employers from using AI in recruitment, hiring, promotion, or other employment management practices if it results in discrimination based on protected classes.

Requires employers to notify employees if AI is used in employment decisions.

Directs the Illinois Department of Human Rights to adopt rules for implementing and enforcing these AI-related provisions, including specifying timelines and means for providing notice.

Takes effect on January 1, 2026.

Casual name: New York S 8828 (RAISE Act, Article 44-B)
Short summary: Enacts the Responsible AI Safety and Education (RAISE) Act, requiring large frontier developers to publish and comply with a frontier AI framework governing catastrophic risk management, publish transparency reports before deploying new frontier models, report critical safety incidents within 72 hours, and file biennial disclosure statements with the Office of the Department of Financial Services.
Long summary:
Requires large frontier developers in New York to publish and maintain a detailed Frontier AI Framework, outlining practices for managing catastrophic risks and ensuring transparency.

Compels developers to report critical safety incidents and updates concerning catastrophic risks regularly to the Office within New York's Department of Financial Services.

Stipulates that a violation of reporting or framework maintenance may result in significant civil penalties, with enforcement overseen by the Attorney General.

Mandates disclosure statements for large frontier developers operating in New York, detailing company ownership and contact information, with renewals every two years.

Establishes the Office of Financial Services' authority to implement further regulations enhancing AI safety and transparency, including the possibility of sharing incident reports with other governmental entities.

Excludes academic institutions and specific consortia from these requirements when engaged solely in research.

Official name: S 1798 Autonomous Vehicle Acceleration Act of 2025 (Standards for autonomous vehicles and other purposes)
Casual name: S 1798 Autonomous Vehicle Acceleration Act of 2025
Short summary: Requires the Secretary of Transportation to update regulations within one year to accommodate autonomous vehicle designs, addressing certification challenges. Develops a roadmap for commercial deployment of Level 4 and Level 5 autonomous vehicles, promoting U.S. leadership and identifying regulatory barriers.
Long summary:
Prescribes the Secretary of Transportation to update Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards to accommodate Level 4 and Level 5 autonomous vehicles, ensuring that traditional human-driver assumptions do not obstruct certification.

Requires addressing certification challenges identified by the Volpe 2016 Report within one year after the Act's enactment.

Instructs the Secretary to develop a roadmap within one year to achieve commercial-scale deployment of Level 4 and Level 5 autonomous vehicles in the U.S., promoting U.S. leadership and identifying barriers to deployment.

Recommends a risk hierarchy and standard of safety for autonomous vehicles.

Mandates a supplemental technology assessment to address new technologies, safety concerns, and updates to the Volpe 2016 Report.

Requires periodic updates to the roadmap and submission of reports to Congress.

Official name: Opinions on Strengthening the Governance of Science and Technology Ethics
Casual name: Opinions on Strengthening the Governance of Science and Technology Ethics
Short summary: Requires work units engaged in S&T activities in AI and other areas to establish S&T ethics review committees and commits the government to formulating S&T ethics norms and guidelines for areas such as AI.
Long summary:
Explains that the National Science and Technology Ethics Commission is responsible for guiding and coordinating the S&T ethics governance system, with the Ministry of Science and Technology overseeing daily operations.

Instructs work units engaged in S&T activities in AI and other areas to form S&T ethics review committees to address ethical risks independently.

Commits the government to formulating S&T ethics norms and guidelines for AI and other areas. 

Calls for strengthening legislative research on S&T ethics in AI and other areas during the 14th Five-Year Plan.

Short summary: Establishes an Artificial Intelligence Task Force to study AI technologies, assess societal impacts, and recommend government actions for ethical use. Involves Executive Branch officials, allows public and expert consultation, and requires a report to the Governor within 12 months.
Long summary:
Establishes the Artificial Intelligence Task Force responsible for studying AI technologies' societal impacts and recommending government actions for ethical use.

Includes the Chief Technology Officer, Chief Innovation Officer, Chief Executive Officer of the Economic Development Authority, and other key officials as members.

Authorizes the Task Force to gather data from state departments and agencies.

Requires executive branch cooperation and assistance to fulfill the Task Force's objectives.

Directs the Task Force to consult with academics, industry professionals, and consumer advocates.

Issues a reporting requirement to the Governor within 12 months of the Order’s enactment, to be shared with the Legislature and public.

Permits additional appointments by the Governor as necessary.

Clarifies the Task Force’s advisory nature in providing advice to the Governor and executive branches.
