Official name: City of San Jose Generative AI Guidelines
Casual name: San Jose Generative AI Guidelines
Short summary: Regulates the use of Generative AI in the City of San José, requiring users to avoid entering confidential information, ensure accuracy, cite AI usage, and create separate City-use accounts. Instructs departments to offer additional rules and engage in AI working groups.
Long summary:
Establishes guidelines for using Generative AI within the City of San José, emphasizing privacy, accuracy, transparency, equity, accountability, and beneficial use.

Requires users to cite AI where substantial content is AI-generated and to verify AI output against trustworthy sources.

Prohibits submission of personal or confidential information into Generative AI platforms and mandates the creation of separate accounts for City-related work using Generative AI.

Subjects AI usage to public records laws, recommending users to opt out of data collection where possible and verify AI-generated content for copyright compliance.

Offers collaborative working groups to enhance AI governance and provides risk assessment criteria for Generative AI use cases.

Encourages active participation in AI workgroups and emphasizes the importance of adapting guidelines as technology and laws evolve.

Official name: Next Generation Military Education Act
Casual name: Next Generation Military Education Act
Short summary: Requires the Department of Defense to develop AI and machine learning courses for military personnel, expand the Digital On-Demand Program to all members and employees, and incorporate AI risks into annual cybersecurity training.
Long summary:
Amends the National Defense Authorization Act to require the Department of Defense to develop and provide distance education courses on artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning for Armed Forces personnel.

Mandates these courses to cover AI literacy, ethical use, data protection, and awareness of AI-generated content.

Requires military departments to ensure access and notify personnel about these courses.

Obligates the Secretary of Defense to report to Congress on the progress of these activities.

Expands participation in the Digital On-Demand Program to all Department of Defense entities and personnel, promoting AI education.

Incorporates AI risks and threats into annual cybersecurity training for Armed Forces and civilian Department of Defense employees.

Requires annual reporting to Congress on the expansion and promotion of the Digital On-Demand Program. 

Defines key terms, including "artificial intelligence" and "Digital On-Demand Program."

Official name: Los Angeles AI Roadmap 2024, Best Practices and Roadmap
Casual name: Los Angeles AI Roadmap 2024, Best Practices and Roadmap
Short summary: Emphasizes AI training for employees and IT developers. Requires departments to set clear objectives before AI deployment and conduct proofs of concept. Advises AI tools remain secure, ethical, and data privacy is protected. Encourages transparency and human-centric AI use.
Long summary:
Establishes two distinct user segments for AI tools: City Employees and IT Professionals, requiring tailored training for each group.

Instructs non-technical department leadership to set clear goals before AI tool deployment.

Encourages piloting AI tools to understand their strengths and weaknesses before widespread use.

Anticipates most AI tools will be accessed through existing software platforms.

Emphasizes the need for adaptable AI tools that align with evolving data and requirements.

Advises staying current on AI tools and frameworks for maximized effectiveness.

Requires comprehensive AI training for both users and developers, highlighting security and ethical considerations.

Insists on cybersecurity and data privacy for AI implementation.

Highlights AI as a long-term investment needing high-quality data and data transparency.

Asserts City data ownership and the need for ethical, transparent, and human-centered AI tools.

Outlines a roadmap for training, deploying AI tools, and developing ethics guidelines for the City.

Implements the Global AI Governance Initiative and promotes consensus and coordinated efforts. 

Supports the formulation and refinement of governance, and tracks trends in AI research, development, and application; with a focus on agile governance.

Short summary: Establishes an AI in Education Task Force to evaluate AI applications in K-12, assess ethical and data privacy implications, and develop policy recommendations. Appoints twelve members and requires reports by December 15, 2024. Dissolves the task force on January 1, 2025.
Long summary:
Establishes an Artificial Intelligence in Education Task Force in Mississippi to evaluate and recommend AI applications in K-12 education.

Requires the State Superintendent of Education to chair the task force, with administrative support provided by the Department of Education.

Comprises twelve members appointed by the Governor, Lieutenant Governor, and Speaker of the House, possessing expertise in education, technology, and data privacy.

Instructs the task force to assess AI's ethical, legal, and data privacy implications, develop policy recommendations, and propose guidelines for AI integration in education.

Tasks the force with identifying workforce needs and strategies for data protection, and fostering collaboration between educational sectors and industries.

Requires submission of interim and final reports detailing findings and recommendations to state officials and public posting of the final report.

Requires CISA to partner with community colleges and technical schools to offer programs and internships aiming to build a skills-based cyber workforce.

Provides full scholarships to eligible students, covering all educational and associated costs.

Specifies eligible institutions and program components, including skills-based exercises and internships.

Directs CISA to conduct outreach initiatives and host recruitment fairs.

Short summary: Requires the Secretary of Commerce to submit a strategic plan for fisheries data modernization, including a description of how the initiative will align with NOAA's AI Strategy.
Long summary:
Directs the Secretary of Commerce, through the Assistant Administrator for Fisheries, to provide a national strategic plan for fisheries data modernization to Congress within 180 days.

Requires the strategic plan to detail how the initiative aligns with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's (NOAA) Artificial Intelligence Strategy.

Directs the Secretary to solicit information from data management and technology experts in developing the strategic plan.

Requires the Secretary to report annually to Congress on progress in implementing the fisheries data modernization efforts.

Official name: Health Equity and Accountability Act of 2024, Sec 1013 ("Task Force on Preventing Bias in AI and Algorithms")
Casual name: Health Equity and Accountability Act of 2024, Sec 1013 ("Task Force on Preventing Bias in AI and Algorithms")
Short summary: Directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to establish a Task Force to provide guidance on preventing AI bias in healthcare. Requires the Task Force to identify risks and submit a report with recommendations for AI implementation and risk mitigation in healthcare.
Long summary:
Directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) to establish a Task Force on Preventing AI and Algorithmic Bias in Health Care to provide guidance on ensuring AI technologies improve health care delivery and do not exacerbate health disparities. 

Mandates that the Task Force be composed of various health and public officials, including experts on health equity and minority health.

Directs the Task Force to examine AI and algorithms in healthcare, identifying risks related to civil rights, civil liberties, and discriminatory bias.

Requires the Task Force to submit a report to Congress within one year detailing findings and recommendations for AI implementation and risk management in healthcare.

Obliges the Task Force to publish the report on the HHS website.

Requires the Task Force to initiate a public comment period of at least 90 days on the Task Force’s duties and activities.

Allows the Chairperson to appoint additional staff without adherence to certain civil service laws and allows federal employees to be detailed to the Task Force.

Official name: Microsoft Responsible AI Standard, v2
Casual name: Microsoft Responsible AI Standard, v2
Short summary: Establishes Microsoft's Responsible AI Standard, requiring AI systems to undergo ongoing evaluations and impact assessments, oversight for adverse impacts, and fit-for-purpose validation, mandating clear documentation on capabilities and limitations, human oversight, and compliance with privacy, security, and accessibility standards.
Long summary:
Mandates Microsoft to conduct Impact Assessments for AI systems early in development to evaluate societal impacts, ensuring AI systems are fit for purpose, with annual updates and reviews for significant adverse impacts.

Demands human oversight by identifying responsible stakeholders, providing necessary tools, and ensuring appropriate documentation for system control and intervention.

Requires intelligibility for decision-making, enabling stakeholders to interpret system outputs and minimize automation bias.

Mandates transparency and communication about system capabilities, limitations, and any AI-generated content.

Ensures fairness by focusing on quality of service and opportunities and minimizing disparities for demographic groups in AI system outputs. 

Emphasizes reliability and safety, requiring evaluation for safe performance within operational ranges, and ongoing monitoring and feedback. 

Insists on compliance with Microsoft’s Privacy, Security, and Accessibility Standards to ensure AI systems are inclusive, secure, and respect privacy.

Casual name: Fraudulent Misrepresentation of Campaign Authority
Collections: U.S. regulations, executive orders, and agency policies

Long summary:
Clarifies that 52 U.S.C. 30124 and 11 CFR 110.16, provisions in the Federal Election Campaign Act prohibiting fraudulent misrepresentation of campaign authority, apply to fraudulent misrepresentation conducted using AI.

Official name: The position paper submitted by the Chinese delegation to CCW 5th Review Conference
Casual name: The position paper submitted by the Chinese delegation to CCW 5th Review Conference
Short summary: Urges international consensus on defining lethal autonomous weapons systems (LAWS) and developing binding LAWS regulation under international law. Warns of LAWS' risks, including harm to civilians, and supports continued discussions within the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW).
Long summary:
Urges extensive discussion on defining and scoping Lethal Autonomous Weapon Systems (LAWS), focusing on autonomy levels, human involvement, and distinctions between civilian and military uses.

Advocates for LAWS to be governed by international humanitarian laws, highlighting uncertainties in distinction, proportionality, and accountability with current systems.

Supports developing a legally binding protocol on LAWS, akin to the Protocol on Blinding Laser Weapons, in order to address legal gaps.

Warns that LAWS increase war's ease and frequency by lowering thresholds and costs, posing risks of indiscriminate harm to civilians.

Calls for caution in using LAWS, particularly to prevent indiscriminate civilian targeting.

Welcomes progress in LAWS discussions within the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) framework and supports continued expert meetings.

Official name: Florida CS/SB 482 (Artificial Intelligence Bill of Rights 2025)
Casual name: Florida CS/SB 482 (Artificial Intelligence Bill of Rights 2025)
Short summary: Restricts contracts with foreign entities for AI technology, mandates rights for Florida residents regarding AI use, including transparency and data protection, and regulates companion chatbots’ interaction with minors. Establishes penalties for violations. Creates "Artificial Intelligence Bill of Rights."
Long summary:
Creates restrictions effective July 2026, prohibiting Florida governmental entities from contracting with entities closely tied to foreign countries of concern for AI technologies unless certain affidavits are provided.

Establishes the "Artificial Intelligence Bill of Rights," granting Florida residents rights regarding AI use, including supervising minor children’s AI use, transparency about AI communications, and rights over personal data and AI-generated likenesses.

Requires companion chatbot platforms to implement parental controls and protections for minors, including disclosure that interactions are AI-generated and instituting penalties for non-compliance by the Florida Department of Legal Affairs.

Mandates clear notifications in interactions between users and AI bots to identify non-human counterparts, with violations actionable by the state.

Regulates AI companies regarding the use of deidentified data, imposing penalties for non-compliance.

Introduces amendments to sections on unauthorized use of AI-generated likenesses, reinforcing the need for consent.

Begins effect on July 1, 2026.

Official name: Position Paper of the People’s Republic of China on Regulating Military Applications of Artificial Intelligence
Casual name: Position Paper of the People’s Republic of China on Regulating Military Applications of Artificial Intelligence
Short summary: Calls for countries to regulate military applications of AI, ensuring prudent development, human control, and compliance with international humanitarian law and ethical norms. Advocates multilateral cooperation and tiered risk management to prevent arms races, proliferation, and misuse, while maintaining global strategic stability.
Long summary:
Calls for countries, especially major powers, to develop and apply military AI prudently, preventing strategic miscalculation and preserving global stability and mutual trust.

Urges countries to refrain from using military AI to start wars, pursue hegemony, or undermine other countries' sovereignty and territorial security.

Calls for military AI weapon systems to comply with international humanitarian law, uphold ethical norms, and minimize collateral casualties and misuse.

Encourages human control and suspension capability over AI weapon systems, alongside secured and restricted use of AI data.

Calls for self-restraint in AI research and development, with human-machine interaction throughout weapons' life cycles and humans as the final responsible party.

Encourages tiered, categorized regulation of military AI and risk research to prevent premature deployment and mitigate proliferation risks.

Advocates for multilateral, inclusive dialogue among diverse stakeholders to establish a universal international governance regime for military AI.

Urges developed countries to assist developing countries' governance capacity while opposing ideological barriers to peaceful technological progress.

Official name: Small Business Artificial Intelligence Training Act of 2024
Casual name: Small Business Artificial Intelligence Training Act of 2024
Short summary: Requires the Secretary of Commerce to develop AI training resources for small businesses, including those in rural and underserved areas. Mandates annual review and updates of resources. Allows grants for AI training. Terminates the program after three years.
Long summary:
Mandates the Secretary of Commerce, in coordination with various agencies, to develop AI training resources for small businesses, including those in rural, Tribal, or underserved areas.

Requires these resources to cover topics such as prompt engineering, financial management, cybersecurity, and government contracting.

Obligates the review and update of these resources every year to ensure relevance and effectiveness.

Coordinates with the Small Business Administration for the distribution of these resources through its network, including development centers and business opportunity centers.

Allows for a grants program to fund training providers using the developed resources.

Demands initial and annual reports to Congress on the progress and impact of the training resources.

Establishes a sunset clause terminating the program three years after the Act's enactment.

Casual name: Agriculture and National Security Act of 2024

Long summary:
Requires the Secretary of Agriculture to submit biennial reports to Congress and the National Security Council assessing gaps in national security efforts related to food and agriculture, including those related to AI.

Official name: California SJR 6
Casual name: California SJR 6 ("Artificial Intelligence")
Short summary: Urges President and Congress to develop an AI Advisory Committee with the push of the Senate and the Assembly of the State of California. Highlights need for AI policy, ethical standards, workforce planning, and innovation. Calls for bridging tech-regulation gaps. Directs resolution to federal and state officials.
Long summary:
Urges the President and Congress to develop a comprehensive Artificial Intelligence Advisory Committee. 

Recognizes that 77% of consumers use artificial intelligence powered by many services and that one-half of the major 10 artificial intelligence startups have been brought to the United States. Notes that research further supports that robots and digital agents will displace blue-collar and white-collar workers. 

Requires the President and Congress to take a role in protecting the nation’s workforce and addressing the future changes that artificial intelligence will bring due to its potential to revolutionize the economy.

Urges officials to recognize that many countries such as Canada, China, United Kingdom and France are developing AI implementation.  

Requires Congress and the President to establish ethical principles when using artificial intelligence. Recognizes that there is a growing gap between regulatory response and the growth of technology. 

Requires the Senate and the Assembly of the State of California to work together in urging the President and Congress to develop an Artificial Intelligence Advisory Committee to develop artificial intelligence policy.

Official name: Department of Energy AI Act
Casual name: Department of Energy AI Act
Short summary: Establishes a centralized AI program within the Department of Energy to develop and deploy advanced AI capabilities across science and national security, including the development of AI models, datasets, and infrastructure. Mandates AI risk evaluation, workforce development, and partnerships, and allocates $2.4 billion annually for five years.
Long summary:
Establishes the Department of Energy AI Act to advance AI capabilities within the Department of Energy (DOE) by creating a centralized AI program focused on research and deployment of AI for science, security, and technology.

Requires the development of AI training datasets, next-generation computing infrastructure, and safe and trustworthy AI models, and directs the creation of eight multidisciplinary AI Research and Development Centers to strengthen U.S. leadership in AI.

Implements an AI Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Program to address safety and security concerns, and allocates funds for STEM education and workforce development, emphasizing AI skill training and diversity.

Establishes a program to use AI to improve federal permitting processes for energy projects.

Directs the Secretary of Energy to assess the impact of data center and advanced computing demand on U.S. energy systems and national security, and to provide recommendations on energy access, domestic deployment, and efficiency improvements.

Official name: California Senate Bill 1381 (2024)
Casual name: California SB 1381 (Crimes: child pornography) (2024)
Short summary: Expands legal prohibitions to include child pornography generated or altered by artificial intelligence. Subjects such AI-generated content to penalties. Allows forfeiture and destruction of such content without a criminal conviction. Becomes operative with AB 1831 enactment.
Long summary:
Expands existing child pornography laws to include materials digitally altered or generated by artificial intelligence.

Prohibits the production, distribution, or possession of AI-generated depictions involving minors engaging in sexual conduct.

Imposes penalties including fines and imprisonment for violations involving AI-generated content depicting minors, including recruiting minors to create such content.

Specifies exemptions for legally emancipated minors; law enforcement; legitimate medical, educational, or scientific activities; and lawful conduct between spouses.

Allows forfeiture of AI-generated depictions involving minors engaging in sexual conduct that is in the possession of city, county, or state officials or agencies.

Allows destruction of AI-generated materials regardless of criminal conviction.

Mandates that the act becomes operative only if AB 1831 is enacted by January 1, 2025.

Official name: AI PLAN Act
Casual name: AI PLAN Act
Short summary: Requires the Secretaries of the Treasury, Homeland Security, and Commerce to submit an annual report to Congress on the risks of use of AI in the commission of financial crimes.
Long summary:
Requires the Secretary of the Treasury, Secretary of Homeland Security, and Secretary of Commerce to submit a joint report to Congress on the risks of use of AI in financial crimes, including fraud and misinformation, within 180 days of enactment and annually thereafter.

Mandates the inclusion in the report of interagency policies, procedures, and resources needed to defend against AI-driven financial crimes.

Directs the report to include the consideration of risks such as deepfakes, voice cloning, foreign election interference, synthetic identities, false market signals, and overall digital fraud.

Requires the subsequent submission of legislative recommendations and best practices to address risks identified within 90 days of each report.

Official name: California Assembly Bill 2013 (2024)
Casual name: California AB 2013 (AI Training Data)
Short summary: Requires developers to disclose training data for generative AI systems publicly by January 1, 2026, and for each subsequent release. Exempts AI systems focused on security, aircraft operation, and national defense. Specifies detailed documentation requirements for datasets, including sources, content types, and modifications.
Long summary:
Defines key terms such as "artificial intelligence," "developer," "generative artificial intelligence," and "synthetic data generation" to clarify the scope and applicability of the regulations.

Mandates developers of generative AI systems, including parties that release a new system or make substantial modifications to a system, released on or after January 1, 2022 to publicly disclose training data documentation on their websites by January 1, 2026, and for each subsequent release.

Requires documentation to include a summary of datasets, sources, purposes, data points, intellectual property status, personal information, any data processing or modifications, and the use of synthetic data generation.

Exempts AI systems solely for security, aircraft operation in national airspace, or national security and defense provided they are only available to federal entities.

Official name: Michigan House Bill 5507
Casual name: Michigan H 5507 (School Aid)
Short summary: Allocates $500,000 for a statewide AI research hub, enhancing expertise on responsible AI use in schools. Supports virtual education, best practices, and policy recommendations. Fosters innovation in instructional technology and virtual learning models for Michigan's education system.
Long summary:
Allocates up to $500,000 to enhance awareness and responsible use of artificial intelligence in schools.

Requires Michigan Virtual University to integrate AI principles in its training programs for educational personnel.

Mandates the Michigan Virtual Learning Research Institute to research and recommend virtual education delivery models leveraging AI.

Instructs the institute to analyze and report on AI-enhanced virtual learning effectiveness by reviewing data from virtual course providers.

Encourages partnerships with districts to study AI-driven competency-based virtual learning models.

Tasks the institute with policy recommendations to the governor on AI and virtual learning implementation.

Designates funds for AI-related professional development programs for educators and stakeholders.

Requires ongoing reports on the implementation of AI in virtual education, including its effectiveness, with a focus on elevating education delivery models in Michigan.

Supports the dissemination of best practices and standards for AI-integrated virtual learning across the state.

Official name: FAA Research and Development Act of 2023, Sec. 215 ("Air Traffic Control Training")
Casual name: FAA R&D Act, Sec. 215 ("Air Traffic Control Training")
Short summary: Requires the assessment of AI, machine learning, and other technologies to improve air traffic control training. Develops a deployment timeline for these technologies. Involves collaboration with stakeholders. Obligates a report to Congress within one year.
Long summary:
Requires the FAA to carry out a research program to modernize and streamline air traffic control training, subject to available appropriations.

Mandates the assessment of advanced technologies, including AI, machine learning, and virtual/augmented reality, to enhance knowledge retention and training effectiveness.

Develops a timeline for deploying proven advanced technologies and processes for accreditation in training programs and facilities.

Includes collaboration with labor organizations and other stakeholders in the research process.

Obligates the Administrator to submit a report to Congress on the research findings within one year of the Act's enactment.

Short summary: Requires the Administrator to review AI and machine learning technologies for airport efficiency and safety. Long summary:
Requires the FAA to conduct a review of current and planned AI and machine learning technologies to enhance airport efficiency and safety.

Mandates the review to cover applications of AI and machine learning specifically in jet bridges, airport service vehicles, and aircraft taxiing.

Allows the Administrator to include other relevant areas that can improve airport efficiency and safety.

Obligates the Administrator to submit a report to Congress within one year, detailing the review's findings.

Includes a required examination of China's domestic application of AI and machine learning technologies in the report.

Official name: Rhode Island SB 2083 (2022)
Casual name: Rhode Island (2022) SB 2083 (Consumer Protection in Eye Care)
Short summary: Regulates AI-based eye assessment mechanisms, requiring patient-provider interaction and verification of recent in-person exams. Forbids AI-generated prescription use alone and imposes penalties for violations. Directs the Department of Health to establish implementing rules and regulations.
Long summary:
Define "assessment mechanism" to include AI and technology used for remote or in-person eye assessments.

Require such mechanisms to offer patient-provider interaction, gather patient history, and acknowledge limitations, including not replacing in-person exams or issuing initial contact lens prescriptions.

Instruct providers using assessment mechanisms to adhere to traditional care standards, verify patient identity and age, ensure recent in-person exams, and maintain patient records.

Establish that using eye assessment data alone for prescriptions is prohibited, and providers must certify prescriptions with their signature and license.

Impose civil penalties up to $10,000 for violations, with rights to hearings and appeals.

Authorize the department of health to implement rules and regulations for enforcement.

Include severability to maintain chapter validity if parts are invalidated.

Official name: Artificial Intelligence Public Awareness and Education Campaign Act
Casual name: Artificial Intelligence Public Awareness and Education Campaign Act
Short summary: Requires the Secretary of Commerce to establish a public awareness and education campaign to enhance AI literacy, identify best practices, and inform the public about AI's prevalence. Tasks the Secretary with consulting stakeholders and updating materials annually, terminating in five years.
Long summary:
Requires the Secretary of Commerce, within 180 days of enactment, to establish a public awareness and education campaign with federal agencies to inform U.S. individuals about AI's prevalence and improve AI consumer literacy.

Directs the Secretary to determine key performance indicators for evaluating the campaign's effectiveness, covering metrics like audience reach and engagement.

Requires facilitating information access on individuals' rights regarding AI and promoting best practices for detecting AI-generated or altered media.

Mandates outreach, including targeted efforts to vulnerable groups like seniors, to highlight AI's prevalence, applications, and limitations.

Instructs consultation with stakeholders across sectors and relevant government officials and submission of annual reports to Congress on campaign activities and effectiveness.

Ensures annual updates to campaign materials, dissemination through various channels, and makes available in multiple languages.

Sets a five-year sunset from enactment for the campaign with no additional funding.

Collaborates with the Small Business Administration for small business-focused campaign elements.

Casual name: New Mexico SM 63 ("Structured Decision-making in Child Abuse")
Short summary: Requests the attorney general to create a task force to study how well the state’s AI-based child welfare decision-making tools are working, gather input from stakeholders, and report findings by August 1, 2024.
Long summary:

Short summary: Amends Iowa law to prohibit knowingly possessing AI-created depictions of identifiable minors in prohibited sexual acts. Treats images of different minors as separate offenses; repeated violations escalate to a class "C" felony.

Official name: Commission Decision Establishing the European AI Office
Casual name: Commission Decision Establishing the European AI Office
Short summary: Establishes the European Artificial Intelligence Office within the Directorate-General for Communication Networks, Content and Technology to implement and enforce the forthcoming AI Regulation. Tasks the Office with evaluating general-purpose AI models, monitoring emerging risks, supporting EU governance and international cooperation on AI, and coordinating with stakeholders, national authorities, and Union bodies.
Long summary:
Establishes the European Artificial Intelligence Office within the Directorate-General for Communication Networks, Content and Technology to oversee AI advancements and enforce the forthcoming AI Regulation.

Tasks the Office with implementing and enforcing the Regulation, including developing tools, methodologies, and benchmarks to evaluate general-purpose AI models and monitor unforeseen risks.

Directs the Office to support prohibited-practice and high-risk AI rules by facilitating information exchange between national authorities, collecting notifications, and establishing information platforms and databases.

Assigns the Office responsibility for assisting the Commission in preparing decisions, implementing and delegated acts, guidance, and common specifications to ensure uniform application of the Regulation.

Tasks the Office with supporting regulatory sandboxes, conducting evaluations, and coordinating an effective governance system, including EU-level advisory bodies and monitoring national authority set-up.

Designates the Office as Secretariat for the AI Board and its subgroups, and as administrative support for the advisory forum and scientific panel.

Requires collaboration with stakeholders—including scientific experts, AI developers, civil society, and social partners—to advance best practices, and establishes a forum for cooperation with the open-source community.

Mandates cross-sectoral cooperation within the Commission, notably with the European Centre for Algorithmic Transparency on evaluating general-purpose AI models, and coordination with other Union bodies and agencies.

Supports international cooperation and promotion of the EU's trustworthy AI approach, including implementation of international agreements on AI.

Finances the Office through redeployment of Directorate-General staff and Digital Europe Programme resources, covering staffing and operational costs.

Enters into force on 21 February 2024, ahead of the Regulation's adoption, with provision for future revision.

Official name: Idaho House Bill 664 (Freedom From AI-Rigged Elections Act)
Casual name: Idaho HB 664 (Freedom From AI-Rigged Elections Act)
Short summary: Prohibits publishing synthetic media in electioneering communications without disclosure. Allows candidates to seek legal relief and damages. Establishes civil liability for content providers and certain media if synthetic content is produced and lacks appropriate disclosure. Requires clear evidence and encourages expedited court proceedings in cases determining liability for the use of synthetically created media in elections. Provides exceptions and severability measures.
Long summary:
Enacts the "Freedom From AI-Rigged (FAIR) Elections Act" to regulate synthetic media in electioneering communications.

Defines "synthetic media" as altered audio or video intended to mislead about real events or speech through advanced digital techniques.

Allows candidates misrepresented by synthetic media to seek injunctive relief and damages against the creators or distributors.

Requires disclosures on synthetic media: a visible text or audible notice stating the media is manipulated.

Places the burden on plaintiffs to prove synthetic media use by clear and convincing evidence.

Holds information content providers liable, not the medium, unless disclosures are altered or removed.

Encourages courts to resolve cases swiftly.

Declares provisions severable to maintain the act's enforceability if parts are invalidated.

Implements the act immediately upon passage due to an emergency declaration.

Official name: Arizona 2024 Senate Bill 1359
Casual name: Arizona SB 1359 (Deepfakes in Election Communications)
Short summary: Prohibits creating and distributing deceptive deepfakes of election candidates without clear AI-generated content disclosure within 90 days before elections. Exempts satire, parody, and interactive computer services. Imposes civil penalties for non-disclosure violations. Defines key terms including "creator" and "synthetic media."
Long summary:
Prohibits the creation and distribution of deceptive and fraudulent deepfakes of election candidates within ninety days before an election unless there is a clear disclosure that the content is generated by artificial intelligence.

Exempts satire, parody, and interactive computer services from this prohibition.

Imposes a civil penalty for each day a deceptive deepfake is distributed without the required disclosure.

Defines a "creator" as a person using AI or digital technology to generate synthetic media, excluding technology providers.

Clarifies "deceptive and fraudulent deepfake" as synthetic media intended to mislead people about a candidate's actions or statements.

Defines "synthetic media" as digitally manipulated images, audio, or video to create realistic but false impressions.

Empowers the President to require U.S. persons to obtain licenses for exporting or transferring critical AI systems and technologies.

Amends the International Emergency Economic Powers Act to align with the updated export control provisions.

Casual name: Department of State Authorization Act, Sec. 931 ("Priority for Australia and UK in Military Sales")
Short summary: Establishes expedited processing for AI technology transfers to Australia, the UK, and Canada under AUKUS. Requires anticipatory release policy for AI and related technologies in military sales. Mandates interagency review and update of related policies and guidance.
Long summary:
Requires the President to institute expedited policies for defense article and service requests from Australia and the United Kingdom under the AUKUS partnership.

Mandates prioritization of these requests over all others, except those from Taiwan and Ukraine.

Instructs the Secretary, in consultation with the Secretary of Defense, to establish an anticipatory release policy for technology transfers to Australia, the UK, and Canada.

Specifies the inclusion of technologies related to submarines, combat systems, hypersonic missiles, cyber capabilities, artificial intelligence, quantum technologies, and other advanced technologies.

Subjects technology transfer reviews to an expedited decision-making process.

Directs the Secretary and the Secretary of Defense to update interagency policies and guidance to incorporate these anticipatory release provisions.

Official name: TAKE IT DOWN Act
Casual name: TAKE IT DOWN Act (2025)
Short summary: Prohibits the use of AI to create or distribute nonconsensual digital forgeries, establishes criminal penalties and civil remedies, and criminalizes related threats. Requires platforms to establish procedures for removal requests of nonconsensual intimate images, and assigns enforcement authority to the Federal Trade Commission.
Long summary:
Prohibits the sharing of nonconsensual intimate visual depictions online, including those created by artificial intelligence (AI), known as digital forgeries. 

Criminalizes the creation and distribution of such depictions without consent, especially targeting AI-altered, identifiable images. 

Imposes penalties, including fines and imprisonment, for offenses involving adults and minors. 

Requires covered platforms to establish a clear removal process within one year of the Act’s enactment, to remove valid nonconsensual intimate images within 48 hours of the request.

Provides liability protections for platforms that remove content in good faith.

Empowers the Federal Trade Commission to enforce compliance, treating noncompliance as an unfair or deceptive act. 

Specifies legal exceptions, including disclosures for lawful or investigative purposes.

Official name: DEFIANCE Act of 2025
Casual name: DEFIANCE Act of 2025
Short summary: Amends U.S. law to allow individuals depicted in intimate digital forgeries to sue creators or distributors. Includes provisions for damages, punitive relief, and privacy protection for plaintiffs. Clarifies that federal, state, and tribal laws remain applicable.
Long summary:
Amends the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2022, to include provisions for civil action against the non-consensual use of intimate digital forgeries created using AI.

Defines "intimate digital forgery" as digitally manipulated depictions of identifiable individuals that are indistinguishable from authentic images.

Allows identifiable individuals depicted in unauthorized intimate digital forgeries to sue for damages in U.S. district courts.

Permits recovery of either liquidated damages up to $250,000 or actual damages, including defendant's profits, depending on the severity of the offiense.

Grants courts the authority to issue protective measures to ensure plaintiffs' privacy, including pseudonyms and sealed documents.

Establishes a statute of limitations for civil actions of 10 years from the individual's awareness of the violation or reaching adulthood.

Clarifies that the Act does not preempt or limit existing Federal, State, or Tribal law and allows for additional protective laws.

Official name: Technical Documentation of National Technical Committee 260 on Cybersecurity of Standardization Administration of China: Basic Safety Requirements for Generative Artificial Intelligence Services
Casual name: Basic Safety Requirements for Generative Artificial Intelligence Services (Technical Documentation)
Short summary: Specifies safety requirements that Chinese generative AI service providers must follow regarding training data, model-generated content, and safety assessments, with an emphasis on guarding against safety risks and illegal and unhealthy information.
Long summary:
Specifies safety requirements for generative AI service providers in China, focusing on corpus safety, model safety, and assessment requirements.

Requires sources of training corpora to be diverse and traceable; directs providers to filter out illegal and unhealthy information in training corpora and comply with intellectual property rights and personal information regulations.

Mandates training for annotators and compliance with functional annotation and safety annotation rules.

Requires providers to monitor the safety of AI-generated content and establish technical measures to improve accuracy and reliability.

Outlines required safety measures for critical AI uses, service transparency, user-entered information collection, supply chain security, and complaint handling.

Directs providers to deny service to users attempting to induce the generation of illegal and unhealthy information; requires safety assessments after model updates and urges regular security audits.

Calls for the creation of a keyword library, generated content test question bank, and bank of test questions that models should refuse to answer, covering safety risks enumerated in the appendix.

Establishes methods for safety assessments and specific benchmarks for corpus safety assessments, generated content safety assessments, and question refusal assessments.

Enumerates 31 safety risks of corpora and generated content, grouped into categories of content that violates socialist values, discriminatory content, commercial violations, violations of rights, and inability to meet safety requirements; defines "illegal and unhealthy information" to include these risks.

Official name: Executive Order on the Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence
Casual name: Executive Order on the Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence (EO 14110)
Collections: U.S. regulations, executive orders, and agency policies;Editors' Picks
Short summary: Directs the federal government to ensure the safety and security of AI systems and take action to protect Americans from their potential risks. Prescribes measures to improve American innovation, competition, and leadership in AI while preserving privacy, mitigating algorithmic discrimination, and addressing labor disruptions. Calls for further responsible deployment of AI in federal government and consumer-facing industries.
Long summary:
Requires federal government to develop and apply standards to ensure the safety and security of AI systems and minimize their risks, including biological risks, cybersecurity risks, and deceptive content risks.

Orders the development of a National Security Memorandum that directs further actions on AI and security.

Directs federal government to support privacy-preserving research and technologies and develop guidance on the collection and usage of commercially available information by federal agencies.

Instructs federal government to prevent algorithmic discrimination by developing guidance and best practices in order to ensure fairness.

Calls for federal government to support the safe, responsible deployment of AI in healthcare, transportation, education, and communications networks.

Requires a report on AI's potential labor-market impacts and the identification of options for strengthening federal support for workers facing labor disruptions

Urges federal government to facilitate the immigration of AI talent to the U.S., catalyze AI research and innovation through a pilot of the National AI Research Resource, and promote competition in the AI ecosystem by providing resources to small businesses.

Directs federal government to maintain U.S. leadership in global AI efforts by expanding multilateral engagements, implementing international standards, and developing guidelines to secure critical infrastructure.

Calls for the advancement of federal government use of AI through the issuance of guidance for agency use of AI, support for agency acquisition of AI products/services, and authorization of rapid hiring of AI professionals.

Official name: NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0
Casual name: NIST AI Risk Management Framework
Authority: National Institute of Standards and Technology
Collections: Editors' Picks;U.S. regulations, executive orders, and agency policies
Short summary: Defines trustworthy AI as valid, reliable, safe, secure, accountable, transparent, explainable, privacy-enhanced, and fair, with managed harmful bias. Outlines an AI risk management development strategy through governance, mapping, measuring, and managing functions.
Long summary:
Articulates characteristics of trustworthy AI, including validity, reliability, safety, security, accountability, explainability, privacy enhancement, and fairness in managing harmful bias. 

Encourages a balance of these characteristics based on AI systems' context of use, noting tradeoffs such as interpretability versus privacy. 

Emphasizes the importance of human judgment in deciding metrics and thresholds for AI trustworthiness. 

Stipulates that trustworthy AI depends on social and organizational behavior, datasets, model choices, and human interactions. 

Mandates addressing AI risks through ongoing testing, monitoring, and balancing accuracy and robustness. 

Calls for clear information and responsible decision-making to ensure safe AI operation. 

Advocates for secure and resilient AI systems that withstand adverse events and protect against unauthorized access. 

Promotes transparency and accountability to enhance confidence in AI systems, with transparency enabling actionable redress. 

Urges explainability and interpretability to improve understanding of AI system operations and outputs. 

Encourages privacy-enhancing technologies to safeguard autonomy and identity, acknowledging tradeoffs with accuracy. 

Highlights fairness in AI, addressing harmful bias and discrimination, and recognizing systemic, computational, and human-cognitive biases. 

Outlines AI risk management framework (AI RMF) functions: GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE, emphasizing a continuous and iterative process. 

Specifies GOVERN function for cultivating risk management culture, policies, and accountability in AI development and deployment. 

Describes MAP function for establishing context and understanding AI system impacts to inform risk management decisions. 

Details MEASURE function for using tools and methodologies to assess AI risks and system trustworthiness. 

Explains MANAGE function for prioritizing and responding to AI risks, maximizing benefits, and managing third-party risks.

Official name: Digital Platform Commission Act of 2023

Short summary: Establishes the Federal Digital Platform Commission to regulate digital platforms, including AI processes, ensuring fairness, transparency, and safety. Long summary:

Establishes the Federal Digital Platform Commission to regulate digital platforms, including social media.

Provides for the creation of a Code Council to develop voluntary or enforceable behavioral codes, technical standards, and other policies related to digital platforms and AI processes.

Mandates oversight of algorithmic processes, including those using AI, for fairness, transparency, and safety.

Obligates platforms to ensure recommendation systems and other algorithmic processes are free from harmful, abusive, anticompetitive, or deceptive biases.

Imposes regular public risk assessments for harmful content distribution and steps to mitigate such harms, including those from algorithmic processes..

Official name: Online Privacy Act of 2023, Sec. 106 ("Right to individual autonomy")
Casual name: Online Privacy Act, Sec. 106 ("Individual autonomy")
Short summary: Prohibits collecting, processing, maintaining, or disclosing personal information for behavioral personalization without consent. Requires annual consent renewals. Mandates non-personalized versions if consent is denied. Allows service denial if non-personalization is infeasible. Exempts small businesses.
Long summary:
Prohibits covered entities from collecting, processing, maintaining, or disclosing personal information for behavioral personalization without affirmative express consent.

Requires covered entities to obtain express affirmative consent before providing behaviorally personalized products or services, and annually thereafter.

Mandates providing non-personalized versions of products or services if consent is denied, or core aspects if full functionality without personalization is infeasible.

Allows denial of products or services if no core aspect can function without personalization and consent is not given.

Permits processing personal information for usability improvements using aggregated data, provided the output is uniform and independent of individual characteristics.

Excludes optimizations aimed primarily at increasing user engagement time from the definition of "usability."

Exempts small businesses from these requirements.

Official name: Illinois SB315 (Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act)
Casual name: Illinois SB315 (Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act)
Short summary: Requires large frontier AI developers in Illinois to establish and publish a frontier AI framework addressing catastrophic risk assessment by 2028, undergo annual independent third-party audits, file an annual disclosure/registration statement, and report critical safety incidents within 72 hours; prohibits false statements about AI risk or framework compliance; establishes escalating civil penalties up to $3,000,000 per violation; and protects whistleblowers who report safety violations.
Long summary:
Requires large frontier developers, starting January 1, 2028, to implement, regularly update, and publish a frontier AI framework incorporating national and industry standards to assess, mitigate, and manage catastrophic AI risks, including cybersecurity protections for model weights.

Requires developers to undergo annual independent third-party audits of compliance, with strict auditor independence safeguards, and to report critical safety incidents to the Illinois Emergency Management Agency and Attorney General within 72 hours (24 hours for imminent risk of death or injury).

Requires developers to publish transparency reports before or concurrent with deploying new or substantially modified frontier models, including catastrophic risk assessment summaries and third-party evaluator involvement in machine-readable format.

Requires large frontier developers, starting January 1, 2027, to file and annually renew a disclosure/registration statement with the Agency identifying ownership, business locations, and points of contact, and pay administration fees, with civil penalties of $1,000 per day for noncompliance.

Prohibits frontier developers from retaliating against or preventing covered employees from disclosing catastrophic risk concerns or Act violations, requiring an anonymous internal reporting process and annual notice of whistleblower rights.

Permits developers to satisfy this Act's requirements by complying with substantially equivalent federal laws, regulations, or guidance documents, provided the federal framework requires comparable incident reporting and independent audits.

Authorizes the Attorney General to enforce compliance through escalating civil penalties of up to $1,000,000 for a first violation and $3,000,000 for subsequent violations, with no private right of action.

Declares AI frontier model regulation an exclusive state power, preempting local Illinois home rule authority, and exempts critical safety incident reports, audit materials, and internal-use risk assessments from disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act.

Long summary:

Requires covered entities to provide limited-access mode for unverified users and verify user age before enabling restricted features.

Prohibits the enablement of restricted features for minors without parental consent and reasonable age verification.

Obligates operators to notify emergency services if they have knowledge of an imminent risk to a user and report incidents to the Attorney General.

Prohibits chatbots from prioritizing engagement metrics over user wellbeing or misleading users about being human.

Enables civil actions and penalties for violations, enforceable by the Attorney General.

Prohibits contractual waivers of rights or remedies under the act.

Requires deletion of age verification data within 24 hours, with specific exceptions.

Official name: California AB 1836
Casual name: California AB 1836 (Use of likeness: digital replica)
Short summary: Amends California Civil Code to require consent for using deceased personalities' likenesses in AI-generated replicas. Exempts certain expressive works. Imposes liability for unauthorized use with fines up to $10,000. Specifies consent requirements and transferrable rights for digital likenesses.
Long summary:
Amends the California Civil Code to impose liability on individuals using a deceased personality's likeness without consent, including AI-generated digital replicas. Requires violators to compensate for unauthorized use, with statutory minimums and profit disgorgement. Excludes certain uses such as news, satire, and fleeting references from consent requirements. 

Recognizes posthumous rights as transferable property interests, extending rights to heirs or designated persons. Limits rights duration to 70 years post-death and outlines specific inheritance rules. Mandates registration with the Secretary of State for enforcing claims, making these registrations public records.

Clarifies that certain artistic and informational works are exempt unless they serve commercial product promotion. Outlines exceptions for media owners unless knowingly complicit in unauthorized use. Enforces consistency with existing law by rendering remedies cumulative. Establishes retroactive application of rights back to those deceased before January 1, 1985.

Official name: Global AI Governance Initiative
Casual name: Global AI Governance Initiative
Short summary: Calls for global cooperation to enhance AI governance, prevent risks, and ensure equitable access. Opposes AI misuse, disinformation, and sovereignty violations. Promotes ethical principles, legal frameworks, and equal rights in AI development. Encourages international collaboration, especially supporting developing countries.
Long summary:
Recognizes that artificial intelligence is a new and developing area of technology for humans and has a profound influence on the progress of human civilization.

Calls on countries to enhance information exchange and technological cooperation for AI governance, focusing on working together to fight against risk and to develop an AI framework to make AI technology secure, reliability, and equitable.

Calls to support the role of AI in promoting sustainable development and tackling global challenges such as climate change and biodiversity conservation.

Opposes using AI for manipulating public opinion, spreading disinformation, or interfering in other nations' affairs.

Urges adherence to international laws and prevention of AI misuse by malicious actors and instead develop principles for AI to use that align with humanities common values of peace, development, equity, justice, democracy and freedom. 

Emphasizes call for global collaboration to make AI technologies open-source and accessible, resisting technological monopolies, drawing ideological lines or forming exclusive groups to obstruct other countries developing AI.

Promotes testing and assessment systems for AI based on risk levels (by carrying out tiered and category based management), ensuring AI remains under human control.

Advocates for laws ensuring privacy and data security in R&D and application of AI and also opposing illegal data practices of personal information.

Stresses fairness and non-discrimination in AI development processes and to avoid bias and discrimination.

Calls for ethical principles and accountability mechanisms to formulate AI ethical guidelines, and build sci-tech ethical review and regulatory system to address ethical concerns in a timely manner.

Encourages wide participation and consensus-based decision-making in AI governance.

Seeks increased representation of developing countries in global AI governance.

Supports UN discussions for an international AI governing institution.

Official name: Candidate Voice Fraud Prohibition Act
Casual name: Candidate Voice Fraud Prohibition Act
Short summary: Amends the Federal Election Campaign Act to prohibit distributing AI-generated audio impersonating candidates' voices with intent to mislead voters, exempting certain media entities and satire. Imposes fines or imprisonment for violations, and requires the Federal Election Commission to issue regulations and reports on compliance.
Long summary:
Prohibits the distribution of political communications containing materially deceptive AI-generated audio that impersonates a candidate’s voice, with actual malice, intended to harm the candidate’s reputation or deceive voters.

Applies to communications distributed within 90 days of a general election or 60 days of a primary, special, or runoff election.

Exempts certain entities from liability such as radio or television stations that air deceptive AI-generated content as part of news coverage or communications that clearly constitute satire.

Defines "materially deceptive audio" as AI-generated impersonation of a candidate’s voice without approval and lacking a clear disclaimer.

Imposes criminal penalties of fines or up to 2 years imprisonment for individuals who knowingly and willfully violate the prohibition.

Requires the Federal Election Commission (FEC) to issue regulations to clarify disclaimer requirements and mandates the submission of annual compliance reports to Congress.

Short summary:
Outlines China's guiding principles for AI governance and previous AI governance actions that China has taken, emphasizing ethics, safety, human control, equal access, security, international cooperation, and peaceful use.

Articulates China's recommendations of establishing AI ethics norms and laws that respect national differences, prioritizing safety and human control of AI systems, ensuring developing countries have equal access to AI, promoting international coordination, using AI to promote sustainable global development, and initiating a UN Security Council study of the impact of AI in conflict.

Highlights China's previous actions related to AI, including issuing an AI development plan, improving norms and standards for ethics and evaluation, and participating in global AI governance; reiterates China's willingness to work with the international community on AI security and other efforts to share the benefits of AI while preventing its risks.
Long summary:
Outlines principles that China believes should guide AI governance, highlights previous AI governance steps that China has taken, and articulates China's commitment to continued international cooperation on AI governance.

Calls for establishing and improving ethical norms and laws to ensure AI is people-centered and used for good, while respecting AI governance differences among countries.

Stresses AI safety and human control, urging the international community to enhance risk awareness, establish accountability structures, and ensure autonomous machine killing does not occur.

Advocates for fairness and inclusiveness, highlighting the importance of ensuring developing countries have equal access to AI and opposing technological hegemony and exclusionary practices.

Promotes openness and inclusiveness, encouraging international and interdisciplinary cooperation on AI development and governance under the UN framework to create an open, non-discriminatory environment.

Calls for peaceful use of AI, underscoring AI's potential to promote sustainable global development and calling for responsible defense policies to prevent AI misuse in military contexts.

Underscores China's commitment to international cooperation on AI governance, referencing past initiatives and ongoing efforts to establish a global framework for AI security governance.

Official name: Disrupt Explicit Forged Images And Non-Consensual Edits Act of 2024
Casual name: DEFIANCE Act of 2024
Short summary: Amends the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2022, to define "digital forgery" as AI-created intimate visual depictions. Allows civil action for non-consensual digital forgeries. Specifies damages and relief. Permits privacy protections. Establishes a 10-year statute of limitations. Ensures non-preemption.
Long summary:
Amends the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2022, to include "digital forgery" as any intimate visual depiction created via AI or other technological means to appear indistinguishable from an authentic visual depiction.

Allows identifiable individuals to bring civil action against those who produce, possess, disclose, or solicit digital forgeries without consent, with knowledge or reckless disregard of the lack of consent.

Specifies relief for plaintiffs, including actual or liquidated damages of $150,000, attorney’s fees, and equitable relief such as injunctions.

Permits courts to issue orders to protect plaintiffs' privacy, including the use of pseudonyms and sealing personal identifying information.

Establishes a 10-year statute of limitations for actions, starting from the discovery of the violation or the individual reaching 18 years of age.

Ensures the Act does not preempt state, federal, or tribal laws that provide at least as much protection.

Directs the municipality to promote the large-scale application of AI throughout society, including in manufacturing, finance, business, logistics, the Internet, education, medicine, elder care, public safety, public health, government services, and the justice system.

Instructs the municipality to conduct security inspections of AI applications and revise regulations as AI evolves.

Calls for the creation of a municipality AI ethics expert committee to develop ethical norms, assess potential AI risks, and advise and educate on AI ethics and safety.

Casual name: Protect Working Musicians Act of 2023
Short summary: Limits liability under antitrust laws for Individual Music Creator Owners who collectively negotiate or refuse licensing to Dominant Online Music Distribution Platforms or companies developing or deploying generative AI. Long summary:

Official name: No AI FRAUD Act
Casual name: No AI FRAUD Act
Short summary: Establishes property rights in likeness and voice, transferable post-mortem for ten years. Prohibits unauthorized cloning and replicas, imposing liabilities. Specifies damages per violation. Allows punitive damages and attorney fees. Provides First Amendment defense. Exempts negligible harm. Sets four-year limitations period.
Long summary:
Establishes property rights for individuals in their likeness and voice, treating them as intellectual property that is transferable and descendible for ten years post-mortem.

Prohibits unauthorized distribution, transmission, or availability of personalized cloning services, digital voice replicas, or digital depictions without the individual’s consent, imposing liabilities for violations.

Specifies that unauthorized use incurs damages of $50,000 per violation for cloning services and $5,000 per violation for voice replicas or depictions, plus actual damages and profits.

Allows for punitive damages and attorney fees for injured parties and invalidates disclaimers as a defense.

Provides a First Amendment defense, balancing public interest with intellectual property rights, and considers commercial use and impact on the value of the original work.

Exempts negligible harm from liability and defines harm to include financial, physical, and severe emotional distress.

Sets a four-year limitations period for civil actions and ensures no preemption of other rights or laws.

Short summary: Amends election law to require disclosure of materially deceptive media in political communications. Exempts satire, parody, and certain news reporting. Allows candidates to seek legal remedies if their likeness is used deceptively. Establishes burden of proof for plaintiffs.
Long summary:
Amends the election law to require disclosure for political communications using materially deceptive media.

Mandates visual disclosures to be legibly printed, stating "This (image, video, or audio) has been manipulated."

Requires audio disclosures to be stated clearly at the beginning, end, and periodically for messages longer than two minutes.

Exempts satire, bona fide news reporting with clear disclosures, stations with consistent disclaimer requirements, and platforms disseminating third-party content in good faith.

Permits candidates depicted in deceptive media to seek legal relief, including court costs, attorney fees, and injunctions against unauthorized dissemination.

Grants courts authority to provide preliminary relief to plaintiffs likely to succeed in proving violations in upcoming elections.

Clarifies that federal law takes precedence over state requirements for media labeling in political communications.

Instructs the City agencies and departments of Boston, excluding Boston Public Schools, to use generative AI responsibly, with guidelines focusing on transparency, accountability, and inclusiveness.

Requires fact-checking and reviewing AI-generated content for public communication to avoid inaccuracies and biases.

Emphasizes disclosing AI usage, including model type and version, to promote trust and transparency.

Prohibits sharing of sensitive or private information in AI prompts to protect residents' data privacy.

Encourages responsible experimentation with generative AI to support efficient, equitable city services while managing risks.

Directs the Department of Innovation and Technology to facilitate learning events and workshops on generative AI.

Advises consultation with relevant city offices and community organizations before publicizing AI-created content to ensure accessibility, accuracy, and sensitivity.

Promotes AI use in drafting documents, summarizing text, coding, and creating multimedia, while highlighting the importance of human oversight and editing.

Encourages engaging stakeholders for potential impacts on arts and society.

Mandates parental or guardian consent for users under 18, requiring platforms to take reasonable steps to verify this consent.

Prohibits the use of algorithmic recommendation systems on individuals under 18, except for contextual suggestions or advertising.

Establishes a Pilot Program for secure digital identification credentials to facilitate age and parental consent verification, overseen by the Secretary of Commerce.

Mandates that fabricated depictions remain in law enforcement custody and are not duplicated during legal proceedings.

Official name: LISTOS Act
Casual name: LISTOS Act
Short summary: Requires large online platforms to ensure consistent enforcement of content moderation, including through automated processes, across languages. Mandates disclosures on processes, establishes an advisory group, authorizes enforcement by the Federal Trade Commission or State Attorneys General, and establishes a pilot program for international research, including tool development, to address non-English online communication inciting harm.
Long summary:
Requires covered platform operators to ensure that content moderation processes are reasonably consistent across languages in which the platform conducts monetization practices, while allowing enforcing entities to consider practical limitations and prohibiting mandates on specific content decisions.

Requires platform operators to report on processes, including automated processes, for content moderation annually to the Federal Trade Commission (Commission) and the public.

Requires platform operators to ensure that user tools for reporting content and automated actions are accessible in all languages offered by the platform.

Establishes the Advisory Group on Language-Sensitive Technologies under the Commission to provide best practices on the application of language-sensitive AI technologies to ensure nondiscriminatory application, and for the Commission to make available the results.

Empowers the Commission and State Attorneys General to enforce compliance, treating violations as unfair or deceptive practices under the Federal Trade Commission Act.

Mandates the Commission to promulgate further regulations for carrying out the Act within 120 days.

Directs the United States Agency for International Development, in coordination with the Department of State, to set up a pilot program supporting international research, including tool development, to address non-English online communication that incites harm, and to report results to Congress and make them publicly available. Authorizes $3,000,000 in each of the fiscal years 2024 and 2025 in appropriations for the program.

Instructs primary and secondary schools to enhance AI education in curricula, encouraging interdisciplinary and practical applications.

Directs the application of AI to enhance student learning, teacher instruction, education governance, scientific research, and smart education infrastructure.

Casual name: Deterring American AI Model Theft Act of 2026

Requires the Secretary of State, in coordination with relevant agencies, to assess and identify foreign entities engaged in such attacks or facilitating them through fraudulent account networks.

Directs the Secretary of Commerce to publish a report on best practices for detecting, preventing, and responding to these attacks.

Maintains an "AI Model Extraction Attackers List" naming identified individuals and entities involved in past attacks, published for public access.

Authorizes the President to impose sanctions under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act on identified entities, with exceptions for humanitarian, intelligence, law enforcement, and national security activities.

Tasks the Under Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Security, in coordination with the End-User Review Committee, to determine placement of identified entities on the Entity List.

Promotes cooperation with closed-source AI model owners to develop best practices against model extraction attacks.

Requires development of a systematic AI curriculum, emphasizing understanding and application of AI at different educational levels.

Encourages interdisciplinary learning and integration of AI education into local and school-specific curricula, with a focus on ethics and proper usage of AI tools.

Directs schools to implement AI education alongside existing subjects and activities, ensuring practical problem-solving skills are taught.

Calls for the creation of universally accessible teaching resources and AI education bases, leveraging digital platforms to share resources.

Encourages development of AI labs and experience centers, promoting a practical learning environment.

Stipulates the need for increasing teacher supply, offering recruitment and training programs.

Promotes diverse AI-related student activities, enhancing skills and innovation.

Mandates local governments and schools to ensure funding, planning, and evaluation measures for AI education implementation.

Emphasizes reducing urban-rural disparities in AI education through resource sharing and support.

Apply provisions to all state agency computer systems, with exceptions for research and personal use systems.

Prohibit uses by state agencies for classifying individuals leading to discrimination, surveillance in public spaces without a warrant, and malicious use of deepfakes.

Allow AI use with human oversight on irreversible decisions, disclosure of AI-generated content, and informing users of AI interactions.

Sever provisions to ensure remaining regulations remain in effect if parts are invalidated.

Recommends agencies apply strong security practices to mitigate risks such as data spills and insecure code generation.

Advises validation and human oversight of all GenAI outputs to mitigate risks of hallucination, bias, and discrimination, particularly toward Māori communities.

Urges agencies to be transparent about GenAI usage and exercise caution when using publicly available AI tools.

Suggests using sandboxes for testing GenAI safely and advises on procurement principles to mitigate vendor-related risks. 

States that this guidance serves as an interim measure while longer-term AI regulatory frameworks are developed.

Official name: Transformational Artificial intelligence to Modernize the Economy against Extreme Weather Act

Long summary:

Requires NOAA to advance AI applications for data assimilation, using AI models to emulate and cross-check numerical weather models.

Requires environmental-impact best practices to minimize the footprint of AI use in each program area.

Provides for public access to data and code developed under the Act, subject to safeguards for national security, intellectual property, and trade secrets.

Official name: Oklahoma H 3642
Casual name: Oklahoma H 3642 (Oklahoma Law on Obscenity and Child Pornography)
Short summary: Defines "child pornography" to include computergenerated images and establishes severe penalties for production and possession. Requires registration as a sex offender for possession of 100+ depictions. Effective November 1, 2024, the act targets explicit computer-generated images involving minors.
Long summary:
Amends Oklahoma laws to enhance penalties for offenses involving child pornography, specifically targeting AI-generated images. 

Defines "child pornography" to include computer-generated images and altered images that depict minors in sexually explicit conduct, regardless of whether the image is real or synthetic. 

Establishes that possessing, distributing, or creating such images, including those utilizing AI technology, is a felony with penalties up to 20 years imprisonment and a $25,000 fine. 

Specifies that possession of 100 or more images constitutes aggravated possession, punishable by life imprisonment and a $10,000 fine, with required sex offender registration.  

Clarifies that AI-generated and computer-altered images count as independent offenses. 

Mandates that this act becomes effective on November 1, 2024.

Requires AI companions to notify users about non-human interactions at the start and every three hours during conversations.

Allows prioritization of technology adoption based on operational needs and budget constraints, with justifications included in reports.

Long summary:

Directs publication of an unclassified public summary of the report on the Department’s website within 60 days, consistent with national security interests.

Instructs the Government Accountability Office (GAO) to evaluate, beginning 18 months after enactment and biennially thereafter, the Department’s implementation of technology transformation projects, including effectiveness of performance and adoption metrics, achievement of operational and security goals, and adequacy of oversight mechanisms for responsible AI deployment.

Requires the Comptroller General to provide recommendations to improve management and evaluation of these technology transformation efforts.

Permits the NSA Director to provide computing resources the Director deems appropriate in support of such collaboration.

Official name: H.R.4640 Stop AI Price Gouging and Wage Fixing Act of 2025
Casual name: H.R.4640 Stop AI Price Gouging and Wage Fixing Act of 2025
Short summary: Prohibits surveillance-based AI systems from determining prices and wages unless specific transparency and fairness criteria are met. Requires Federal Trade Commission and Equal Employment Opportunity Commission to enforce provisions. Grants states and individuals the right to pursue legal actions.
Long summary:
Prohibits surveillance-based price and wage setting using AI-based automated decision systems. 

Requires transparency and clear criteria for data usage if AI adjusts consumer prices or worker wages based on location or cost of living.

Instructs entities using AI for these purposes to publicly disclose data procedures 180 days in advance and provide consumers and workers means to correct data inaccuracies.

Empowers the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) to enforce these provisions, treating violations as unfair acts under the FTC Act.
