Casual name: S.2528 Unleashing AI Innovation in Financial Services Act 2025
Short summary: Establishes AI Innovation Labs within financial regulatory agencies to enable regulated entities to test AI projects. Permits alternative compliance strategies. Requires agencies to review applications and issue guidelines. Mandates annual reporting on AI test projects' outcomes to Congress without disclosing proprietary information.
Long summary:
Establishes AI Innovation Labs under financial regulatory agencies to allow experimentation with AI test projects without the burden of enforcement actions.

Requires regulated entities to submit detailed applications for AI test projects, including alternative compliance strategies, risk assessments, and economic impact estimates.

Instructs financial regulatory agencies to review applications within 120 days and approve those meeting the criteria for innovation, public interest, and risk management.

Allows financial regulatory agencies the authority to extend approval deadlines by 120 days and mandates automatic approval if no determination is made after this extension.

Prohibits enforcement of certain regulations on approved AI projects except in cases of fraud, unsafe practices, or significant risks.

Requires financial agencies to ensure data security for AI test project information and mandates them to promulgate regulatory procedures for AI projects.

Obliges financial agencies to report annually to Congress on AI test project outcomes, omitting proprietary information.

Official name: S.2506 SkyFoundry Act of 2025
Casual name: S.2506 SkyFoundry Act of 2025
Short summary: Require the Secretary of Defense to establish the SkyFoundry Program for rapid development of unmanned aircraft systems, leveraging alternative acquisition and public-private partnerships. Permit expedited regulatory approvals and prioritize domestic industrial base support under the Defense Production Act.
Long summary:
Requires the Secretary of Defense to establish the SkyFoundry Program to rapidly develop, test, and manufacture small unmanned aircraft systems, potentially expanding to other autonomous systems.

Directs administration of the Program through the Secretary of the Army and integrates it into the Defense Industrial Resilience Consortium.

Leverages alternative acquisition mechanisms to accelerate system development and production.

Establishes a Government-owned innovation facility for research and development and a production facility for manufacturing, both operated by United States Army Materiel Command.

Allows entering into multiyear contracts or public-private partnerships for augmented support.

Prioritizes using or modifying existing Army Depot facilities for the Program, with requirements for facility size and location.

Ensures the U.S. retains intellectual property rights to jointly developed technologies.

Utilizes Defense Production Act authorities to support domestic industrial base capacity for these systems.

Permits expedited approvals and potential waivers of regulatory requirements to facilitate rapid Program operations.

Official name: S.2455 Transparency and Responsibility for Artificial Intelligence Networks Act 2025
Casual name: S.2455 TRAIN Act 2025
Short summary: Establishes an administrative subpoena process permitting copyright owners to request records from AI model developers. Requires developers to disclose training materials to ascertain copyright use. Sets penalties for noncompliance and bad-faith requests, while ensuring confidentiality of disclosed records.
Long summary:
Creates a process for copyright owners to obtain administrative subpoenas to determine if their works were used in training artificial intelligence models.

Defines key terms such as 'artificial intelligence model,' 'developer,' and 'generative artificial intelligence model.'

Allows copyright owners or their representatives to request subpoenas from U.S. district courts to require AI developers to disclose training materials involving copyrighted works, provided they have a good faith belief that their works were used.

Restricts subpoena requests to the requester’s own copyrighted works.

Requires developers to disclose requested materials if a subpoena is issued properly.

Prohibits disclosure of information obtained through subpoenas without proper authorization.

Establishes a rebuttable presumption against developers who fail to comply with subpoenas.

Permits courts to impose sanctions on parties who request subpoenas in bad faith in accordance with Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.

Official name: H.R.4321 Supporting Modern Approaches in Recovery Technology for Traumatic Brain Injury Act 2025
Casual name: H.R.4321 SMART for TBI Act 2025
Short summary: Amends law to require the Secretary of Defense to establish a working group for developing a strategy using AI and digital health technologies to treat traumatic brain injuries. Identifies capability gaps, analyzes current efforts, and recommends advancements and investment plans.
Long summary:
Amends the James M. Inhofe National Defense Authorization Act to require the Secretary of Defense to develop a strategy using digital health technologies for treating traumatic brain injuries.

Establishes a working group to develop this strategy, consisting of Armed Forces members, Department of Defense civilian employees, and external experts in relevant fields.

Requires the strategy to identify capability gaps in treating traumatic brain injuries that AI and digital technologies could address, analyze current efforts using AI and commercial technologies, and recommend advancements to improve treatments.

Includes a plan for recommending investments to enhance digital health technologies for traumatic brain injuries.

Directs the Secretary to brief congressional defense committees on this strategy by September 30, 2026.

Official name: Arizona 2024 House Bill 2394
Casual name: Arizona HB 2394 (Digital Impersonation of Candidate for Public Office)
Short summary: Prohibits digital impersonation using AI to deceive voters in Arizona elections. Allows candidates or citizens to seek declaratory relief within two years of impersonation. Shields service providers from liability for third-party content. Requires clear and convincing evidence for relief.
Long summary:
Amends Arizona Revised Statutes to prohibit digital impersonation using AI techniques.

Allows candidates or citizens to take legal action against digital impersonation within two years of awareness.

Mandates proof of unauthorized publication and lack of clear indication of impersonation to prevail in court.

Restricts legal action to originators of paid advertisements containing impersonations.

Exempts interactive computer service providers from liability for third-party content.

Permits filing for preliminary declaratory relief in superior court with expedited ruling requirements.

Specifies conditions for granting preliminary relief, such as immediate elections or significant harm.

Allows further injunctive relief and damages for impersonations involving sexual or criminal content.

Sets standards of proof as clear and convincing evidence for relief actions.

Defines "digital impersonation" as AI-manipulated media designed to deceive, excluding parody or artistic expression.

Operates as an emergency measure effective immediately to protect public peace and safety.

Official name: FinCEN Modernization Act of 2023
Casual name: FinCEN Modernization Act of 2023
Short summary: Cites the Act as the "FinCEN Modernization Act of 2023." Requires FinCEN to establish research and information-sharing programs on technological advances. Mandates exploration of beneficial innovations. Obligates adoption of necessary technologies. Enables information exchange. Authorizes non-standard transactions. Compels annual reporting to Congress.
Long summary:
Cites the Act as the "FinCEN Modernization Act of 2023."

Requires FinCEN to establish research, development, and information-sharing programs focusing on technological advances like machine learning and data analytics.

Mandates FinCEN to explore and evaluate technological innovations beneficial for financial systems and detect illicit activities.

Obligates FinCEN to adopt necessary technologies for monitoring cryptocurrencies and addressing money laundering and cyber threats.

Enables FinCEN to exchange information with other Treasury offices and federal departments.

Authorizes FinCEN to enter into non-standard transactions and accept contributions, gifts, or donations to support technological advancements.

Compels FinCEN to submit an annual report detailing transactions, contributions, and their justifications and purposes to relevant Congressional committees.

Official name: S 2750 Strengthening Artificial intelligence Normalization and Diffusion By Oversight and eXperimentation Act 2025
Casual name: S 2750 SANDBOX Act 2025
Short summary: Requires the Director of the Office of Science and Technology Policy to establish a Federal regulatory sandbox program for AI, allowing applicants to test AI innovations by obtaining temporary waivers or modifications on specific legal provisions.
Long summary:
Requires the Director of the Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP) to establish a Federal regulatory sandbox program for artificial intelligence (AI). 

Allows entities developing or deploying AI systems to apply for temporary waivers or modifications of specific legal or regulatory requirements in order to test AI technologies within the sandbox.

Establishes an application process requiring applicants to describe the AI system, testing plan, regulatory barriers, and potential risks such as health and safety harms, economic impacts, and unfair trade practices.

Directs relevant federal agencies to review applications and assess the risks and benefits of proposed AI testing before approving sandbox participation.

Authorizes the OSTP Director to approve, deny, modify, or revoke waivers and to impose conditions on sandbox participation.

Requires monitoring and evaluation of sandbox activities, including compliance with participation conditions and mitigation of identified risks.

Allows the Director to review compliance, revoke waivers, or terminate participation if participants fail to meet the terms of their agreement.

Facilitates coordination between the federal sandbox program and state-level AI regulatory initiatives where appropriate.

Requires reporting to Congress on sandbox activities, outcomes, and recommendations for regulatory changes.

Establishes the 12-year duration and operational terms of the sandbox program.

Official name: Israel's Policy on Artificial Intelligence: Regulations and Ethics
Casual name: Israel's Policy on Artificial Intelligence: Regulations and Ethics
Short summary: Identifies seven challenges arising from the use of AI in the private sector; provides guidelines to support responsible AI innovation and guide sector-specific regulation of private sector AI usage.
Long summary:
Provides guidelines for regulation of private sector AI uses, focusing on responsible innovation and the idea that innovation, ethics, and regulation are complementary.

Identifies discrimination, human oversight, explainability, disclosing AI interactions, robustness and security, accountability and legal liability, and privacy as key challenges that AI regulation should consider.

Urges sector-specific regulation and consistency with international approaches.

Advocates a risk-based approach, incremental development, and experimentation in AI regulation.

Encourages the use of "soft" tools and multistakeholder cooperation in AI regulation.

Recommends adopting ethical AI principles based on the OECD AI Principles, focusing on human-centric AI, equality, transparency, reliability, accountability, and using AI to promote growth.

Proposes the creation of an AI Policy Coordination Center to advise regulators, promote inter-agency coordination, monitor implementation of regulation, and lead international representation at AI forums.

Recommends mapping AI uses and associated challenges and risks in regulated sectors.

Calls for the establishment of forums for regulators and public participation to ensure coordination and open discussion of AI regulation.

Urges government departments to engage actively international forums to develop AI regulation and standards.

Encourages the government to develop tools to support responsible AI, including a risk management framework.

Official name: Pay Flexibility, Incentive Pay, and Leave and Workforce Flexibility Programs for Artificial Intelligence (AI), AI-enabling, and Other Key Technical Employees (OPM)
Casual name: Pay Flexibility, Incentive Pay, and Leave and Workforce Flexibility Programs for Artificial Intelligence (AI), AI-enabling, and Other Key Technical Employees (OPM)
Collections: U.S. regulations, executive orders, and agency policies
Short summary: Allows federal agencies to use various pay and workforce flexibility programs to recruit and retain AI talent without needing approval from the Office of Personnel Management.
Long summary:
Grants federal agencies discretionary authority to use various pay flexibility, incentive pay, and leave and workforce flexibility programs to recruit, relocate, and retain AI employees.

Permits agencies to offer recruitment, relocation, and retention incentives for AI positions of up to 25% of basic pay; allows agencies to request permission from the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) to increase such incentives to 50% based on critical needs.

Enables agencies to repay student loans as a recruitment or retention incentive, with limits of $10,000 annually and $60,000 total per employee.

Allows agencies to set higher pay rates for employees with superior qualifications or employees filling special needs; permits agencies to request OPM approval for special rates and critical position pay.

Authorizes agencies to offer leave accrual incentives, alternative work schedules, and remote work to enhance recruitment and retention of AI employees.

Encourages collaboration between hiring managers and Chief Artificial Intelligence Officers to design agency-specific recruitment and retention strategies.

Official name: Combating Cartels on Social Media Act of 2023
Casual name: Combating Cartels on Social Media Act of 2023
Short summary: Requires the Secretary of Homeland Security to assess and counter cartel recruitment on social media by developing a national strategy, consulting with operators and communities, creating reporting mechanisms, and designating an official within CBP to manage and share intelligence
Long summary:
Requires the Secretary of Homeland Security to assess within 180 days how transnational criminal organizations use covered services, including social media and other online platforms, for recruitment and other illicit activities, and to evaluate existing government and operator responses

Mandates submission of a National Strategy to combat illicit recruitment activity by Transnational Criminal Organizations on social media and online platforms within one year

Proposes improvements in cooperation between government entities and social media operators, enhanced intelligence analysis, and proactive law enforcement efforts, international partnerships, and targeted outreach to youth in border communities

Requires establishment of a centralized mechanism for reporting recruitment efforts by transnational criminal organizations to the Department of Homeland Security

Excludes any legislative recommendations not enacted by strategy submission date, including encryption policies and Section 230 reforms

Instructs the Secretary to consult with various federal, state, and local entities, as well as social media companies and experts during strategy development and implementation

Mandates semiannual reporting on the implementation of the strategy and its progress to appropriate congressional committees for five years

Designates a specific official within U.S. Customs and Border Protection to manage intelligence related to recruitment activities and to facilitate voluntary information reporting from social media operators

Official name: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026, Section 7337 ("National Academy of Sciences report on uncrewed systems and use of data")
Casual name: FY2026 NDAA, Section 7337 ("National Academy of Sciences report on uncrewed systems and use of data")
Short summary: Requires the Commandant to arrange for the National Academy of Sciences to assess uncrewed maritime domain technologies for the Coast Guard, focusing on benefits, costs, operational impacts, and necessary adjustments. Instructs report submission to Congress within one year.
Long summary:
Require the National Academy of Sciences to assess uncrewed, autonomous, or remotely-controlled maritime technologies for Coast Guard use.

Directs the Academy to describe benefits and limitations of such systems for ocean observation, vessel monitoring, weather observation, search and rescue, intelligence, and communications.

Requires the Academy to assess how these technologies can guide Federal investment priorities by considering costs, reliability, versatility, and lifecycle; how new and emerging technologies can lower costs and manpower while expanding Coast Guard capabilities and efficiency.

Requires the Academy to evaluate progress from research to effective operations since the 2020 study on unmanned systems and identify necessary adjustments in Coast Guard authorities and procedures to incorporate uncrewed technologies.

Requires the Academy to submit the assessment to Congressional committees within one year of agreement; encourages usage of existing Coast Guard reports for cost formulation in the assessment.

Official name: Digital Defense Content Provenance Act of 2023
Casual name: Digital Defense Content Provenance Act
Short summary: Establishes a Defense Department education course on digital content provenance, training specialists on authentication standards and forgery risks. Launches a pilot program to test industry standards for verifying media authenticity in official DoD content, and requires reporting on progress, effectiveness, and potential permanence.
Long summary:
Requires the Department of Defense to establish a course at the Defense Information School to provide education on digital content provenance for DoD media content, covering challenges from digital content forgery, industry-open technical standards, and techniques for secure digital content documentation.

Mandates a report on the curriculum development and implementation plan for the course, including resource needs.

Initiates a pilot program to assess the feasibility of using industry-open technical standards for digital content provenance in DoD media.

Directs the pilot program to verify digital content provenance, apply technology solutions, assess historical records, and develop effectiveness measures.

Requires a report detailing findings, consultations, effectiveness, and recommendations on the pilot program's permanence.

Casual name: Stop Fentanyl at the Border Act
Short summary:
Appropriates $1,090,000,000 to U.S. Customs and Border Protection for technology improvements to enhance fentanyl interdiction.

Appropriates $223,000,000 to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to expand fentanyl interdiction and disrupt transnational criminal networks.

Mandates submission of reports by March 31, 2028, on impacts of Border Patrol Processing Coordinator positions and equipment needs.

Creates penalties for damaging or evading border controls, with fines and imprisonment up to 5 years for violations aimed at financial gain or furthering criminal organizations.
Long summary:
Appropriates $1,090,000,000 to U.S. Customs and Border Protection for technology improvements, including non-intrusive inspection scanning systems and anomaly detection algorithms, to enhance fentanyl interdiction at land borders.

Appropriates $223,000,000 to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to expand efforts to interdict fentanyl and disrupt transnational criminal networks, including funds for additional special agents and joint surge operations.

Mandates submission of reports by March 31, 2028, detailing impacts of Border Patrol Processing Coordinator positions, equipment needs for outbound inspections, and summaries of non-intrusive inspection technology at land ports of entry.

Creates penalties for knowingly damaging or evading border controls, with fines and imprisonment up to 5 years for violations aimed at securing financial gain or furthering criminal organizations.

Official name: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026, Section 224 ("National Security and Defense Artificial Intelligence Institute")
Casual name: FY2026 NDAA, Section 224 ("National Security and Defense Artificial Intelligence Institute")
Short summary: Authorize the Secretary of Defense to establish AI Institutes focused on national security. Directs support for interdisciplinary AI research, partnership, innovation ecosystems, and workforce development.
Long summary:
Allows the Secretary of Defense to establish one or more artificial intelligence research institutes focused on national security and defense.

Requires each institute to address foundational or cross-cutting AI challenges relevant to defense and national security.

Directs institutes to form partnerships across federal agencies, academia, nonprofit research organizations, state and local governments, and industry.

Requires institutes to foster innovation ecosystems that translate research into applications and products that enhance national security and defense capabilities.

Requires support for research and development that spans multiple institutions of higher education and organizations.

Requires institutes to support interdisciplinary research and workforce development in AI and related disciplines within the United States.

Long summary:

Requires agencies to submit quarterly reports detailing hires made under direct hire authority, including the number of job announcements, qualified applicants, and hires.

Allows OPM to request information and assess agency use of direct hire authority, with the possibility of modification or termination.

Permits use of excepted service Schedule A appointments for non-technical, temporary staffing to support implementation of Executive Order 14110 ("Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence").

Prohibits use of direct hire authority or Schedule A authority beyond December 31, 2028.

Official name: Interim Measures for the Management of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services
Casual name: Interim Measures for the Management of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services
Short summary: Regulates generative AI services in mainland China, emphasizing legal compliance, societal ethics, and security. Encourages innovation while preventing discrimination and protecting personal information. Mandates providers to ensure content accuracy, transparency, and user privacy. Enforces penalties for non-compliance.
Long summary:
Establishes legal framework for the use and governance of generative AI services in mainland China, promoting innovation while ensuring security and compliance with national values.

Applies to public generative AI services generating text, images, audio, video, but excludes non-public research and development.

Mandates adherence to laws, ethical standards, and the protection of intellectual property, personal information, and societal values.

Encourages independent innovation and international cooperation in AI technology, emphasizing lawful data handling and quality improvement.

Requires providers to ensure information security, sign service agreements with users, and prevent misuse by minors and illegal activities.

Obligates providers to label AI-generated content, maintain service stability, and establish complaint mechanisms.

Imposes oversight by relevant state departments, requiring security assessments for AI with social mobilization potential.

Specifies penalties for non-compliance, including warnings, service suspension, and legal action for serious violations.

Takes effect on August 15, 2023, with provisions for foreign investment compliance.

Official name: HHS Public Benefits and AI
Casual name: HHS Public Benefits and AI
Authority: Department of Health and Human Services
Collections: U.S. regulations, executive orders, and agency policies
Short summary: Encourages state and local governments to use AI responsibly in public benefits administration. Recommends risk assessment, fairness, transparency, human oversight, and privacy protection. Emphasizes equity, accountability, and civil rights compliance. Supports developing frameworks and resources for AI governance and innovation.
Long summary:
Requires the United States Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to promote responsible AI use in public benefits administration by State, Local, Tribal, and Territorial Governments (STLTs).

Encourages STLTs to align with the principles of the National Institute of Standards and Technology AI Risk Management Framework and the Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights.

Recommends STLTs assess AI systems for equitable outcomes, notify recipients about AI use, and ensure human oversight and appeal processes.

Supports STLTs in developing AI policies and practices through guidance, technical assistance, and resources.

Urges STLTs to focus on safeguarding privacy, civil rights, and safety, and to provide opt-out options for AI systems.

Emphasizes the need for transparency, public engagement, and governance to manage AI-associated risks.

Directs HHS to work with STLTs and other agencies to ensure AI systems in public benefits programs are safe, equitable, and efficient.

Official name: California AB 412
Casual name: California AB 412 (Generative artificial intelligence: training data: copyrighted materials)
Short summary: Regulates GenAI developers in California by requiring them to document copyrighted materials used to train AI models, make available a mechanism for rights owners to request information regarding the use of covered materials, and respond to rights owners’ information requests within 30 days.
Long summary:
Defines terms for the purposes of this article, including approximate content fingerprint and artificial intelligence. 

Requires GenAI developers to document and identify covered materials used for training their models, including the rights owner of each covered material.

Mandates that developers provide information on their websites that enable the generation of fingerprints that are compatible with covered materials used to train a GenAI model and are generated using accepted industry standards.

Instructs GenAI developers to make available on their websites a mechanism allowing rights owners to request information about developers' use of covered materials.

Obliges developers to assess and respond to rights owners’ requests within 30 days; states that each day after the 30-day period a developer fails to provide a rights owner with the required information constitutes a discrete violation.

Limits rights owners to one request per quarter to the same developer concerning the same model and permits rights owners to bring civil actions against developers who do not comply with this article, including actual damages, injunctive relief, and attorney’s fees.

Exempt models trained using data that the developer makes publicly available, models developed and used for noncommercial academic governmental research, models not trained with covered materials, or models trained using covered materials owned by the developer, from the requirements of this article.

Official name: Google DeepMind Frontier Safety Framework Version 1.0
Casual name: Google DeepMind Frontier Safety Framework Version 1.0
Short summary: Establishes protocols for identifying and mitigating severe AI risks from Critical Capability Levels (CCLs) in domains like Autonomy, Biosecurity, Cybersecurity, and Machine Learning R&D. Implements security and deployment mitigations to manage risks, evolving with insights and future research.
Long summary:
Establishes protocols within the Frontier Safety Framework to address severe risks from future foundation models' capabilities.

Defines "Critical Capability Levels" (CCLs) to identify when AI models pose heightened risks, focusing initially on Autonomy, Biosecurity, Cybersecurity, and Machine Learning R&D.

Implements periodic evaluations to detect when models approach CCLs and articulates developing mitigation plans.

Proposes security mitigations to prevent model weight exfiltration and deployment mitigations to control access and expression of critical capabilities.

Outlines graded mitigation and security protocols based on AI capabilities and risks from potential misuse. 

Plans to implement the framework by early 2025 and expects it to evolve with emerging risks and insights.

Commits to periodically reviewing and updating the framework as understanding of AI risks and benefits improves.

Official name: Canada Artificial Intelligence and Data Act (Companion document)
Casual name: Canada Artificial Intelligence and Data Act (Companion document)
Short summary: Proposes AIDA to regulate high-impact AI systems, discusses implementation strategies, presenting a roadmap to ensure effective enforcement of AIDA to ensure safety, accountability, and human rights protection for citizens. Empowers the Minister to enforce compliance and prohibits harmful AI uses, establishing penalties. Establishes an AI and Data Commissioner in order to enforce compliance. Advocates repeated consultation with stakeholders for regulation development.
Long summary:
Proposes the Artificial Intelligence and Data Act (AIDA) to regulate AI in Canada, focusing on high-impact AI systems.

Empowers the Minister of Innovation, Science, and Industry to enforce AIDA, supported by a new AI and Data Commissioner.

Prohibits the reckless and malicious use of AI that causes harm, introducing new criminal law provisions.

Aligns with international norms, such as the EU AI Act, and integrates with existing Canadian laws.

Mandates businesses to identify, assess, and mitigate risks associated with high-impact AI systems.

Requires transparency, fairness, safety, and accountability in AI systems.

Introduces administrative penalties and criminal offences for non-compliance.

Plans a consultation process for the development of regulations, seeking input from stakeholders.

Establishes mechanisms for human oversight and monitoring of AI systems.

Targets AI systems impacting services, biometric identification, behavior influence, and health and safety.

Official name: Opinion on Strengthening Science and Technology Ethics Governance
Casual name: Opinion on Strengthening Science and Technology Ethics Governance
Short summary: Strengthens governance and ethics in AI by establishing legal systems, ethical principles, and review mechanisms. Requires risk assessment, transparency, and compliance with national and international standards. Promotes education and awareness, ensuring responsible AI innovation and preventing ethical violations. Enhances global cooperation.
Long summary:
Mandates embedding ethical requirements throughout scientific and technological activities, including AI, ensuring responsible innovation.

Requires adherence to rule of law in ethics governance, constructing a legal system for AI ethics.

Promotes agile governance for AI, dynamically adjusting to ethical challenges and risks.

Emphasizes the importance of openness and cooperation in global AI ethics governance.

Directs institutions to establish ethics committees for AI and sensitive areas, ensuring compliance with ethical standards.

Urges development of norms and guidelines for AI ethics, enhancing transparency and stakeholder participation.

Establishes the National Committee for Ethics in Science and Technology to guide AI ethics governance.

Mandates strict review and regulation of AI ethics, including risk assessment and compliance with international standards.

Calls for monitoring and early-warning systems for ethical risks in AI, ensuring rapid response to challenges.

Requires education and training on AI ethics for scientific personnel, raising awareness and ensuring adherence to ethical standards.

Official name: TAME Extreme Weather and Wildfires Act
Casual name: TAME Extreme Weather and Wildfires Act
Short summary: Directs the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration to curate training datasets and develop and integrate AI weather models for forecasting and fire environment modeling, while providing technical assistance to forecasters. Encourages public-private partnerships and workforce development, and requires public access to data where feasible while safeguarding national security and intellectual property.
Long summary:
Mandates the development of comprehensive weather forecasting training datasets, built on existing federal datasets where practicable, to support AI weather modeling; permits NOAA to develop and test its own global AI weather model, with annual progress reports to Congress.

Requires NOAA to advance AI applications for data assimilation, using AI models to emulate and cross-check numerical weather models.

Directs technical assistance for AI weather model adoption, including inventorying non-federal AI models, developing best practices for combining AI and numerical model outputs, supporting forecasters and emergency managers, and establishing a common reforecast-analysis framework.

Creates a fire environment modeling program using AI and observational/synthetic data to warn communities and responders, predict and detect wildfires, forecast fire propagation, and monitor smoke and related hazards.

Encourages public-private and academic partnerships, including novel co-investment strategies and shared intellectual property arrangements, to advance AI-driven environmental forecasting.

Directs workforce development, calling for NOAA to recruit and sustain an AI-skilled workforce through public-private training collaborations.

Requires environmental-impact best practices to minimize the footprint of AI use in each program area.

Provides for public access to data and code developed under the Act, subject to safeguards for national security, intellectual property, and trade secrets.

Supports continued research, observational data collection, and numerical weather modeling alongside AI development, ensuring traditional forecasting methods remain funded.

Official name: Responsible AI safety and education act
Casual name: New York A6453 (RAISE Act)
Collections: Editors' Picks;U.S. state and local documents
Short summary: Amends the general business law to establish the Responsible AI Safety and Education Act (RAISE Act), compelling transparency, safety protocols, and mandatory disclosures for frontier AI models. Enables state enforcement through penalties, prohibiting deployments that pose critical harm risks. Applies to frontier models in New York.
Long summary:
Amends New York's general business law to introduce the Responsible AI Safety and Education (RAISE) Act, implementing transparency requirements for deploying AI frontier models.

Requires large AI developers to implement and retain a written safety and security protocol that must be published with redactions and submitted to the Attorney General and Homeland Security.

Stipulates annual reviews of the protocol to accommodate any advancements.

Requires prompt reporting of safety incidents to authorities within 72 hours.

Prohibits knowingly making false or misleading statements concerning AI documentation.

Empowers the Attorney General to bring civil actions for violations, with penalties up to $30 million for repeated offenses.

Confirms that the Act applies exclusively to frontier AI models developed or operating in New York State.

Casual name: Increasing AI Capacity Across the Federal Government: AI Talent Surge Progress and Recommendations
Collections: U.S. regulations, executive orders, and agency policies
Short summary: Reports on the National AI Talent Surge's progress in recruiting AI professionals into government; offers further recommendations for building an AI workforce and AI capacity across the federal government.
Long summary:
Reports on the progress of the National AI Talent Surge, launched in Executive Order 14110, in recruiting AI professionals into government service.

Indicates that tech talent programs saw a 288% increase in AI applications in the first month of the talent surge; provides AI talent recruitment statistics for Presidential Innovation Fellows, U.S. Digital Corps, U.S. Digital Service; highlights the success of cross-government AI career fairs.

Reports that the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) authorized additional hiring authorities and issued guidance on pay and workforce flexibilities to improve recruitment and retention of AI talent.

Describes OPM and the AI and Tech Task Force's efforts to train recruiters who hire AI talent.

Summarizes how the task force is building AI competency and literacy among the federal workforce, including ensuring the workforce understands the benefits, risks, and limitations of AI and can use AI safely and responsibly.

Recommends federal funding increases for AI talent, creating a cross-agency technical recruiting team, and institutionalizing tech talent programs to further build AI capacity across the federal government.

Recommends improving USAJOBS, granting additional hiring authorities, and piloting skills-based hiring for AI positions.

Proposes a federal AI scholarship-for-service program and encourages the tech ecosystem to cultivate public service.

Recommends a global AI talent exchange.

Official name: Executive Order on Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence
Casual name: Executive Order on Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence
Collections: Editors' Picks;U.S. regulations, executive orders, and agency policies
Short summary: Establishes an AI Litigation Task Force to challenge state regulations hindering United States Artificial Intelligence (AI) dominance. Directs an evaluation to identify state laws that mandate ideological bias or alter truthful model outputs. Restricts state access to federal funding, such as the Broadband Equity Access and Deployment program, unless states comply with a proposed national policy framework designed to preempt conflicting state-level AI mandates.
Long summary:
Establishes a national policy to sustain United States leadership and global dominance in Artificial Intelligence (AI) by creating a "minimally burdensome" federal framework intended to replace a "patchwork" of conflicting state regulations

Directs the Attorney General to form an AI Litigation Task Force within 30 days to challenge state laws that unconstitutionally regulate interstate commerce or conflict with the national objective of AI supremacy,.

Mandates the Secretary of Commerce to conduct an evaluation of existing state AI laws within 90 days to identify "onerous" mandates that conflict with federal policy, specifically targeting those that require models to alter their truthful outputs or compel disclosures that violate the First Amendment.

Restricts state eligibility for remaining Broadband Equity Access and Deployment (BEAD) program funding, specifically making states with "onerous" AI laws ineligible for non-deployment funds. 

Instructs executive agencies to assess discretionary grant program to determine if they can condition funding on states either not enacting conflicting AI laws or entering into binding agreements to not enforce existing ones during the performance period.

Requires the Federal Communications Commission to consider a Federal AI reporting and disclosure standard to preempt conflicting State laws.

Directs the Federal Trade Commission to issue a policy statement on preempting State laws that require deceptive modifications to AI outputs.

Mandates preparation of a legislative recommendation for a Federal AI policy framework, allowing certain State AI laws on topics like child safety to remain.

Official name: H.R. 9626, To direct the Department of Defense to develop a plan for the establishment of a secure computing and data storage environment for the testing of artificial intelligence trained on biological data, and for other purposes.
Casual name: H.R. 9626, DOD Secure Computing and Data Storage Plan Development
Short summary: Establishes a secure AIxBio sandbox for testing AI trained on biological data. Designates the Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering to manage it. Involves selecting defense-applicable projects and facilitating partnerships with DoD and academic labs to bring these projects to fruition and application for military use. Requires reporting to Congress on evaluation of possible successful projects within one year of the enactment of this legislation.
Long summary:
Mandates the Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering to develop a plan for a secure computing and data storage environment, termed the "AIxBio sandbox," to facilitate the testing of AI models trained on biological data.

Requires the AIxBio sandbox to utilize existing Department of Defense infrastructure when feasible and designates the Under Secretary of Defense for managing and overseeing its activities.

Directs the Under Secretary to select projects for the sandbox that demonstrate potential defense applications at the intersection of AI and biotechnology, such as medical countermeasures and biomanufacturing.

Establishes mechanisms for collaboration between Department of Defense laboratories and academic institutions to support AIxBio projects, with streamlined processes that will facilitate efficient and fruitful partnerships.

Obligates the Under Secretary to report and brief Congress on the plan within one year of the Act's enactment.

Official name: Safe and Responsible AI in Australia Consultation, Interim Response
Casual name: Safe and Responsible AI in Australia Consultation, Interim Response
Short summary: Considers mandatory safety guardrails for high-risk AI applications. Plans to consult on regulatory frameworks, including testing and transparency. Advocates international collaboration on AI safety and indicated future regulatory actions by the Australian government to improve AI safety, especially in high-risk use cases. Focuses on balancing innovation with risk management, enhancing privacy laws, and addressing misinformation and detrimental content that may. appear as a product of generative AI use.
Long summary:
Proposes strengthening existing laws and considering new legislation to address AI-related risks, particularly in high-risk settings.

Considers mandatory safety guardrails for AI systems in high-risk contexts, focusing on testing, transparency, and accountability.

Plans to work with industry to develop a voluntary AI Safety Standard and explore options for voluntary labelling and watermarking of AI-generated materials.

Emphasizes a risk-based regulatory framework to ensure proportionality and avoid unnecessary burdens on low-risk AI applications so as to balance innovation with safety considerations.

Commits to collaborating with international partners, aligning with global standards, in accordance with initiatives like the Bletchley Declaration on AI safety, and modeled after regulatory practices adopted by the US, Canada and Singapore.

Supports investments in AI capability development and aims to maximize AI benefits, including through initiatives funded by the 2023–24 Budget.

Establishes an interim expert advisory group to explore AI guardrail options and harmonizes efforts with state and territory governments.

Official name: Transformational Artificial intelligence to Modernize the Economy against Extreme Weather and Wildfires Act
Casual name: TAME Extreme Weather and Wildfires Act 2025
Short summary: Directs NOAA to develop and curate AI weather models and training datasets to improve forecast accuracy and disaster response, while promoting public-private partnerships and technical assistance for emergency managers. Authorizes funding through 2030 and public data access, subject to safeguards for national security and intellectual property.
Long summary:
Directs NOAA's Under Secretary to develop and curate comprehensive weather forecasting training datasets, building on existing federal Earth system datasets where practicable, in consultation with federal agencies and technical experts.

Authorizes the development and testing of global, regional, and local AI weather models.

Permits exploring AI to enhance dissemination of weather and wildfire risk information and evaluate communication effectiveness for improved public understanding and preparedness.

Requires continued support for observational data collection, numerical weather modeling, and data assimilation alongside AI development.

Directs exploration of advanced AI applications, including ensemble forecasting and improved impact-based decision support.

Requires technical assistance, best practices, and a common reforecast-analysis framework for evaluating AI and numerical weather models, delivered through the National Weather Service.

Permits an independent study on AI weather models' impacts on the weather enterprise.

Encourages novel public-private-academic-international partnerships and co-investment strategies to accelerate AI adoption in weather and wildfire forecasting.

Requires a plan for public access to operational and experimental AI weather models, data, and documentation at no cost, subject to safeguards for national security, intellectual property, and NOAA's mission to protect lives and property.

Mandates biennial reports to Congress on program activities through 2035, along with a one-time report assessing risks from foreign access to U.S. weather data.

Authorizes appropriations of $105 million for fiscal year 2026 and $25 million annually for fiscal years 2027–2030.

Casual name: Supercritical Geothermal Research and Development Act
Short summary: Amends the Energy Independence and Security Act to incorporate machine learning in geothermal research. Establishes a supercritical geothermal research program focusing on supercritical conditions. Requires periodic updates to geothermal data repositories. Authorizes funding for research and development through 2030.
Long summary:
Amends the Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007 to include machine learning algorithms in geothermal research and development.

Establishes a supercritical geothermal research and development program within the Geothermal Technologies Office, focusing on well completion, permeability, materials, sensors, and water-rock geochemistry.

Requires the creation of a repository for geothermal data, with periodic updates for data standardization and accessibility.

Mandates a memorandum of understanding for data sharing regarding geothermal development among federal departments.

Directs the Secretary of the Interior to drill deep exploration boreholes for geothermal mapping.

Establishes a next-generation geothermal center of excellence to coordinate research, development, and workforce initiatives.

Authorizes $5 million annually from 2026 to 2030 for these activities.

Updates geothermal resource assessments quadrennially to include supercritical geothermal regions.

Requires progress reports on geothermal resource potential and commercialization barriers.

Official name: Lummis-Gillibrand Payment Stablecoin Act (Sec. 1-3)
Casual name: Lummis-Gillibrand Payment Stablecoin Act (Sec. 1-3)
Short summary: Prohibits issuing algorithmic payment stable coins. Requires registration or authorization for issuing payment stable coins in the U.S. Limits issuance by non-depository trust companies to $10 billion. Establishes safe harbors for limited issuance and foreign regulatory equivalence. Adjusts thresholds for inflation.
Long summary:
Prohibits any person from issuing, creating, or originating an algorithmic payment stablecoin in the United States.

Mandates that payment stablecoins can only be issued by a registered non-depository trust company with a limit on nominal value or an authorized depository institution as a national payment stablecoin issuer.

Prohibits the offer or sale of payment stablecoins in the United States except by a U.S. person living in the U.S.

Requires the Board to adjust the issuance threshold for inflation every four years.

Directs the Board to establish safe harbor regulations, allowing limited issuance of payment stablecoins under specific conditions and fostering innovation and competition.

Allows safe harbor status for issuers regulated by equivalent foreign authorities.

Intends the section to have extraterritorial effect, extending its reach beyond U.S. borders.

Official name: S 2142 Ground and Orbital Launched Defeat of Emergent Nuclear Destruction and Other Missile Engagements Act of 2025
Casual name: S 2142 GOLDEN DOME Act 2025
Short summary: Directs the Secretary of Defense to accelerate development and deployment of AI and machine learning for missile defense, including an information fusion platform for threat detection and early warning. Establishes a Program Manager with authority for acquisitions and integration of these technologies.
Long summary:
Directs the Secretary of Defense to accelerate the development of AI and machine learning-based platforms for detecting threats to enhance homeland defense capabilities under the "GOLDEN DOME Act of 2025."

Accelerates the use of AI in non-kinetic capabilities to counter missile and unmanned system threats.

Instructs the Secretary to integrate AI technologies for information fusion and threat awareness across various domains, including air, land, space, and maritime.

Accelerates development of AI-driven autonomous agents to defend against cruise missiles and unmanned systems.

Promotes AI applications in resilient positioning, navigation, and timing solutions and supply chain mapping.

Exploits AI for advanced sensor fusion and error correction to improve missile defense systems. 

Utilizes commercial and AI technologies to speed up testing, development, and deployment processes.  

Provides substantial funding for these initiatives, emphasizing national security and defense advancements through technological innovation.

Official name: S2381 Preventing Recurring Online Abuse of Children Through Intentional Vetting of Artificial Intelligence Data Act of 2025
Casual name: S2381 PROACTIV AI Data Act of 2025
Short summary: Require the Director of the National Institute of Standards and Technology to develop a framework for detecting, removing, and reporting child pornography in datasets for AI training. Protect AI developers and data collectors from liability if adhering to the framework.
Long summary:
Requires the Director of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to develop and publish a voluntary framework for detecting, removing, and reporting child pornography in datasets used for training artificial intelligence systems. 

Collaborates with federal agencies and organizations like the National Science Foundation and the Department of Justice in developing this framework. 

Ensures the framework provides guidelines and best practices to AI developers and data collectors, excluding deployers and users, for identifying and managing child pornography in datasets. 

Solicits input from academic, governmental, and civil organizations, while allowing public commentary on the framework.

Limits liability for AI developers and data collectors who comply with the framework, except in cases of misconduct, such as gross negligence or intentional malice.

Supports research into new methods for handling child pornography in datasets, coordinated by the National Science Foundation.

Official name: S 2600 A bill to require a Defense Science Board study on optimal organizational structure for digital solutions 2025
Casual name: S 2600 Defense Science Board Study 2025
Short summary: Directs the Secretary of Defense to have the Defense Science Board evaluate optimal organizational structures for digital solutions, including AI systems, within the Office of the Secretary of Defense and military departments. Requires recommendations by February 2027.
Long summary:
Instructs the Secretary of Defense to direct the Defense Science Board to conduct a study on the optimal organizational structure for digital solutions engineering within the Office of the Secretary of Defense and military departments.

Requires the study to assess existing structures and effectiveness, consider potential organizational courses of action, and recommend the most suitable structure for supporting digital engineering, including artificial intelligence systems.

Specifies that recommendations should address capability requirements, governance framework, unique hiring and acquisition authorities, and transition steps for implementation.

Directs the report to be submitted to the Secretary of Defense by February 1, 2027, and subsequently to congressional defense committees.

Defines "digital solutions engineering" as involving the development and sustainment of AI systems, software applications, and other digital technologies for the Department of Defense.

Official name: S 2676 Cloud Labs to Advance Biotechnology Act of 2025
Casual name: S 2676 Cloud LAB Act of 2025
Short summary: Instructs the Director of the National Science Foundation to establish a cloud laboratory network for generating and analyzing biological data using AI. Requires collaboration with other agencies, grants for cloud labs, and ensures research security and equitable access.
Long summary:
Requires the Director of the National Science Foundation to establish a cloud laboratory network program, focusing on supporting biotechnology research through remote-controlled laboratories equipped with advanced robotics.

Obligates the Director to develop an implementation plan examining existing cloud laboratories, outlining grant programs, and ensuring equitable access.

Ensures the network aids in collecting high-quality biological data for AI model training and other analyses while fostering collaboration among researchers.

Establishes an advisory board to recommend data priorities, ensure cybersecurity measures, and promote equitable access.

Directs awarding of grants for developing phase II and phase III cloud laboratories, with operational and competitive award timelines.

Mandates annual reports to Congress on the pilot program's progress.

Terminates the advisory board and the program 12 years after enactment.

Official name: S2606 A bill to require the Commander of United States Cyber Command to complete development of a roadmap for industry collaboration on artificial intelligence-enabled cyber capabilities for cyberspace operations of the Department of Defense, and for other purposes 2025
Casual name: S2606 US Cyber Command AI Industry Collaboration Roadmap 2025
Short summary: Requires the Commander of United States Cyber Command to complete a roadmap for AI-enabled cyber capabilities, coordinating with multiple defense entities. Establishes a framework for collaboration with industry, addressing security, contracting, and development. Mandates annual briefings to Congress.
Long summary:
Require the Commander of United States Cyber Command to complete a roadmap by August 1, 2026, for industry collaboration on AI-enabled cyber capabilities. 

Coordinate roadmap development with key Department of Defense (DoD) and other agency leaders.

Establish a framework for private sector and DoD coordination to integrate AI into cyberspace operations through convening AI developers and cybersecurity experts, and facilitating information exchange.

Address course management for research partnerships, collaborative development, engagement strategy, and industry contract mechanisms.

Include in the roadmap implementation milestones, technology transition methods, infrastructure costs, and organizational considerations.

Mandate that the Commander of United States Cyber Command provide an initial briefing to congressional defense committees by November 1, 2026.

Require annual updates on roadmap activities to be provided to congressional defense committees each year from FY 2028 through December 31, 2030.

Official name: CA AB 1064
Casual name: CA AB 1064 September 2025 (Leading Ethical AI Development for Kids Act)
Short summary: Establishes the LEAD for Kids Act, prohibiting companion chatbots from causing psychological harm to children. Requires operators to ensure safety guardrails to prevent self-harm encouragement from chatbots, unsolicited mental health therapy advice, illegal activity, or explicit content. Allows Attorney General and individuals to seek penalties for violations.
Long summary:
Prohibits operators from making companion chatbots available to children unless they prevent harms such as encouraging self-harm, violence, substance abuse, illegal activity, or engaging in erotic interactions.

Requires operators to ensure chatbots do not prioritize user validation over factual accuracy or safety.

Mandates that chatbots do not offer unsupervised mental health therapy or discourage professional help.

Allows the Attorney General to impose civil penalties, injunctive relief, and recover attorney’s fees for violations.

Permits children or their guardians to sue operators for actual and punitive damages, as well as attorney’s fees and injunctive relief.

Defines “companion chatbots” and sets specific criteria for their operation regarding children under 18.

Applies severability to maintain the validity of remaining provisions if any are invalidated.

Official name: Responsible AI Disclosure Act of 2024
Casual name: Responsible AI Disclosure Act of 2024
Short summary: Requires covered agencies to study and report on artificial intelligence (AI) data methodologies, assess compliance with federal laws, and recommend regulatory changes. Authorizes these agencies to mandate that regulated entities and AI vendors disclose specific information regarding model training data, design, and function.
Long summary:
Mandates a study by covered agencies to establish and recommend standards for artificial intelligence (AI) data categorization, AI model training practices, and data source identification.

Requires an assessment of AI model design, functionality, and compliance with federal laws, including anti-discrimination and consumer protection requirements.

Obligates the issuance of a report to specified congressional committees within six months of enactment, detailing the study's findings and recommending potential legislative or regulatory revisions regarding AI disclosures.

Authorizes covered agencies, following the report's issuance, to mandate AI data reporting and public or vendor-to-entity disclosures by regulated entities and vendors, specifically concerning data sources, synthetic data ratios, and model functionality.

Defines "covered agencies" as key federal financial regulatory bodies, and "regulated entities" as the specific financial institutions overseen by these respective agencies.

Casual name: Guidance on Application of the Fair Housing Act to the Advertising of Housing, Credit, and Other Real Estate-Related Transactions through Digital Platforms
Authority: Department of Housing and Urban Development
Collections: U.S. regulations, executive orders, and agency policies
Short summary: Provides guidance on how the Fair Housing Act applies to the use of AI in targeting and delivering housing-related advertisements; recommends that advertisers and ad platforms disable certain targeting features and regularly audit AI systems to reduce the risk of discriminatory outcomes.
Long summary:
Explains how the Fair Housing Act applies to housing-related advertising via AI and algorithmic systems on digital platforms, particularly by prohibiting discriminatory advertising practices based on protected characteristics such as race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, or disability.

Warns that AI-enabled audience targeting and algorithmic delivery tools can unintentionally lead to discrimination by excluding or targeting groups based on protected characteristics.

Recommends that ad platforms conduct regular audits of audience targeting tools and consider disabling custom and mirror audience functions for housing-related ads to ensure compliance with the Fair Housing Act.

Recommends that advertisers and platforms manage discriminatory risks by using separate processes and interfaces for housing-related ads and monitoring ad delivery outcomes for bias.

Advises that ad platforms document and publicly share information on ad targeting functions and internal auditing.

Official name: Federal Senate Bill of Law No. 21, of 2020
Casual name: Brazil Federal Senate Bill of Law No. 21, of 2020
Short summary: Establishes a framework of aims, foundation, and principles for AI governance in Brazil, defines guidelines for future regulations, including risk-proportionate regulation. Prioritising human rights, environmental protection, transparency, non-discrimination, competitiveness, and the balancing of innovation and self-regulation with safety requirements for high-risk systems.
Long summary:
Establishes foundations and principles for AI development and applications in Brazil and guidelines for the promotion and performance of public authorities. 

Defines AI systems as computational processes that, from goals defined by humans, can learn from data to perceive, interpret, and interact with the external environment, excluding automation solely guided by predefined parameters without learning capability.

Declares that AI implementation in Brazil is aimed at technological development, sustainable and inclusive economic development, societal well-being, competitiveness, increased participation in the value chain, improved public services, innovation, and environmental protection.

Declares that the foundations for AI development and implementation in Brazil are scientific and technological development, free enterprise and competition, human rights and democratic values, freedom of expression and communication, non-discrimination, recognition of the dynamic nature, the encouragement of self-regulation, protection of privacy, information security, national defence and sovereignty, freedom of business models, preservation of AI systems' security, stability, and functionality, free competition, and freedom from abusive market practices.

Declares that the principles for AI development and application in Brazil are beneficial purpose, human centrality, non-discrimination, neutrality, transparency, security and prevention, responsible innovation, and data availability.

Requires the Brazilian government to observe guidelines on necessity, sector context, specific risks, proportionality, evidence-based decision-making, public consultations, and regulatory impact analysis, as well as subjective liability rules when regulating the implementation of AI.

Establishing a tiering of the risk-based management guidelines, encouraging flexible regulatory techniques and responsible innovation in low-risk AI, and granting legal government power to inquire into high-risk AI's security and prevention, and mandating liability for AI-harm in consumer relations and for public service providing legal entities.

Established guidelines for the Brazilian government's performance regarding the usage and promotion of AI, including promotion of trust in AI, investment in research and development, promotion of interoperability, incentives for adoption, incentives for job market restructuring, educational innovation, stimulus for innovation-promoting regulation, stimulus for multi-stakeholder governance collaboration, promotion of international cooperation, as well as transparency and ethical usage. 

Mandates sectoral bodies and entities to apply the law and to monitor AI risk management, establish rights, duties, and responsibilities, and recognize self-regulatory institutions.

Grants exclusive authority to the federal Union for legislating on AI

Official name: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence Part 1: Digital Replicas July 2024
Casual name: Copyright Office Part 1 Digital Replicas 2024
Short summary: Recommends Congress establish a federal right to protect individuals from unauthorized digital replicas, make the right licensable but not assignable with civil remedies, apply secondary liability with conditioned safe harbor for OSPs, include First Amendment accommodations, avoid full preemption of state publicity rights, and rely on the Copyright Office as a resource for Congress and other branches in considering these recommendations and future developments
Long summary:
Recommends that Congress establish a federal right to protect individuals from the distribution of unauthorized digital replicas during their lifetimes. 

Proposes that this right be licensable and subject to guardrails but not assignable, with remedies such as monetary damages and injunctive relief available. 

Recommends applying traditional rules of secondary liability, with a safe harbor for online service providers suitably conditioned.

Suggests explicit First Amendment accommodations in the law.

Advises against full preemption of state laws, recognizing well-developed state rights of publicity. 

Offers the Copyright Office as a resource for Congress, the courts, and the executive branch in implementing these recommendations and addressing future developments.

Official name: Measures for Labeling of AI-Generated Synthetic Content
Casual name: Measures for Labeling of AI-Generated Synthetic Content
Short summary: Requires clear labeling of AI-generated synthetic content in China through both explicit user-facing indicators and implicit metadata, mandates service providers and platforms to verify, disclose, and preserve such labels, and ensures compliance through regulatory oversight.
Long summary:
Requires online information service providers to label AI-generated synthetic content with both explicit and implicit labels, ensuring that users can easily recognize AI-generated content.

Mandates explicit, user-visible labeling on text, image, audio, video, and virtual scene content, and requires that such labels remain when content is downloaded, reproduced, or exported.

Instructs service providers to embed implicit labels in digital file metadata, indicating the content’s origin and attributes, and encourages the use of digital watermarks.

Mandates content transmission platforms to verify metadata for implicit labels and add notifications if AI-origin is detected or suspected.

Obligates application distribution platforms to assess apps for compliance with generative AI services and labeling.

Requires service providers to include labeling methods and specifications in user agreements.

Permits exceptions for omitting explicit labels if users assume responsibility, with logs stored for a period of six months.

Requires service providers to comply with relevant laws, administrative regulations, and national standards, and to provide labeling materials during algorithm filings and safety assessments to help prevent illegal or criminal misuse.

Sets penalties for non-compliance to be enforced by the relevant regulatory authorities.

Casual name: Illinois SB2203 (Preventing Algorithmic Discrimination Act)
Short summary: Prohibits AI system deployers in Illinois from causing  or using systems that result in algorithmic discrimination against individuals or groups of individuals. Requires annual impact assessments and governance programs to manage AI risks.
Long summary:
Enacts the Preventing Algorithmic Discrimination Act in Illinois to combat discrimination by automated decision tools. 

Defines "algorithmic discrimination" as resulting from AI tool usage that causes discrimination against protected classes.

Requires deployers to perform annual impact assessments on automated tools by January 2027, analyzing potential biases and preventing discrimination. 

Mandates notifications to individuals affected by AI decisions, with options for alternative processes. 

Requires an alternative process for those that request AI tools not be used in a decision.

Obliges deployers to establish comprehensive governance programs to manage discrimination risks, requiring technical safeguards and annual compliance reviews. 

Mandates public availability of policies on AI tool usage and discrimination management. 

Prohibits use of tools resulting in algorithmic discrimination, with civil actions allowed from January 2028 for violations, including compensatory damages and legal fees. 

Obliges deployers to submit impact assessments to the Attorney General, with fines for non-compliance. 

Integrates enforcement with the Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices Act.

Short summary: Establishes a "Cross-Functional Team" led by the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Officer for artificial intelligence (AI) model assessment in the Department of Defense (DOD). Mandates designation of functional leads for AI applications in DOD. Requires assessment of major AI systems by 2028, followed by a congressional briefing and ends the team by 2030.
Long summary:

Requires the Team to create a standardized assessment framework comprising performance standards, testing procedures etc, and governance structure for AI models used by the Department. Duties also include developing guidelines, assessment levels based on risk, and collaboration mechanisms for AI models.

Mandates inclusion of representatives from various defense branches and commands to ensure comprehensive oversight.

Instructs the Secretary of Defense to designate functional leads for AI applications, taking into account expertise and capability to set standards.

Obligates the assessment of all major AI systems using this framework by specific deadlines.

Specifies the termination of the Cross-Functional Team by December 31, 2030, with a transition plan to a successor entity within the Department.

Requires periodic congressional briefings on progress and activities related to these initiatives, and reports by Secretary of Defense after the termination.

Define "covered artificial intelligence" as AI developed by Chinese company DeepSeek or High Flyer and entities associated with High Flyer.

Classify entities on specific lists or subject to foreign influence as "covered artificial intelligence companies."

Specify the meaning of "artificial intelligence" by referencing existing federal definitions.

Casual name: USDA Framework for State, Local, Tribal, and Territorial Use of Artificial Intelligence for Public Benefit Administration
Collections: U.S. regulations, executive orders, and agency policies
Short summary: Outlines USDA's approach to supporting state, local, tribal, and territorial agencies in responsibly using AI to administer USDA nutrition benefits, ensuring that such uses of AI protect rights and safety, advance equity, uphold USDA accountability, and advance responsible innovation.
Long summary:
Outlines how USDA's Food and Nutrition Service (FNS) will work with state, local, tribal, and territorial agencies (SLTT) to ensure that AI used to administer USDA nutrition benefits is deployed responsibly.

Prioritizes protection of civil rights and safety, establishing FNS notification and approval requirements for uses of AI that impact rights or safety.

Requires SLTT agencies to assess and mitigate factors that contribute AI bias, discrimination, and inequitable outcomes; stipulates that this assessment should include consultation with civil rights offices and affected groups.

Requires SLTT agencies to provide opt-out options for public-facing AI systems.

Advocates for transparency and accountability, requiring SLTT agencies to notify the public when AI is being used and provide channels for reporting inaccurate information or adverse actions taken by AI systems.

Stresses human oversight, requiring SLTT agencies to ensure that staff who conduct oversight of AI functions are sufficiently trained and have the authority to override inaccurate decisions.

Prohibits AI from making adverse decisions in benefits administration without human validation.

Encourages responsible innovation, requiring SLTT agencies to identify reliability thresholds before deploying AI and to monitor whether these thresholds are met before, during, and after implementation.

Directs SLTT agencies to use representative training datasets, follow privacy and security best practices to protect data, and collaborate with tribes on data sovereignty.

Requires FNS programs to establish AI governance processes aligned with this framework.

Official name: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026, Section 3117 ("Appropriate scoping of artificial intelligence research within the National Nuclear Security Administration")
Casual name: FY2026 NDAA, Section 3117 ("Appropriate scoping of artificial intelligence research within the National Nuclear Security Administration")
Short summary: Limits funding for AI research within the National Nuclear Security Administration to nuclear security missions. Allows AI research programs elsewhere within the Department of Energy or other Federal agencies, provided it doesn't interfere with nuclear security missions or facilities.
Long summary:
Amends the Atomic Energy Defense Act to specify that funds appropriated for AI research and development by the National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) can only support the Administration's nuclear security missions.

States that this funding limitation does not prohibit the establishment of national security AI research programs within other areas of the Department of Energy or other federal agencies.

Allows the use of NNSA resources for an enduring national security AI program by external entities, provided support is given on a full cost recovery basis and does not interfere with the nuclear security missions of involved facilities.

Official name: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026, Section 1534 ("Digital sandbox environments for artificial intelligence")
Casual name: FY2026 NDAA, Section 1534 ("Digital sandbox environments for artificial intelligence")
Short summary: Requires the Secretary of Defense, via the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Officer, to establish an AI sandbox task force by April 2026 to facilitate AI experimentation and deployment. Identifies members and duties, with termination by January 2030.
Long summary:
Establishes a Task Force on artificial intelligence sandbox environments by April 1, 2026, under the Secretary of Defense through the Chief Digital and AI Officer.

Tasks the Task Force to develop and deploy AI sandbox environments for experimentation, training, and deployment across the Department of Defense.

Requires AI sandbox environments to be designed for use by personnel with varying technical proficiencies, facilitate familiarization with AI capabilities, and accelerate responsible AI adoption.

Chairs the Task Force with the Chief Digital and AI Officer and includes key officials from the Department of Defense, military departments, and combatant commands.

Requires the Task Force to standardize AI sandbox requirements across the Department of Defense, catalog and align existing solutions, improve efficiency and approvals, and provide clear guidance and resources to support users of all technical skill levels.

Requires a briefing to congressional defense committees by August 1, 2026.

Terminates the Task Force on January 1, 2030.

Defines key terms including "artificial intelligence" and "artificial intelligence sandbox environment."

Long summary:
Encourages the Secretaries of Defense, Army, Navy, and Air Force to use AI and machine learning technologies to facilitate audits of the Department of Defense's financial statements for fiscal year 2026.

Oversees the Director of the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office, in coordination with the Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering and the Inspector General, in adopting AI and machine learning technologies to support financial management and enterprise business operations.

Official name: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026, Section 547 ("Pilot program for generative artificial intelligence and spatial computing for performance training and proficiency assessment")
Casual name: FY2026 NDAA, Section 547 ("Pilot program for generative artificial intelligence and spatial computing for performance training and proficiency assessment")
Short summary: Instructs the Secretary of the Navy to develop a pilot program for generative AI and spatial computing in training. Requires assessment of feasibility compared to other methods. Directs a report on program results 90 days post-termination.
Long summary:
Instructs the Secretary of the Navy to develop and implement a pilot program using generative AI and spatial computing for immersive training and proficiency assessment within 90 days of enactment.

Requires the program to develop content for at least five occupational specialties and compare the feasibility and effectiveness of these methods with traditional training, especially regarding cost and time efficiency.

Terminates the program one year after the date of establishment.

Requires the Secretary of the Navy to submit a report to congressional defense committees within 90 days after program termination, detailing program results, effectiveness analysis, and any cost or time savings achieved.

Short summary: Facilitates integration of commercial AI for logistics into two Department of Defense exercises in 2026. Directs the Secretary of Defense to brief Congress on exercise specifics and AI integration impact on readiness and operations.
Long summary:
Facilitates the integration of commercially available AI capabilities into logistics operations of the Department of Defense (DoD) during fiscal year 2026 exercises.

Requires the Secretary of Defense to identify and choose AI products designed for logistics that comply with DoD data security protocols.

Ensures the selected AI products can adapt to software changes rapidly and prioritizes products from small or nontraditional firms.

Expedites approvals for secure data use and ensures compliance with DoD cybersecurity policies for these exercises.

Mandates an interim briefing by March 1, 2026, detailing the exercises, participating commanders, AI capabilities used, timelines, resource needs, and assessment metrics.

Requires a post-exercise briefing by the commander on the integration, effectiveness, and recommendations for further AI development in DoD operations.

Casual name: Leading Ethical AI Development (LEAD) for Kids Act April 2025
