Official name: Modernizing Wildfire Safety and Prevention Act of 2024, Section 405 ("Joint Office of the Fire Environment Center (Report Recommendations 104, 105, 106)")
Casual name: Modernizing Wildfire Safety and Prevention Act of 2024, Section 405 ("Joint Office of the Fire Environment Center (Report Recommendations 104, 105, 106)")
Short summary: Establishes a Joint Office to test AI/ML for fire management, supporting risk modeling and resource allocation. Requires collaboration with local entities and data sharing. Ensures development of decision support tools and air quality monitoring, with a $150 million annual budget.
Long summary:
Establishes the Joint Office of the Fire Environment Center within one year, under the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

Requires the Data Services branch to test AI and machine learning technologies to aid fire management, suggesting resources based on real-time fire conditions.

Mandates the provision of science-based, data-rich services for fire management, including predictive and decision-support tools.

Develops a technological common operating environment to integrate air quality data and other public health information.

Forms a 12-member board governing the Joint Office, including federal and non-federal wildfire community representatives.

Empowers the Joint Office to contract with government and private entities for necessary supplies and services.

Authorizes $150 million annually from fiscal years 2025 to 2034 for the Joint Office's operations.

Official name: NO FAKES Act of 2024
Casual name: NO FAKES Act of 2024
Short summary: Establishes rights for individuals over digital replicas of their voice or likeness, requiring consent for creation and use. Imposes liability for unauthorized replication. Provides safe harbors for online services complying with takedown notices. Limits preemption of existing state laws.
Long summary:
Establishes the right for individuals to authorize the use of their voice or visual likeness in digital replicas, treating it as a property right that is licensable but not assignable during the individual's life.

Allows post-mortem transfer and licensing, enabling rights to be inherited and renewed under specific conditions.  

Imposes civil liability for the knowing unauthorized production, distribution, or public display of digital replicas, with specific exclusions for news, historical, parody, and public interest uses.  

Provides notice-and-takedown safe harbors for online services that promptly remove unauthorized replicas, provided they register a designated agent.  

Classifies the right as intellectual property to exempt it from Section 230 platform immunity, and preempts conflicting state laws except those addressing sexually explicit or election-related deepfakes.

Applies liability only to conduct and contracts occurring after the enactment date, while granting the replication right retroactively to deceased individuals' estates.

Official name: A bill to establish protections for individual rights with respect to computational algorithms, and for other purposes.
Casual name: Artificial Intelligence Civil Rights Act of 2024
Short summary: Prohibits discriminatory use of AI algorithms and mandates pre- and post-deployment evaluations. Requires transparency in algorithm use. Enforces compliance through Federal Trade Commission oversight, state actions, and private lawsuits. Establishes resources for algorithm auditing and consumer awareness initiatives.
Long summary:
Prohibits developers and deployers of AI algorithms from causing or contributing to discrimination based on protected characteristics.

Mandates developers and deployers to conduct pre-deployment evaluations and annual impact assessments of AI algorithms to identify potential harms or disparate impacts.

Requires independent audits of AI algorithms and obligates developers to provide relevant information to deployers for compliance.

Imposes transparency obligations, including public disclosures of AI practices and consumer rights, in multiple languages and accessible formats.

Grants the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) enforcement authority, including rulemaking, with violations treated as unfair or deceptive acts.

Provides a private right of action for individuals, enabling lawsuits for violations and barring pre-dispute arbitration agreements.

Establishes federal resources for algorithm auditing, including a new occupational series and additional personnel for the FTC to handle AI-related issues.

Official name: Massachusetts House Docket 4053 (2025)
Casual name: Massachusetts HD 4053 (protecting consumers in interactions with AI systems)
Short summary: Establishes consumer protections against AI-induced discrimination. Requires developers and deployers of high-risk AI systems to document, assess, and mitigate algorithmic discrimination risks, and mandates notification to consumers about AI-influenced decisions.
Long summary:
Amends state law to introduce Chapter 93M, mandating consumer protections in interactions with artificial intelligence (AI) systems.

Requires developers and deployers of high-risk AI systems to use reasonable care to prevent algorithmic discrimination and disclose foreseeable risks.

Defines "high-risk AI systems" as those influencing consequential decisions in areas like education, employment, and healthcare.

Mandates developers to provide detailed documentation about AI system data usage, limitations, and discrimination mitigation measures.

Obligates deployers to establish risk management policies aligned with recognized standards, and perform annual impact assessments.

Demands transparency from deployers by notifying consumers before consequential decisions are made using high-risk AI systems, and offering appeal opportunities for adverse decisions.

Empowers the attorney general with exclusive enforcement authority, classifying violations as unfair trade practices.

Allows attorney general to create rules for implementing these requirements, ensuring alignment with national standards.

Official name: JSP 936 V1.1 Dependable Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Defence (part 1: directive)
Casual name: JSP 936 V1.1 Dependable Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Defence (UK MoD)
Short summary: Requires the Ministry of Defense’s development and use of AI to be governed by national and international law and to align with the principles of human centricity, responsibility, understanding, bias and harm mitigation, and reliability; provides guidance on AI ethics governance, AI lifecycle agnostic requirements, quality, safety, and security, and AI assurance.
Long summary:
Explains the Ministry of Defense’s adopted definition of AI, the scope of the document, and the delegation of responsibilities for TLB Holders and Chief Executives, and requires the JSP to be applied by all MOD staff in all phases of the AI lifecycle.

Requires the MOD’s development and use of AI to be governed by national and international law and to align with the principles of human centricity, responsibility, understanding, bias and harm mitigation, and reliability. 

Provides requirements related to AI ethics governance, including that each TLB appoint a RAISO and that large AI projects with significant ethical risks have an ethics manager and an independent ethics assurance mechanism.

Addresses the teaming of humans with AI by mandating the adoption of a Human Centered Design approach across AI systems’ lifecycles, encouraging the identification of AI systems’ workforce implications, and providing guidance on the training implications of AI.

Explains AI development and use lifecycle concepts, such as DevOps, and provides guidance on lifecycle agnostic requirements, including those related to planning, data collection and control, and AI verification and validation.

Requires safety risk analysis, security risk analysis, and other measures to ensure  requirements related to AI quality, safety, and security. 

Obliges AI suppliers to deliver products at a level of confidence that is commensurate with their use, and provides guidance on AI assurance.

Official name: Delaware House Bill 333
Casual name: Delaware  H 333  (Artificial Intelligence Commission )
Short summary: Establishes the Delaware AI Commission to recommend AI-related legislative and executive actions, develop guidelines, encourage AI use in agencies, and ensure AI safety and rights compliance. Requires an annual report and conducts a Generative AI inventory. Expires in 10 years.
Long summary:
Establishes the Delaware Artificial Intelligence (AI) Commission to make legislative and executive recommendations on AI.

Mandates the development of statewide AI processes, principles, and guidelines for government agencies.

Encourages the use of AI in agencies to improve service delivery and ensures AI usage does not violate individual rights.

Requires an inventory of Generative AI use within state agencies to identify high-risk areas.

Comprises a 19-member commission, with appointments from state officials, academia, and the private sector.

Requires the commission to submit an annual report on activities, goals, and policy recommendations.

Places the commission within the Department of Technology and Information, with staffing support from the Chief Information Officer.

Sets an expiration of the Act 10 years after enactment unless extended by the General Assembly.

Official name: H.R. 3447 Chip Security Act
Casual name: Chip Security Act 2025
Short summary: Requires the Secretary of Commerce to mandate chip security mechanisms for location verification before exporting integrated circuit products. Obligates reporting of tampering or diversion. Mandates the assessment and development of additional security mechanisms, considering national security and export compliance objectives.
Long summary:
Mandates the Secretary of Commerce to issue standards for chip security mechanisms on integrated circuit products within 180 days of the Act's enactment.

Requires covered integrated circuit products to be outfitted with location verification chip security mechanisms before export, reexport, or in-country transfer within 180 days of enactment.

Obligates exporters to report any unauthorized change in product location, user, or tampering incidents to the Under Secretary of Industry and Security.

Calls for an assessment within one year to identify additional security mechanisms needed to enhance Export Control Reform Act compliance and prevent unauthorized use.

Directs the Secretary to develop secondary security requirements based on assessment findings and report to Congress with a roadmap for implementation.

Authorizes the Secretary to verify ownership and location of exported products and maintain records of product locations and current end-users, requiring license holders to provide necessary information.

Requires annual assessments of new chip security mechanisms and recommends export control modifications to expand permissible destinations for secure products.

Official name: TAME Extreme Weather Act
Casual name: TAME Extreme Weather Act
Short summary: Mandates the use of AI by Federal agencies to improve weather forecasts, grid resilience, and resource deployment for extreme weather. Orders the development of AI weather models, enhanced emissions monitoring, and a fire modeling program.
Long summary:
Mandates federal agencies to use AI to adapt to extreme weather, improving weather forecasts, electrical grid resilience, resource deployment, and public-private partnerships.

Requires National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration to develop and curate an Earth system reanalysis dataset, build on existing datasets, and develop AI weather models.

Directs NOAA to explore advanced AI applications for weather forecasting, including data assimilation and model emulation.

Tasks NOAA with providing technical assistance on AI weather models and developing best practices and public datasets.

Establishes programs using AI for wildfire detection, emissions monitoring, and illegal wood product tracking, requiring dataset curation and public access to AI code and data.

Instructs the Department of Energy to optimize energy grids using AI, develop environmental review documents, and ensure public access to AI models and training datasets.

Includes provisions to exclude public access to models, training datasets, or related systems for national security purposes.

Official name: Artificial Intelligence Risk Evaluation Act of 2025
Casual name: Artificial Intelligence Risk Evaluation Act of 2025
Short summary: Requires the Secretary of Energy to establish the Advanced Artificial Intelligence Evaluation Program within 90 days. The program is required to offer standardized and classified testing of AI systems for likelihood of incidents.
Long summary:
Requires the Secretary of Energy to establish the Advanced Artificial Intelligence Evaluation Program to evaluate advanced AI systems using standardized testing protocols. Requires the implementation of testing protocols that match or exceed real-world AI Jailbreaking techniques. 

Mandates that each artificial intelligence system developer shall participate in the program and provide to the Secretary any relevant materials and informations to carry out the program. 

The above materials may include the underlying code of the advanced artificial intelligence system, data used to train the system, model weights or other parameters, the interface engine, or any kind of detailed information regarding the training. Any penalties for the obligation to participate will be fined no less than $1,000,00 per day.

Instructs the program to offer standardized testing and evaluation of advanced AI systems. Implements testing including adversarial testing by red teams with expertise to malicious actors. 

Obligates the Secretary to submit to Congress a detailed report of the recommendation, drawing directly from empirical data, insights, and lessons learned from the program..

Sets a program termination date 7 years post-enactment unless Congress renews it.

Casual name: FY2026 NDAA, Section 1515 ("Incorporation of artificial intelligence considerations into cybersecurity training")
Short summary: Requires the Secretary of Defense, via the Chief Information Officer, to revise cybersecurity training for Armed Forces and civilian employees to include AI-related cybersecurity challenges within one year of the Act’s enactment.
Long summary:
Requires the Secretary of Defense, through the Department of Defense's Chief Information Officer, to revise mandatory cybersecurity training.

Includes content addressing unique cybersecurity challenges posed by artificial intelligence.

Sets a deadline of one year from the enactment date of this Act for these revisions to be implemented.

Applies to both members of the Armed Forces and civilian employees within the Department of Defense.

Official name: California SB 53
Casual name: California SB 53 March 2025 (CalCompute and Whistleblowers)
Collections: Editors' Picks;U.S. state and local documents
Short summary: Establishes a consortium to create "CalCompute," advancing AI in a responsible, equitable manner. Prohibits developers from retaliating against whistleblowers who disclose AI risks. Requires developers to notify employees of their rights, offering whistleblowing avenues and legal protections against retaliation.
Long summary:
Establishes a consortium to create CalCompute, a public cloud computing framework promoting safe and ethical AI.

Mandates CalCompute to foster research benefiting the public and expanding access to computational resources.

Obligates submission of a report by January 1, 2027, detailing CalCompute's framework, including infrastructure analysis, costs, governance, and workforce recommendations.

Introduces whistleblower protections for employees disclosing critical AI risks, including practices leading to severe harm, damage, or misinformation.

Mandates developers to establish anonymous internal reporting processes and ensures responsive investigation.

Authorizes courts to grant attorney’s fees, shift burdens of proof to developers, and issue injunctive relief in whistleblower cases, prioritizing employee protections.

Official name: California AB 979 (California Cybersecurity Integration Center: artificial intelligence)
Casual name: California AB 979 (California Cybersecurity Integration Center: AI)
Short summary: Establishes the California AI Cybersecurity Collaboration Playbook by January 1, 2027, to enhance cybersecurity through information sharing on AI threats. Requires state protection of sensitive information, with mandatory and voluntary participation mechanisms, while safeguarding individual privacy and business confidentiality.
Long summary:
Instructs the California Office of Emergency Services to develop a California AI Cybersecurity Collaboration Playbook by January 1, 2027, to enhance information sharing and bolster defenses against AI-related cyber threats.

Requires review of federal standards and best practices, including the Joint Cyber Defense Collaborative AI Cybersecurity Collaboration Playbook, to inform California's playbook.

Mandates that the playbook include mechanisms for mandatory information sharing on AI threats and vulnerabilities by state contractors, and allows voluntary sharing by other entities.

Prohibits public disclosure of sensitive information related to cyber threats or AI vulnerabilities, ensuring confidentiality and compliance with security requirements.

Defines the California Cybersecurity Integration Center as the central hub for state cybersecurity activities, coordinating with various governmental and private entities to reduce cyber incident impacts.

Asserts strong state interest in protecting IT systems due to their critical role and need for confidentiality to prevent system attacks.

Official name: TTC Joint Roadmap on Evaluation and Measurement Tools for Trustworthy AI and Risk Management
Casual name: TTC Joint Roadmap on Evaluation and Measurement Tools for Trustworthy AI and Risk Management
Short summary: Proposes a joint U.S.-EU roadmap to advance shared AI terminology and taxonomies, cooperate on international technical standards, build a shared repository of trustworthy AI metrics and tools, and develop mechanisms for tracking and evaluating existing and emerging AI risks, with short- and long-term implementation steps organized around three expert working groups.
Long summary:
Outlines a U.S.-EU Joint Roadmap to advance trustworthy AI and risk management through three workstreams: shared terminology, international standards cooperation, and risk monitoring.

Encourages risk-based approaches, aligning existing EU and U.S. methodologies, including the EU AI Act and the U.S. AI Bill of Rights. 

Calls for the development of shared terminologies and taxonomies for key AI risk concepts, drawing on existing work from U.S., EU, and international standards-setting bodies.

Advocates for U.S.-EU leadership in international AI standards development, emphasizing transparency, inclusiveness, and multi-stakeholder participation.

Proposes a publicly accessible shared repository of metrics and methodologies for measuring AI trustworthiness and risk, and calls for studies to characterize the existing landscape of trustworthy AI tools.

Suggests the creation of a continuously updated tracker of existing and emerging AI risks based on use cases, incident data, and empirical harms.

Calls for the development of interoperable tests and evaluations of frontier AI systems to measure trustworthiness.

Calls for the creation of three expert working groups on terminology, standards, and risk monitoring, with dedicated work plans and stakeholder consultation processes to advance short- and long-term objectives.

Official name: Colorado HB 1263 (Conversational Artificial Intelligence Service Operator Requirements)
Casual name: Colorado HB 1263 (Conversational AI Service Operator Requirements)
Short summary: Defines "conversational artificial intelligence service" and requires operators to disclose AI use to minors and prohibit harmful content. Imposes annual reporting to the Attorney General on crisis response protocols. Prohibits false professional endorsements and provides consumer transparency guidelines from January 1, 2027.
Long summary:
Defines "conversational artificial intelligence service" as AI systems simulating human conversation, excluding certain applications like developer tools and voice assistants.

Requires operators of these AI services to use methods to identify minor users and disclose interactions' artificial nature starting January 1, 2027.

Prohibits rewards that increase minors' engagement with AI services and mandates measures to prevent AI from generating explicit, emotional, or harmful content for minors.

Instructs operators to implement protocols responding to self-harm or suicidal prompts by directing users to crisis services, excluding law enforcement.

Bans any representation of AI outputs as endorsed by licensed professionals.

Mandates annual reports from operators on crisis notifications and protocol efficacy submitted to the Attorney General's Office from July 1, 2027.

Ensures protection of confidential information and prohibits inconsistency with constitutional rights.

Official name: Colorado SB 25-288 (Intimate Digital Depictions Criminal & Civil Actions)
Casual name: Colorado SB 25-288 (Intimate Digital Depictions Criminal & Civil Actions)
Short summary: Prohibits unauthorized disclosure of intimate digital depictions created using generative AI. Allows civil action for those harmed by unauthorized disclosures. Defines responsibilities and exemptions for technology providers and broadcasters. Extends legal protections to depicted individuals' privacy and authorship rights.
Long summary:
Incorporates the "Preventing Unauthorized Disclosure of Intimate Digital Depictions Act," establishing civil causes of action for unauthorized disclosure of AI-generated intimate depictions if harm results.

Defines "generative AI" as AI used for creating content, emphasizing its legal significance.

Exempts certain disclosures made in good faith for public interest, law enforcement, or legal purposes.

Excludes liability for interactive computer services and media platforms under specific conditions.

Amends laws regarding the exploitation of minors, explicitly criminalizing AI-generated exploitative material involving minors.

Addresses juvenile offenses involving AI-modified intimate images, incorporating educational programs and diversion.

Allows plaintiffs in civil actions to use pseudonyms for privacy protection.

Empowers the Attorney General to implement rules for the Act's enforcement.

Ensures alignment with the federal "Communications Decency Act."

Establishes significant damages and legal costs as potential remedies for victims.

Official name: Colorado SB 25-318 (Artificial Intelligence Consumer Protections)
Casual name: Colorado SB 25-318 (AI Consumer Protections)
Short summary: Regulates high-risk AI systems in Colorado, defining "algorithmic discrimination" and requiring developers and deployers to mitigate risks, provide disclosures, and conduct impact assessments. Authorizes the attorney general to enforce these provisions and adopt necessary rules.
Long summary:
Defines algorithmic discrimination as AI use violating anti-discrimination laws, including the Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act and major federal acts.

Requires developers of high-risk AI systems to provide detailed documentation, including intended uses and risks, to deployers by 2027.

Obligates deployers to implement risk management policies and conduct annual impact assessments for high-risk AI systems starting 2027 to mitigate algorithmic discrimination risks.

Mandates deployers to disclose to consumers the use and impact of high-risk AI systems when making consequential decisions, ensuring transparency and providing an appeals process.

Empowers the attorney general to enforce compliance, investigate violations, and potentially adopt rules for implementing the statute.

Exempts certain small developers and deployers from specific obligations and outlines conditions under which information may be withheld.

Does not apply to certain AI systems acquired by federal agencies or those necessary to comply with federal law.

Official name: California SCR 82 (Relative to Artificial Intelligence in Public Higher Education 2025)
Casual name: California SCR 82 (Relative to AI in Public Higher Education 2025)
Short summary: Encourages the University of California's President and California State University's and Community Colleges' Chancellors to form a workgroup. Reviews AI use in academics, ensuring ethical standards. Involves faculty, staff, students, and AI experts in strategy discussions and reporting findings.
Long summary:
Encourages the President of the University of California, the Chancellor of the California State University, and the Chancellor of the California Community Colleges to create a workgroup comprising faculty, staff, and administrators to evaluate the use of artificial intelligence in higher education.

Directs the workgroup to discuss strategies and best practices for the acceptable use of AI, emphasizing academic honesty, ethical standards, and the mitigation of plagiarism.

Advises the workgroup to focus on AI's role in student academic support and faculty professional development.

Recommends collaboration with faculty, students, external higher education experts, and associated student bodies for insights.

Suggests the workgroup develop a report detailing their agreed-upon strategies and practices for AI use in academics.

Instructs the Secretary of the Senate to distribute this resolution to relevant academic senate chairs and the author.

Official name: Content Origin Protection and Integrity from Edited and Deepfaked Media Act of 2024
Casual name: Content Origin Protection and Integrity from Edited and Deepfaked Media Act of 2024
Short summary: Requires transparency in AI-generated content, mandates development of standards for content provenance, and prohibits tampering with provenance information. Enforces compliance through FTC and state actions. Penalizes unauthorized AI training using non-consensual content. Establishes public-private partnerships for developing standards.
Long summary:
Mandates the development of standards for content provenance and detection of synthetic and synthetically-modified content through a public-private partnership.

Requires tools used commercially to create synthetic or synthetically-modified content to provide the option of including machine-readable content provenance information, with security measures to prevent tampering.

Prohibits knowingly removing or altering content provenance information in furtherance of unfair or deceptive acts.

Prohibits the non-consensual use of content with attached provenance information for training AI systems, requiring express consent and adherence to copyright terms.

Empowers the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and state attorneys general to enforce the Act, treating violations as unfair or deceptive acts.

Permits private parties to bring civil actions for violations involving content provenance information.

Ensures the Act does not alter existing copyright rights and includes provisions for severability, maintaining the Act’s effectiveness even if parts are invalidated.

Official name: Massachusetts House Bill 4885
Casual name: Massachusetts H 4885 (Firearm Laws), Section 148
Short summary: Establishes a special legislative commission to investigate emerging firearm technologies, including the risks and impacts of using digital firearm manufacturing code for machine learning and AI. Requires a report with findings and recommendations by March 1, 2025.
Long summary:
Establishes a special legislative commission to study emerging firearm technology, including personalized and microstamp technologies.

Requires the commission to evaluate the risks associated with using digital firearm manufacturing codes for machine learning and artificial intelligence.

Mandates the investigation of the accuracy, effectiveness, and utility of personalized firearm and microstamp technologies.

Instructs the commission to review any legal or constitutional issues relating to these technologies.

Tasks the commission with evaluating the commercial availability of these technologies for new and existing firearms.

Directs the commission to assess the feasibility and utility of a tax incentive program for personalized firearm technology.

Obliges the commission to submit its study and recommendations, including legislative suggestions, by March 1, 2025.

Official name: New York 2025-A768
Casual name: New York 2025-A768 (NY AI Consumer Protection Act)
Short summary: Establishes AI consumer protection with documentation, audits, and risk management requirements for high-risk AI decision systems. Mandates developer disclosures, consumer notifications, and opportunities to contest AI-based decisions.
Long summary:
Enacts the New York Artificial Intelligence Consumer Protection Act to manage risks of  AI decision systems. 

Requires developers to ensure systems do not cause algorithmic discrimination through regular bias and governance audits conducted by independent third parties retained by developers and deployers. 

Obligates deployers to notify consumers when high-risk AI systems make significant decisions that affect them and to provide explanations and recourse for adverse decisions. 

Imposes a risk management program for deployers to identify and mitigate potential discrimination. 

Grants the Attorney General exclusive enforcement authority to investigate compliance and bring actions for violations. 

Establishes a red-teaming affirmative defense, allowing developers and deployers who discover violations to avoid liability if such violations are cured within 60 days and the Attorney General is notified. 

Establishes exceptions for preempting federal law compliance and protects trade secrets from disclosure.

Official name: Anthropic Responsible Scaling Policy
Casual name: Anthropic Responsible Scaling Policy
Short summary: Establishes AI Safety Level Standards (ASLs) for AI model testing, deployment and security. Requires ASL-2 standards for current models, with ASL-3 for higher-risk capabilities like Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) weapon development or autonomous R&D. Implements Capability Thresholds to trigger safeguard upgrades. Outlines regular assessments, reviews, and transparency requirements.
Long summary:
Establishes AI Safety Level (ASL) Standards to guide safe deployment and security for current and future AI models, categorizing measures into Deployment and Security Standards.

Requires all current models to meet ASL-2 standards, focusing on safe usage and protection from unauthorized access.

Introduces Capability Thresholds to determine when stronger safeguards (ASL-3 or higher) are needed, specifying Required Safeguards for particular risks including Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) capabilities and Autonomous AI R&D.

Mandates comprehensive assessments to ensure models remain below Capability Thresholds, with stricter ASL-3 standards implemented if thresholds are surpassed.

Outlines internal governance practices including a Responsible Scaling Officer role, transparency measures, and procedures for noncompliance whistleblowing.

Commits to public transparency, expert input, and notifying US Government if standards beyond ASL-2 are needed.

Official name: OpenAI Preparedness Framework (Beta)
Casual name: OpenAI Preparedness Framework (Beta)
Short summary: Introduces OpenAI's Preparedness Framework to track, evaluate, forecast, and mitigate catastrophic AI risks. Establishes processes for risk evaluation, unknown risk identification, safety baselines, and cross-functional advisory. Limits model deployment or development based on risk levels. Forms a dedicated Preparedness team and Safety Advisory Group to oversee safety measures and decision-making.
Long summary:
Commits to continually evaluating and forecasting key areas of risk along several Tracked Risk Categories and indicating current pre- and post-mitigation risk in a Scorecard.

Commits to establishing safety baselines where only models with a post-mitigation score of "medium" or below can be deployed and only models with a post-mitigation score of "high" or below can be developed further.

Announces creation of a Safety Advisory Group to assist OpenAI leadership and Board of Directors with making safety decisions by overseeing risk assessments and handling emergency scenarios via fast-track process.

Tasks Preparedness team with conducting research, evaluations, and forecasting of risks, submitting regular reports to the Safety Advisory Group, coordinating with other OpenAI teams on recommended mitigations, and managing safety drills and third-party auditing.

Official name: California SB 384 (Preventing Algorithmic Price Fixing Act: Prohibition on Certain Price-Setting Algorithm Uses 2025)
Casual name: California SB 384 (Preventing Algorithmic Price Fixing Act 2025)
Short summary: Prohibits the use, sale, or licensing of price-setting algorithms processing nonpublic data if intended for competitors in the same market. Assigns enforcement to the Attorney General and others, allowing penalties per violation. Defines 'artificial intelligence' for regulatory purposes.
Long summary:
Prohibits individuals from selling, licensing, providing, or using a price-setting algorithm intended for use by competitors in the same market if nonpublic input data is used to set prices, supply levels, rents, or occupancy levels.

Permits an affirmative defense for users who show reasonable due diligence, such as obtaining written assurances that the algorithm does not process nonpublic input data.

Specifies that each user and each month of a violating algorithm's use constitutes a separate violation.

Authorizes the Attorney General, district attorneys, or city or county attorneys to file civil actions for violations, seeking damages, injunctive relief, restitution, or civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation.

Declares conflicting contracts void.

Confirms this section does not limit antitrust laws' applicability.

Defines key terms such as "artificial intelligence," "nonpublic input data," "price-setting algorithm," and "competitors" within the context of the act.

Official name: California SB 500 (Autonomous Vehicles: Zero Emissions 2021)
Casual name: California SB 500 (Autonomous Vehicles: Zero Emissions 2021)
Short summary: Regulates autonomous vehicles in California by requiring manufacturer certifications, insurance, and Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) application approval. Requires additional safety measures and documentation, and mandates zero-emission status for certain vehicles starting in 2031. Allows DMV to impose specific rules and requirements.
Long summary:
Defines "autonomous vehicle" as any vehicle equipped with technology meeting Levels 3, 4, or 5 of SAE standards allowing driving without human monitoring.

Requires testing on public roads with a driver capable of manual control and a $5 million insurance or bond from the manufacturer.

Prohibits public road operation without Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) application approval, certifying safety features and insurance coverage.

Directs the DMV to adopt regulations by January 2015, including insurance and safety standards for autonomous vehicle testing.

Mandates public hearings for regulations concerning driverless operation.

Allows DMV to require a driver in the vehicle if deemed necessary.

Requires informing purchasers about data collected by the autonomous technology.

Mandates zero-emission for autonomous vehicles under 8,501 pounds from the model year 2031, beginning rulemaking after 2027.

Specifies that National Highway Traffic Safety Administration regulations override conflicting state laws.

Official name: California SB 480 (Autonomous vehicles 2025)
Casual name: California SB 480 (Autonomous vehicles 2025)
Short summary: Regulates autonomous vehicles (AVs), defining "autonomous technology" and operations on public roads. Requires AV manufacturers to certify safety standards compliance, insurance coverage of $5 million, and testing. Mandates the Department of Motor Vehicles to adopt relevant regulations and allows ADS marker lamps.
Long summary:
Amends the Vehicle Code to establish regulations for autonomous vehicles and their technology.

Defines "autonomous technology" and "autonomous vehicle" following SAE International standards, distinguishing them from vehicles with basic driver-assistance features.

Permits the operation of autonomous vehicles on public roads for testing by designated individuals if specific conditions are met, including possessing the proper driver's license and insurance.

Requires manufacturers to submit an application to the Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) for the operation of autonomous vehicles, including certifications on safety, insurance, and technology standards.

Instructs the DMV to adopt regulations for insurance, application submissions, and safety standards for autonomous vehicles, consulting experts as needed.

Authorizes the DMV to impose additional requirements for vehicles operating without a driver present.

Requires manufacturers to disclose data collection practices to purchasers and potentially pay fees covering DMV processing costs.

Specifies the addition of ADS marker lamps for autonomous vehicles and mandates zero-emission operation for vehicles of certain specifications starting in 2030.

Official name: California SB 503 (Health Care Services: Artificial Intelligence 2025)
Casual name: California SB 503 (Health Care Services: AI 2025)
Short summary: Requires developers and deployers to identify, mitigate, and monitor AI systems in healthcare for biased impacts. Obligates them to report compliance efforts annually. Instructs the department to publish these reports online. Effective from January 1, 2027.
Long summary:
Add Section 1339.76 to the Health and Safety Code.

Require developers and deployers to identify and mitigate artificial intelligence systems with biased impacts in clinical decision-making or health care resource allocation.

Instruct deployers to monitor these AI systems regularly and take steps to reduce bias.

Specify no requirement for the department to independently inspect AI systems; developers and deployers ensure compliance and maintain documentation.

Obligate developers, starting January 1, 2027, to report compliance efforts to the department before making AI systems available.

Require deployers to submit annual compliance reports to the department starting January 1, 2027.

Mandate the department to publish these reports online.

Define terms such as "biased impact," "deployer," "developer," and "artificial intelligence."

Clarify that compliance with this section supplements other state laws and does not serve as a defense against discrimination claims.

Official name: California SCR 17 (Relative to Artificial Intelligence 2023)
Casual name: California SCR 17 (Relative to Artificial Intelligence 2023)
Short summary: Affirms California Legislature's commitment to President Biden's safe AI vision and the "Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights." Commits to examine and implement these principles in state legislation and policies on automated systems use and deployment.
Long summary:
Affirms the California Legislature's commitment to President Biden’s vision for safe AI and the principles outlined in the "Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights."

Commits to examining and implementing the principles of Safe and Effective Systems, Algorithmic Discrimination Protections, Data Privacy, Notice and Explanation, and Human Alternatives, Consideration, and Fallback in state legislation and policies.

Addresses significant challenges posed by automated systems to democracy and public rights, such as unsafe, biased systems in healthcare and discriminatory algorithms in hiring and credit decisions.

Recognizes the potential benefits of AI, including increased efficiency in agriculture and revolutionary industrial advancements through data analysis.

Instructs the Secretary of the Senate to transmit copies of this resolution to the author for distribution.

Official name: Guidance on Algorithmic Discrimination and the New Jersey Law Against Discrimination
Casual name: Guidance on Algorithmic Discrimination and the New Jersey Law Against Discrimination
Short summary: Prohibits algorithmic discrimination under New Jersey's Law Against Discrimination (LAD) by covered entities. Holds entities liable for discriminatory outcomes from automated tools. Addresses disparate treatment, disparate impact, and failure to provide reasonable accommodations related to AI use.
Long summary:
Clarifies that the New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (LAD) applies to algorithmic discrimination through automated decision-making tools similarly to traditional discrimination.

Prohibits any form of discrimination facilitated by automated tools, regardless of intent or third-party involvement in tool development.

Requires covered entities, like employers and housing providers, to avoid disparate treatment and disparate impact discrimination in using these tools.

Mandates that entities provide reasonable accommodations to avoid discriminatory impacts, even if automated tools fail to recognize accommodations.

Holds entities liable for discrimination resulting from their use of third-party developed tools, emphasizing the importance of evaluating these tools for bias.

Encourages developers and vendors to design and test automated tools to minimize discriminatory outcomes, thus reducing liability risk under the LAD.

Reiterates the LAD's comprehensive protections against discrimination, regardless of the technology used, and provides resources for understanding these protections.

Official name: California SB 243 (Companion Chatbots 2025)
Casual name: California SB 243 (Companion Chatbots 2025)
Short summary: Regulates companion chatbots by requiring operators to disclose their artificial nature, implement protocols against suicide-related content, and apply heightened protections for minors. Mandates annual reporting to the Office of Suicide Prevention and subjects violators to civil liability.
Long summary:
Defines "companion chatbot" as an AI system with a natural language interface capable of sustaining relationships across multiple interactions, excluding customer service bots, video game bots limited to game-related topics, and stand-alone voice assistant devices.

Requires operators to issue clear disclosures when a reasonable person could mistake the companion chatbot for a human.

Mandates operators maintain and publicly post protocols to prevent suicide-related content by issuing crisis service notifications.

Obligates operators to disclose to minors that interactions are with AI, send break reminder notifications at least every three hours during ongoing interactions, and prohibit chatbots from generating sexually explicit content.

Requires annual reporting of crisis notifications and protocols to the Office of Suicide Prevention, effective July 1, 2027.

Permits individuals injured by violations to seek injunctive relief, damages, and attorneys' fees.

Official name: Illinois HB 3506
Casual name: Illinois HB 3506 (AI Safety and Security Protocol Act)
Collections: Editors' Picks;U.S. state and local documents
Short summary: Requires developers to establish, publish, and adhere to safety and security protocols and conduct regular risk assessments and third-party audits. Imposes civil penalties for violations up to $1,000,000.
Long summary:
Mandates developers to produce, implement, and publish a "safety and security protocol" to respond to critical risks, along with quarterly risk assessment reports.

Defines "critical risk" as deriving from the development or deployment of foundation models in a manner which could cause serious injury, death, or financial loss.

Defines "foundation model" as an AI model applicable to many different contexts and capable of self-supervision in training.

Requires an annual third-party audit to assess compliance with these protocols.

Allows redactions in published documents for protecting trade secrets or public safety, with unredacted versions available to the Attorney General.

Imposes civil penalties up to $1,000,000 for violations, with consideration of the severity and potential materialization of critical risks.

Establishes whistleblower protections and procedures for reporting internal risks related to AI development.

Authorizes the Attorney General to seek injunctive relief if a developer's activities pose imminent threats to public safety.

Emphasizes the cumulative nature of this Act, not limiting duties or remedies under other laws.

Official name: California ACR 96 Relative to the 23 Asilomar AI Principles 2023
Casual name: California ACR 96 Asilomar AI Principles 2023
Short summary: Supports the 23 Asilomar AI Principles as guiding values for AI development and policy. Emphasizes safety, transparency, value alignment, shared benefit, and privacy. Urges cooperation among AI researchers and policymakers, and promotes avoiding an AI arms race.
Long summary:
Expresses support by the California Legislature for the Asilomar AI Principles to guide the development of artificial intelligence and related public policy.

Supports creating AI with beneficial intelligence, ensuring robust systems that align with human values.

Encourages collaboration between AI researchers and policymakers and cooperation among AI developers to maintain safety standards.

Emphasizes AI safety, transparency in system failures and judicial use, and designer responsibility for AI implications.

Advocates for AI systems to respect human dignity, privacy, cultural diversity, and to empower people while sharing economic prosperity.

Stipulates human control over AI decision-making and discourages AI arms races.

Calls for cautious planning for advanced AI development, focusing on mitigating catastrophic risks.

Urges that superintelligence development serves ethical ideals and benefits all humanity.

Requests the Chief Clerk of the Assembly to distribute the resolution appropriately.

Official name: California AB-1170, SEC. 46 (AI in Education Working Group 2025)
Casual name: California AB-1170, SEC. 46 (AI in Education Working Group 2025)
Short summary: Requires the Superintendent to convene a working group to develop AI usage guidelines for educational settings. Instructs the group to assess AI use in schools, develop model policies, and report findings by 2027. Specifies transparency, privacy, and academic integrity provisions.
Long summary:
Amends the Education Code to define "artificial intelligence" and establish a working group, convened by the Superintendent, for the safe and effective use of AI in education. 

Requires development of guidance on AI use that benefits pupils and educators, a model policy on AI in local educational agencies, and practices supporting educators’ effective use of AI.

Includes diverse stakeholders in the working group, with at least half being credentialed teachers.

Assesses current and future AI use, conducting public meetings for feedback, and identifying human-centered and replacement AI examples.

Details AI's impact on educational quality, pupil data security, and teacher employment.

Develops AI guidance and model policies addressing academic integrity, data privacy, acceptable uses, and avoiding inequities.

Submits a report to the Legislature by January 1, 2027, presents findings, and posts guidance online. 

Dissolves the working group post-report submission and repeals this section on January 1, 2031.

Official name: California SB 7 (Employment: Automated Decision Systems 2025)
Casual name: California SB 7 (Employment: Automated Decision Systems 2025)
Short summary: Regulates employers' use of automated decision systems (ADS) in workplaces for employment-related decisions, requiring notice and human oversight. Prohibits retaliation against workers exercising rights. Enforces compliance through the Labor Commissioner and allows civil penalties for violations.
Long summary:
Requires employers in California to notify workers and their authorized representatives if an Automated Decision System (ADS) is used for employment-related decisions, excluding hiring, providing notice 30 days in advance and maintaining an updated ADS list.

Prohibits employers from using ADS to violate labor laws, infer protected status, or take actions against workers exercising their rights.

Mandates human review and additional information for discipline, termination, or deactivation decisions based on ADS.

Allows workers to request their own data used for ADS-related decisions annually.

Prohibits retaliation against workers invoking protections under this regulation and establishes enforcement by the Labor Commissioner and public prosecutors.

Imposes a civil penalty of $500 for violations and ensures compliance with the California Consumer Privacy Act.

Exempts parties under collective bargaining agreements with explicit waivers from coverage, and retains obligations toward federal regulatory requirements.

Official name: California AB-1170, SEC. 35 (Generative AI Training Data Documentation 2025)
Casual name: California AB-1170, SEC. 35 (Generative AI Training Data Documentation 2025)
Short summary: Requires developers to publicly post data documentation for generative AI systems released after 2022, covering datasets used, unless systems focus solely on security, aircraft operation, or national defense. Specifies details including data sources, purposes, and modifications.
Long summary:
Requires developers of generative AI systems or services made publicly available in California to post documentation about the data used for training these systems on their websites by 2026.

Specifies the documentation must include a summary of datasets, sources, and how they support the system's purpose.

Requires disclosure on dataset data points, whether datasets include copyrighted or personal information, modifications made, and whether synthetic data is used.

Exempts AI systems aimed solely at ensuring security and integrity, operating aircraft in national airspace, or developed for national security and defense purposes for federal entities from these documentation requirements.

Official name: Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act (HB 149)
Casual name: Texas Responsible AI Governance Act (2025 Update) (HB 149)
Link to document: https://www.legis.state.tx.us/BillLookup/Text.aspx?LegSess=89R&Bill=HB149 - wait until docx version is available
Collections: Editors' Picks;U.S. state and local documents
Short summary: Establishes the Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act, prohibiting AI systems from inciting harm, manipulation, political viewpoint discrimination, and unlawful discrimination against protected classes; requires government agencies to disclose AI use to consumers; establishes the Artificial Intelligence Council and a regulatory sandbox program; and authorizes the Attorney General to enforce compliance and impose civil penalties.
Long summary:
Regulates AI systems in Texas under the Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act.

Prohibits AI systems from inciting harm, criminality, manipulation, or discrimination based on political viewpoints or protected classes.

Establishes the Artificial Intelligence Council and a regulatory sandbox program for controlled AI testing.

Requires government disclosure to consumers when AI is used in interactions.

Instructs the attorney general to enforce regulations, manage complaints, and impose fines for non-compliance.

Prohibits government use of AI for social scoring or capturing biometric identifiers in violation of rights.

Mandates that AI must not produce certain unlawful content and must adhere to consumer protections and data privacy.

Official name: Illinois HB 4844 (2024), Section 90 ("Generative AI and Natural Language Processing Task Force")
Casual name: Illinois HB 4844, Sec 90 ("Generative AI and Natural Language Processing Task Force")
Short summary: Directs the Illinois Department of Innovation and Technology to establish a Generative AI and Natural Language Processing Task Force to investigate and report on generative AI and natural language processing software.
Long summary:
Amends the Illinois Department of Innovation and Technology Act to establish a Generative AI and Natural Language Processing Task Force within the Department of Innovation and Technology.

Investigates generative AI and natural language processing software and producing a report on findings.

Specifies the composition of the Task Force, which includes legislative appointees from both chambers and both parties, with the Speaker of the House and Senate President appointees serving as co-chairs.

Includes a range of state officials as members, including the Secretary of Innovation and Technology, State Superintendent of Education, heads of the Illinois Community College Board and Board of Higher Education, and the Attorney General.

Includes Governor-appointed members representing teachers, principals, cybersecurity experts, AI experts, statewide business associations, and statewide labor associations, as well as the Statewide Chief Information Security Officer.

Official name: Wisconsin Act 2023-123 (Artificial Intelligence Content Disclosure)
Casual name: Wisconsin Act 2023-123 (AI Content Disclosure)
Short summary: Requires the disclosure of AI generative content in political advertisements. Amends the 11.1303 title to define synthetic media. Enforces fines for violations.
Long summary:
Amends the 11.1303 title to define synthetic media.

Defines synthetic media as audio or video produced in part by generative artificial intelligence.

Requires that any issue advocacy communications that contain any AI should include a writing stating "Contains content generated by AI".

Requires the label to be visible through each portion containing synthetic media.

States that compliance does not create any exemption from civil or criminal liability.

Enforces fines of up to $ 1,000 for each violation.

Mandates that the liability only affects the person responsible for the communication.

Official name: California AB 682 (Health Care Coverage Reporting 2025)
Casual name: California AB 682 (Health Care Coverage Reporting 2025)
Short summary: Requires health care plans and insurers to report claims that use AI, detailing processed and denied claims, costs, and demographic categories. Directs public website postings and allows regulatory rules on forms and content, ensuring privacy protections.
Long summary:
Regulates health care service plans and insurers in California to report annual claims data, requiring detail on claims processed or reviewed with artificial intelligence or predictive algorithms.  

Requires health care service plans, by February 1, 2026, and insurers, by February 1, 2028, to publicly report prior authorization data online, including approval and denial rates for standard and expedited requests, and timeframes for decisions.  

Obliges plans to include data on AI-assisted decisions in annual payment and dispute resolution reports starting February 1, 2027, disaggregated by demographics from 2029.  

Instructs the director and commissioner to create rules and regulations for report forms and content, ensuring compliance with privacy laws, including the Confidentiality of Medical Information Act and HIPAA.  

Allows directors and commissioners to reject and require correction of inadequate reports, with financial penalties for noncompliance by insurers.

Official name: California AB 3061 (Vehicles: Autonomous Vehicle Incident Reporting 2024)
Casual name: California AB 3061 (Vehicles: Autonomous Vehicle Incident Reporting 2024)
Short summary: Adds Section 38760 to California's Vehicle Code, requiring autonomous vehicle manufacturers to report collisions, disengagements, and traffic violations from July 31, 2025. Mandates quarterly reports on vehicle miles and incidents. Requires data publication and redaction by the DMV starting January 1, 2028.
Long summary:
Adds Section 38760 to the California Vehicle Code to enhance transparency and public safety concerning autonomous vehicles.

Requires autonomous vehicle manufacturers, beginning July 31, 2025, to report collisions and disengagements to the Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) when vehicles operate in autonomous mode on public roads.

Mandates the inclusion of detailed incident information in reports, such as collision narratives, road conditions, and vehicle permits.

Obligates manufacturers to submit quarterly summaries of incidents, vehicle miles traveled, immobilizations, and unresolved traffic citations.

Instructs the DMV, starting July 1, 2025, to maintain and, from January 1, 2028, publish incident reports while redacting personal and proprietary information.

Permits the DMV to establish additional regulations and assess fees to recover costs related to implementing these requirements. 

Ensures public access to data and supports safe deployment of autonomous vehicles through comprehensive reporting and regulatory oversight.

Official name: California AB 723 (Real Estate: Digitally Altered Images: Disclosure 2025)
Casual name: California AB 723 (Real Estate: Digitally Altered Images: Disclosure 2025)
Short summary: Require real estate brokers or salespersons using AI-altered images in advertisements to disclose alterations and provide access to original images. Define "digitally altered image" as modified through AI or software, excluding minor edits like lighting and color adjustments.
Long summary:
Add Section 10140.8 to the California Business and Professions Code to require real estate brokers or salespersons to disclose when images in advertisements are digitally altered.

Define "digitally altered image" as one altered through photo editing software or AI, affecting elements like fixtures, furniture, or views.

Exclude from this definition alterations that use common photo editing adjustments such as lighting or cropping that do not alter property representations.

Require advertisements with digitally altered images to include a statement and link to access unaltered images.

Oblige brokers or salespersons to provide access to original images if they control the website on which the advertisement is posted.

State that no reimbursement is required under this act, as it pertains to creating or changing the definition or penalty of a crime.

Official name: Arkansas HB 1876 (Ownership of Model Training and Content Generated by a Generative Artificial Intelligence Tool 2025)
Casual name: Arkansas HB 1876 (Ownership of Model Training and Content Generated by a Gen AI Tool 2025)
Short summary: Assigns ownership of AI-generated content to the input provider, unless infringing on existing intellectual property. Grants model training ownership to data providers, with conditions. Treats AI work done by employees under employer direction as employer-owned, adhering to specific criteria.
Long summary:
Amends Arkansas law to establish ownership of content and models generated through generative AI tools.

Grants ownership of AI-generated content to the person providing the input, conditional on the content not infringing on existing intellectual property.

Assigns ownership of trained AI models to the person providing the training data, provided the data is lawfully acquired and ownership rights have not been transferred by contract.

Specifies that if an employee uses generative AI as part of their employment duties, the employer owns the resulting content and trained models, provided the work is within the scope of employment and under employer control.

Clarifies that the section does not confer ownership over content that infringes on existing copyrights or intellectual property rights.

Official name: Illinois House Bill 53 (2021)
Casual name: Illinois HB 53 (2021)
Short summary: Amends the Artificial Intelligence Video Interview Act to require employers using AI for video interviews to collect and report applicants' race and ethnicity data to the Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity. Requires the Department to analyze and report potential racial bias annually.
Long summary:
Amends the Artificial Intelligence Video Interview Act by requiring employers using AI to analyze video interviews for in-person interview selection to collect demographic data.

Requires the collection of race and ethnicity data of applicants selected and not selected for interviews, as well as of those hired.

Obligates employers to report this demographic data annually to the Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity by December 31.

Requires the Department to analyze this data and determine any racial bias in the AI use.

Instructs the Department to report findings of racial bias to the Governor and General Assembly by July 1 each year.

Official name: Illinois House Bill 2557 (2019)
Casual name: Illinois HB 2557 (AI Video Interview Act)
Short summary: Requires employers in Illinois using AI for video interview analysis to notify applicants, explain AI functionality, and obtain consent. Prohibits sharing videos except with necessary evaluators. Instructs employers to delete videos upon applicant request within 30 days.
Long summary:
Requires employers in Illinois to notify job applicants if artificial intelligence will analyze their video interviews and to provide information on how the AI works, including characteristics it evaluates.

Requires employers to obtain applicants' consent before using AI to evaluate them.

Prohibits employers from using AI analysis on applicants who do not consent.

Permits sharing of applicant videos only with individuals necessary for evaluating the applicant's fitness for the position.

Obliges employers to delete video interviews and instruct any recipients to do the same, including backup copies, within 30 days if the applicant requests it.

Official name: PATHS Act
Casual name: PATHS Act
Short summary: Extends the Department of Homeland Security's authority to use transaction mechanisms involving AI technology until 2028, requiring notification and briefing to congressional committees. Reduces the contract award threshold from $4,000,000 to $1,000,000.
Long summary:
Extends the use of other transaction authority for research and development acquisition under the Homeland Security Act of 2002 from September 30, 2024, to September 30, 2028.  
   
Mandates notification to congressional committees within 72 hours after the use or extension of transaction authority involving artificial intelligence (AI) technology.  
   
Requires the Secretary of Homeland Security to offer a briefing explaining the reason for using or extending AI-related transaction authority.  
   
Reduces the maximum amount for covered contract awards under the James M. Inhofe National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023 from $4,000,000 to $1,000,000.

Official name: Louisiana SCR 49
Casual name: Louisiana (2023) SCR 49 (Study Impact of AI)
Short summary: Urges the Joint Legislative Committee on Technology and Cybersecurity to study AI's impact on operations, procurement, and policy. Requires a written report with recommendations submitted to relevant committees 60 days before Louisiana's 2024 Regular Session; encourages the committee to solicit input from several governmental and industry entities.
Long summary:
Urges the Joint Legislative Committee on Technology and Cybersecurity to study the impact of artificial intelligence on operations, procurement, and policy in Louisiana.

Requires the committee to submit a written report of its findings to the House Committee on Commerce and the Senate Committee on Commerce, Consumer Protection and International Affairs at least sixty days before the 2024 Regular Session.

Instructs the report to propose recommendations and legislative proposals to aid government and businesses in leveraging AI benefits while protecting consumers.

Encourages the committee to seek input from the Department of Economic Development, the office of technology services, Division of Administration, the Department of Justice, and industry partners.

Transmits a copy of the resolution to the Joint Legislative Committee on Technology and Cybersecurity.

Official name: Ensuring Safe and Ethical AI Development Through SAFE AI Research Grants
Casual name: SAFE AI Research Grants
Short summary: Requires the National Academy of Sciences to establish a grant program for the development of safe AI models and AI research; directs and outlines the submission of a proposal for the program in accordance with guiding principles.
Long summary:
Requires the National Academy of Sciences to establish a grant program for the development of safe AI models and AI research.

Mandates the development of guiding principles and ethical considerations for the grant program.

Directs the Director of the National Academy of Sciences to submit a detailed proposal of the grant program to relevant Congressional committees within one year, including a budget, proposed appropriation request, and an evaluation of existing AI models and methodologies.

Official name: Department of State Authorization Act of 2023, Sec. 941 ("Reporting Related to the AUKUS Partnership")
Casual name: Department of State Authorization Act, Sec. 941 ("Reporting Related to AUKUS")
Short summary: Requires the President to report non-binding instruments related to the AUKUS partnership. Mandates biennial reports on AI and other tech collaboration under Pillar Two, assessing efforts in AI, quantum, cyber, and other advanced capabilities.
Long summary:
Requires the Secretary, in coordination with officials within the Secretary of Defense and others, to submit a biennial report on the AUKUS partnership starting one year after enactment.

Requires assessments of trilateral collaboration efforts in areas including underseas capabilities, quantum technologies, artificial intelligence and autonomy, advanced cyber capabilities, hypersonic technologies, electronic warfare, innovation, and information sharing.

Official name: Framework for Artificial Intelligence Diffusion
Casual name: AI Diffusion Rule (US BIS)
Collections: Editors' Picks;U.S. regulations, executive orders, and agency policies
Short summary: Controls the export of AI chips and models outside the United States. Establishes a country-based tiering system to determine applicable restrictions, exceptions, and conditions, including security and reporting safeguards. Creates validated end-user programs to govern exports of AI chips to most countries. Defines an adjustable compute-based threshold for export-controlled AI models.
Long summary:
Imposes export controls on AI models, excluding publicly available models, and expands licensing requirements for AI chips to additional countries.

Establishes three tiers of countries for purposes of determining applicable export restrictions, including eighteen countries able to import AI chips without restrictions (tier 1); countries able to import AI chips through validated end-user (VEU) programs, limited-volume exceptions, and licensing, but otherwise subject to restrictions (tier 2); and countries subject to ongoing restrictions, including arms-embargoed countries (tier 3).

Establishes a Data Center Validated End User (DC VEU) program to govern compute exports related to major AI infrastructure development in second-tier countries, with different pathways and restrictions depending on data center operator nationality. Imposes cybersecurity, physical and personnel security, and sourcing mandates on DC VEU participants, as well as reporting requirements.

Imposes specific computing power deployment restrictions on companies operating in second-tier countries, including relative ratios and numerical caps.

Controls the export of AI models developed using compute above a given threshold, to be adjusted over time based on assessments of publicly available models. Requires cloud computing providers to implement security measures preventing the unauthorized training of models otherwise subject to export controls.

Official name: New York Senate Bill 1042
Casual name: New York SB 1042 (Unlawful Dissemination of Intimate Images)
Short summary: Amends the penal law to criminalize dissemination or publication of digitized intimate images without consent. Defines "digitization" as realistic alteration using images of another person or computer-generated images. Repeals subdivision 2-a of section 245.15.
Long summary:
Amends the penal law to include the unlawful dissemination or publication of intimate images created or altered by digitization.

Defines "digitization" as altering an image realistically using other persons' images or computer-generated images.

Defines unlawful dissemination of intimate images, including AI-generated or digitally altered images, as intentional, non-consensual acts causing emotional, financial, or physical harm to individuals.

Mandates that the actor knew or should have known that the person depicted did not consent to the dissemination or publication.

Repeals subdivision 2-a of section 245.15 of the penal law.

Specifies that the act takes effect on the sixtieth day after becoming law.

Casual name: Washington SB 5152 (Synthetic Media)
Short summary: Defines "synthetic media" in political campaigns as manipulated media creating false impressions. Permits candidates to seek legal relief against such media use. Requires disclosure of manipulation. Holds sponsors liable, not media, unless disclosure is altered. Encourages prompt court rulings.
Long summary:
Defines "synthetic media" as manipulated images, audio, or video that create a false impression of a real individual's appearance, speech, or conduct.

Allows candidates to seek injunctive relief or damages if their appearance, speech, or conduct is altered using synthetic media in electioneering communications.

Requires disclosure for synthetic media, stating, "This (image/video/audio) has been manipulated," with specific guidelines for visibility and audibility.

Places the burden of proof on plaintiffs to demonstrate synthetic media use by clear and convincing evidence.

Encourages courts to expedite proceedings related to synthetic media disputes.

Holds sponsors, but not mediums, liable unless mediums alter content or remove required disclosures.

Exempts interactive computer services from being treated as publishers of third-party content, except under specific conditions.

Mandates the public disclosure commission to adopt rules supporting this chapter without constituting violations under existing campaign finance laws.

Official name: Mississippi Senate Bill 2577

Short summary: Criminalizes dissemination of AI-generated deepfakes within 90 days of an election, without consent, intending to harm candidates or influence elections. Long summary:
Establishes criminal penalties for wrongful dissemination of deepfakes, defined as realistic digital alterations of images or audio using AI or other technologies, particularly if used to influence elections.

Criminalizes dissemination within 90 days of an election without consent and with intent to harm a candidate or election outcome.

Imposes penalties of up to five years imprisonment or $10,000 fines for violations intended to incite violence or deter voting, with lesser penalties for other cases.

Allows injunctive relief actions by various parties, including the Attorney General and affected candidates, to prevent violations and remove disseminated deepfakes.

Exempts certain broadcasters and publishers, including those involved in bona fide news reporting or satire, from liability.

Requires clear labeling of deepfakes as a defense to prosecution.

Takes effect on July 1, 2024.

Casual name: Fix Our Forests Act, Section 303 ("Public-private wildfire technology deployment and demonstration partnership")
Short summary: Establishes a pilot program for deploying innovative wildfire technologies. Prioritizes AI, quantum sensing, and other emerging technologies. Long summary:

Requires coordination between selected private entities and federal agencies for real-time technology testing during wildfire mitigation.

Prioritizes entities involved in the Fire Weather Testbed or developing emerging technologies like AI and quantum sensing.

Mandates public outreach to invite applications from entities to demonstrate technologies.

Obligates annual reporting to Congress on program participants, technologies demonstrated, costs, outreach, and recommendations for technology adoption.

Specifies the program's authority will terminate seven years after enactment.

Short summary: Establishes a Fireshed Center to assess and predict fire and smoke using AI and data tools. Promotes coordination, data sharing, and streamlined processes among federal agencies and other entities. Disseminates AI-based decision support products for fire risk reduction and recovery.

Utilizes artificial intelligence and data tools to assess and predict fire and smoke at the wildland-urban interface for improved management, risk reduction, and recovery.

Promotes data sharing and coordination across federal, state, local, tribal, and private sectors.

Reduces duplication and fragmentation in predictive services and decision support related to wildland fires.

Streamlines procurement and cybersecurity processes.

Develops and disseminates publicly accessible data, models, and technologies for fire risk reduction and recovery planning.

Maintains the Fireshed Registry and supports its operations with personnel and services from the U.S. Geological Survey and the Forest Service.

Short summary: Requires the University of Hawaii to establish a two-year program using AI to develop a wildfire forecast system. Appropriates $1,000,000 for this purpose. Mandates reporting on program effectiveness and recommendations before the 2026 legislative session.
Long summary:
Mandates the University of Hawaii to establish a two-year program for developing a wildfire forecast system using artificial intelligence.

Obligates the University of Hawaii to report on the program's effectiveness and provide findings, recommendations, and any proposed legislation to the legislature before the 2026 regular session.

Casual name: Hawaii SB 2687 (Deceptive Media)
Short summary: Prohibits reckless distribution of materially deceptive media using AI during elections. Exempts certain broadcasters and services and requires disclaimers for manipulated media. Establishes criminal penalties and civil remedies for violations.
Long summary:
Prohibits the reckless distribution of materially deceptive media, including deepfake and generative AI content, during election periods, to protect candidates' reputations and electoral prospects.

Establishes criminal penalties for violations, including petty misdemeanors, misdemeanors for repeat offenses, and class C felonies for intent to cause violence or harm.

Allows exceptions for broadcasters and online services that did not create the deceptive media, or if disclaimers indicate manipulation.

Mandates that disclaimers must be clearly visible and in the same language as the media, with specific requirements for video, image, and audio content.

Provides civil remedies for individuals or organizations harmed by deceptive media, including damages, attorney's fees, and injunctive relief.

Empowers the attorney general, campaign spending commission, and other authorities to enforce these provisions and seek injunctions.

Defines "artificial intelligence" and "materially deceptive media" for clarity and enforcement purposes.

Official name: California SB 295 (California Preventing Algorithmic Collusion Act of 2025)
Casual name: California SB 295 (California Preventing Algorithmic Collusion Act of 2025)
Short summary: Prohibits persons from distributing, recommending, or using pricing algorithms — including those derived from machine learning or other AI techniques — that process competitor data to coordinate prices or commercial terms among competitors in the same market with exceptions for credit score tools, and authorizes civil enforcement including penalties of up to $25,000 per violation.
Long summary:
Enacts the California Preventing Algorithmic Collusion Act of 2025, prohibiting the distribution or use of pricing algorithms — including those derived from machine learning or AI techniques — by two or more competitors if the algorithms process competitor data to set prices or commercial terms in the same market.

Establishes an affirmative defense for persons who exercised reasonable due diligence before using such algorithms, including obtaining written assurances that the algorithm does not process competitor data.

Specifies that each authorized user, each recommendation, and each calendar month of use constitutes a separate violation.

Exempts algorithms using competitor data collected more than one year prior, and credit scoring tools subject to the Fair Credit Reporting Act not used for direct coordination among competitors.

Authorizes the Attorney General, district attorney, county counsel, or city attorney to seek restitution, punitive damages, civil penalties of up to $25,000 per violation, and injunctionary relief through civil actions.

Specifies that contracts violating this chapter are void and that existing antitrust laws remain applicable.

Casual name: Executive Order on Preventing Woke AI In The Federal Government

Short summary: Directs federal agency heads to procure large language models (LLMs) that adhere to two principles: truth-seeking and ideological neutrality. Requires developers to not intentionally encode partisan or ideological judgments into an LLM’s outputs. Instructs the Office of Management and Budget to issue guidance for implementation, acknowledging technical limitations and allowing exceptions for national security systems.
Long summary:
Requires agency heads to procure only large language models (LLMs) that adhere to "Unbiased AI Principles," emphasizing truth-seeking and ideological neutrality.

Defines LLMs as generative AI models that generate natural-language responses to user prompts.

Instructs the Director of the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) to, within 120 days, issue guidance for implementing these principles, considering technical limitations, transparency, and avoiding over-prescription.

Mandates agency heads to ensure Federal contracts for LLMs include compliance with the Unbiased AI Principles, allowing vendor decommissioning costs for noncompliance.

Allows agencies to specify criteria for applying these principles to other AI models and exempts national security systems where appropriate.

Instructs the Secretary of Education and other Federal entities to support the use of AI in educational settings to improve outcomes.

Directs the Secretary of Labor to increase AI-related Registered Apprenticeships and promote AI skill development through the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act (WIOA).

Encourages agencies to prioritize AI in educational grant programs.
