Official name: Bureau of Industry and Security Information Technology Modernization Act
Casual name: BIS IT Modernization Act
Short summary: Requires the Bureau of Industry and Security to integrate AI, machine learning, and advanced tools into IT systems. Mandates data fusion and analytics for export controls. Enhances data sharing and security. Allocates $25 million annually through 2028 for modernization.
Long summary:
Require the Bureau of Industry and Security to adopt advanced data and analytics tools to improve export licensing, assess global industrial ties, and detect evasive trade patterns.

Requires the Bureau to adopt and use modern data sharing and capabilities to exchange data securely and effectively with industry.

Directs the Bureau to enable the integration of AI and machine learning over time and to expedite Entity List actions and enforcement related to tracking military end users in high-risk countries.

Obligates the Bureau to expedite Entity List decisions and strengthen enforcement targeting military end users in countries of concern.

Collaborate with relevant agencies to map the PRC’s defense industrial base, military-civil fusion strategy, and its commercial ties with Russia.

Demands the modernization of the Bureau’s IT systems through 2029 by implementing a unified platform that enables seamless case management and analysis of external trade data.

Adopt advanced data analytics and sharing tools to streamline export licensing, strengthen enforcement and Entity List decisions, track military end users, and securely share data with partners.

Evaluate technology solutions based on their ability to improve efficiency, reduce costs, strengthen security, enable secure data sharing, and enhance user experience.

Instructs the Under Secretary to reassess staffing needs and consult Congress on personnel adjustments during the modernization.

Authorizes $25 million annually from 2025 to 2028 for these initiatives.

Official name: Utah SB 226 (Artificial Intelligence Consumer Protection Amendments 2025)
Casual name: Utah SB 226 (Artificial Intelligence Consumer Protection Amendments 2025)
Short summary: Requires suppliers and regulated professionals using generative artificial intelligence in consumer transactions and high-risk interactions to disclose AI use; provides a safe harbor for compliant disclosers; grants the Division of Consumer Protection enforcement and rulemaking authority; and establishes civil and administrative penalties for violations.
Long summary:
Defines key terms including generative artificial intelligence, high-risk artificial intelligence interaction, regulated occupation, and related terms governing the scope of the chapter's application to consumer transactions and regulated services.

Establishes that generative artificial intelligence cannot be used as a defense against consumer protection law violations administered by the Division of Consumer Protection.

Requires suppliers to disclose generative artificial intelligence use to consumers upon request in consumer transactions, and requires individuals in regulated occupations to prominently disclose AI use in high-risk interactions verbally or in writing before the interaction begins.

Provides a safe harbor from enforcement actions for suppliers that clearly and conspicuously disclose generative artificial intelligence use at the outset and throughout consumer interactions, and grants the Division of Consumer Protection rulemaking authority to specify forms and methods of disclosure.

Grants the Division of Consumer Protection enforcement authority, including administrative fines of up to $2,500 per violation, civil penalties of up to $5,000 per violation, and court remedies including injunctions, disgorgement, and attorney fees.

Specifies that this chapter does not displace any other remedy or right authorized under state or federal law.

Repeals the existing provision governing generative artificial intelligence's impact on consumer protection liability and the Artificial Intelligence Policy Act effective July 1, 2027.

Official name: Promoting United States Leadership in Standards Act of 2025
Casual name: Promoting US Leadership in Standards Act of 2025
Short summary: Directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology and the Department of State to promote U.S. participation in AI standards development. Establishes a web portal and pilot program to support hosting domestic AI standards meetings, with grants for eligible organizations.
Long summary:
Mandates the Director of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), in coordination with the Secretary of State, to brief Congress on U.S. participation in AI standards development and opportunities for federal support.

Requires the establishment of a web portal to inform U.S. industry and federal agencies about international AI standards efforts and participation opportunities.

Establishes a pilot program to support AI standards meetings in the U.S. by awarding grants to eligible entities, specifying eligibility criteria for these grants, and defining allowable costs.

Requires annual briefings to Congress on the pilot program's effectiveness.

Directs the development of recommendations for permanent implementation of the program if deemed feasible within two years.

Official name: Utah Senate Bill 149, Chapter 70
Casual name: Utah SB 149, Chapter 70 (Artificial Intelligence Policy Act)
Short summary: Establishes the Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy to oversee AI development. Creates an AI Learning Laboratory for research and regulatory evaluation. Permits regulatory mitigation agreements for AI testing. Criminalizes offenses committed with AI aid. Repeals the Act on May 1, 2025.
Long summary:
Establishes the Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy to oversee the AI Learning Laboratory Program, which analyzes AI technologies' risks, benefits, and regulatory implications.

Mandates the creation of regulatory mitigation agreements, allowing participants to operate under modified regulations while testing AI technologies.

Sets eligibility requirements for regulatory mitigation, including technical expertise, financial resources, and risk management plans.

Requires participants to report consumer harm, privacy breaches, or unauthorized data usage, with potential removal from the program for violations.

Allows an initial 12-month regulatory mitigation period, with a possible 12-month extension.

Defines using generative AI to commit offenses as a punishable act.

Specifies the program's repeal on May 1, 2025.

Takes effect on May 1, 2024.

Official name: Utah Senate Bill 149, Section 13-2-12
Casual name: Utah SB 149, Section 13-2-12 (Impact of generative AI on liability for violation of consumer protection law)
Short summary: Prohibits using generative AI as a defense for consumer protection violations. Requires disclosure of AI interactions in regulated occupations. Imposes fines up to $2,500 per violation. Authorizes courts to issue injunctions, order disgorgements, and impose additional penalties.
Long summary:
Establishes that using generative artificial intelligence (AI) is not a defense against violations of consumer protection laws.

Mandates disclosure when generative AI interacts with a person, requiring clear communication that the interaction is with AI, not a human.

Requires providers of regulated occupations to disclose when generative AI is used in service provision.

Prohibits service provision of regulated occupations via generative AI without meeting legal requirements.

Stipulates that disclosures be made verbally at the start of oral interactions and electronically before written exchanges.

Empowers the Division of Consumer Protection to enforce these provisions, including imposing fines up to $2,500 per violation.

Allows the division to seek court actions, which may result in injunctions, disgorgement of funds, or additional fines.

Permits civil penalties up to $5,000 for violating administrative or court orders, enforceable by the attorney general.

Official name: AI Development Practices Act of 2024
Casual name: AI Development Practices Act of 2024
Short summary: Amends the National Institute of Standards and Technology Act to require developing voluntary AI development guidelines. Focuses on risk management, communication practices, and collaboration. Involves public reporting, security measures, and international standards alignment. Mandates committee briefings 18 months post-enactment.
Long summary:
Amends the National Institute of Standards and Technology Act to require the development of voluntary guidelines for AI system development, release, and assessment.

Mandates the Director of NIST to collaborate with public and private organizations to provide guidance for guidelines to help with development. 

Defines methods and guidelines for developing AI risk tolerances for variety of cases in regards to AI such as security risks, economic risks and social risks.

Requires categorization of practices related to security, safety, fairness, privacy, and other attributes of AI systems.

Obligates the Director to implement duties focused on voluntary risk management for a trust worthy AI, ensure that voluntary guidance is developed based on international and business standards, prohibits prescribing specific technologies, and requires collaboration with different entities such as public, industry, and academic entities for guidance development.

Demands a report to Congress within 18 months after enactment on new materials or systems programs, and follow policy recommendations that could improve communication and coordination between private-public sector coordination.

Defines "artificial intelligence red teaming" as structure process that tests systems through adversarial methods to identify vulnerabilities, risks, and undesirable behaviors.

Defines "artificial intelligence system" for clarity on meaning given in section 7223 of the Advancing American AI Act.

Official name: Utah SB 96 (Emerging Technology Talent Initiative 2020)
Casual name: Utah SB 96 (Emerging Technology Talent Initiative 2020)
Short summary: Establishes a Deep Technology Talent Initiative to develop programs in deep technology, including AI, at Utah higher education institutions. Requires proposals vetted by an Advisory Council. Allocates $5 million for program funding and oversight by the State Board of Regents.
Long summary:
Enacts a Deep Technology Initiative in Utah to promote education and workforce development in emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence.

Requires the State Board of Regents to develop and oversee a deep technology talent initiative with funding to expand relevant educational programs.

Directs institutions of higher education to submit proposals for deep technology programs in partnership with employers, detailing program structure, participation, and funding needs.

Tasks the Deep Technology Talent Advisory Council with reviewing and prioritizing proposals for funding, evaluating aspects like workforce needs, partnerships, and cost-effectiveness.

Compels the Board to review Advisory Council recommendations and allocate funding by September 1 each fiscal year, incorporating legislative oversight through reports to committees.

Establishes a $5,000,000 allocation from the Workforce Development Restricted Account to support the initiative, ensuring funds meet established criteria and goals.

Official name: Autonomous Vehicle Accessibility Act/AV Accessibility Act
Casual name: Autonomous Vehicle Accessibility Act/AV Accessibility Act
Short summary: Prohibits states from issuing licenses for Level 4 or 5 ADS-equipped vehicle operation that discriminate against individuals with disabilities. Requires the Secretary to study infrastructure improvements for accessible ride-hail ADS-equipped vehicles. Authorizes $5 million for this study.
Long summary:

Defines key terms including “disability,” “public transportation,” and “ride-hail ADS-equipped vehicle.”

Prohibits states from issuing licenses for Level 4 or Level 5 ADS-equipped vehicles in a manner that discriminates against individuals with disabilities, in accordance with the ADA.

Mandates the Secretary of Transportation to commission a study through the National Academies to identify changes needed in public transportation infrastructure to improve accessibility for individuals with disabilities using ride-hail ADS-equipped vehicles.

Authorizes $5,000,000 for the completion of the accessibility infrastructure study, available until expended.

Casual name: DOS Foreign Operations Appropriations Act, Title VII ("General Provisions"), Sec. 7032 ("Democracy Programs")
Short summary: Include AI challenges in the President's democracy strategy within 180 days, focusing on digital security, countering disinformation, and AI-related democracy threats. Allocate funds for digital security and counter-disinformation initiatives as part of broader democracy programs.
Long summary:
Requires the allocation of $2,900,000,000 for democracy programs from various appropriations, including $159,240,000 for the Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights, and Labor.

Mandates the submission of a comprehensive five-year strategy for democracy promotion abroad within 180 days, addressing digital security, countering disinformation, and AI-related challenges.

Prohibits foreign governments from having prior approval over the implementation of democracy programs and protects the confidentiality of implementing partners in undemocratic countries.

Allocates $30,000,000 to protect civil society activists and journalists and $20,000,000 for international freedom of expression and independent media.

Requires the regular informing of the National Endowment for Democracy about planned and supported democracy programs.

Casual name: TORPEDO Act of 2023,  Sec. 12 (Expedited release of advanced technologies to Australia, Canada, and the United Kingdom through the foreign military sales program)
Short summary: Expedites the release of AI and other advanced technologies to Australia, Canada, and the UK through the Foreign Military Sales program. Establishes a fast-track decision-making process for AI capabilities, with a presumption of approval, and anticipatory release policy.
Long summary:
Requires the Secretary of State, in coordination with the Secretary of Defense, to compile a list of pre-cleared military technologies and platforms for sale to Australia, Canada, and the UK within 90 days of enactment and annually thereafter.

Expedites the processing of Foreign Military Sales requests from Australia, Canada, and the UK.

Mandates the creation of an anticipatory release policy for key Foreign Military Sales capabilities, including AI, hypersonic missiles, cyber capabilities, and quantum technologies, with a presumption of approval.

Requires the review and update of interagency policies to incorporate these anticipatory release provisions.

Official name: California AB 2930 (Automated decision systems)
Casual name: California AB 2930 (Automated decision systems)
Short summary: Requires deployers and developers of automated decision systems to conduct impact assessments to mitigate algorithmic discrimination. Mandates notification to natural persons affected by these systems. Establishes enforcement mechanisms through the Civil Rights Department. Excludes cybersecurity technology.
Long summary:
Regulates the use of automated decision systems, focusing on preventing algorithmic discrimination based on protected classifications.

Requires deployers and developers to conduct impact assessments before deploying or making these systems available, and annually thereafter.

Mandates notification to individuals affected by consequential decisions made by automated systems, including an explanation and the opportunity for alternative processes.

Obligates deployers and developers to publicly disclose policies on the use and risk management of automated decision systems.

Prohibits using systems identified as posing algorithmic discrimination risks until mitigated.

Allows the Civil Rights Department to investigate violations, request impact assessments, and bring civil actions, potentially resulting in penalties for violations involving discrimination.

Exempts cybersecurity technologies and ensures confidentiality of trade secrets in impact assessments. 

Mandates compliance with existing anti-discrimination laws, ensuring cumulative protections and remedies.

Official name: California AB 1405 (Artificial intelligence: auditors: enrollment)
Casual name: California AB 1405 (AI auditors)
Short summary: Establishes the AI Auditors’ Enrollment Fund and details requirements for AI auditors in California. Requires auditors to enroll and adhere to industry standards. Prohibits conflicts of interest and unauthorized disclosure of information. Requires the Government Operations Agency to manage enrollments and misconduct reports.
Long summary:
Establishes the AI Auditors’ Enrollment Fund, administered by the Government Operations Agency, to oversee the regulation of AI auditors.

Requires AI auditors to enroll with the agency, pay enrollment fees, and provide detailed information about their practices by January 1, 2027.

Mandates AI auditors to adhere to widely recognized industry standards and avoid conflicts of interest, including prohibiting employment with auditees within 12 months of an audit.

Obliges auditors to provide detailed reports post-audit to auditees, explaining results and compliance recommendations while retaining documentation for at least 10 years.

Prohibits auditors from disclosing confidential information without authorization, except under specified legal circumstances, and prohibits retaliation against employees who report non-compliance.

Instructs the agency to publish auditor information publicly and retain and share misconduct reports for enforcement purposes, beginning January 1, 2027. 

Clarifies that this chapter doesn’t impede audits required by other statutes prior to January 2027, when Section 11549.86 expires.

Official name: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026, Section 907 ("Defense science board study on optimal organizational structure for digital solution and software delivery")
Casual name: FY2026 NDAA, Section 907 ("Defense science board study on optimal organizational structure for digital solution and software delivery")
Short summary: Requires the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026 to direct the Defense Science Board to conduct a study evaluating and recommending the most optimal organizational structure to align and maximize the output of digital solutions engineering and software delivery activities across the Department of Defense. It requires an assessment of existing organizational structures, an evaluation of potential courses of action, recommendations on optimal organizational structures, and transition recommendations for its implementation.
Long summary:

Requires policies to be established by Director of National Intelligence for artificial intelligence capabilities to amends the statute by updating a subsection reference, redesigning subsection (b) as subsection (c), and inserting a new subsection after subsection (a).

Requires the policy to create a plan on for private individuals or companies to notify federal agencies about specific risks or threats involving artificial intelligence. 

Assessing that articifical intelgience systems demonstrate increased capabilities in the generation of synthetic media and computer programming, has growing capablities for large-scale artificial intelligence models to be used by individuals, businesses, and governments, have dramatically increased the adoption, and the risks of misuse or failure increase as Artificial intellgince becuase more accessable.

Official name: 2023 UK AI Safety Summit Response (Microsoft)
Casual name: 2023 UK AI Safety Summit Response (Microsoft)
Short summary: Describes Microsoft's responsible AI development and deployment framework, encompassing multi-layered governance, red teaming and evaluation practices, cybersecurity and data input controls, and transparency mechanisms; establishes a joint Microsoft-OpenAI Deployment Safety Board for pre-release frontier model review; and supports a coordinated global licensing regime for frontier models.
Long summary:
Establishes a joint Microsoft-OpenAI Deployment Safety Board (DSB) for pre-release frontier model capability review, and supports a globally coordinated licensing regime for frontier model oversight.

Implements multi-layered responsible AI governance through the Responsible AI Council, Responsible AI Division Leads, and iterative risk mapping, measurement, and management across the product lifecycle.

Describes and implements red teaming practices at model and application levels, including AI-specific metrics and post-deployment monitoring pipelines.

Establishes cybersecurity controls for AI systems including Security Development Lifecycle (SDL)-based threat modeling, model weight encryption, access controls, and the Adversarial ML Threat Matrix developed with MITRE.

Describes Microsoft's Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure process and establishes a new AI-specific bug bounty program and responsible disclosure framework through the Frontier Model Forum.

Outlines data input controls, privacy practices, and General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) compliance for AI systems, and commits to defending customers against copyright claims through the Copilot Copyright Commitment.

Describes stakeholder-specific transparency and disclosure mechanisms and commits to an annual responsible AI transparency report and cross-industry collaboration through the Frontier Model Forum.

Establishes Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA)-based provenance standards and watermarking for identifying AI-generated content, and commits to expanding these capabilities across Microsoft products.

Implements iterative post-deployment abuse monitoring and misuse prevention, with continuous adjustment of security controls in response to new misuse patterns.

Describes AI safety research investments through the Accelerate Foundation Models Research (AFMR)= grant program and commits to expanding academic access to AI computing resources through the National AI Research Resource.

Official name: S3193 Algorithm Accountability Act 2025
Casual name: S3193 Algorithm Accountability Act 2025
Short summary: Amends Section 230 to impose a duty of care on social media platforms in the design and operation of recommendation algorithms, holding them liable for foreseeable bodily harm and removing liability protections for violations. Allows affected individuals to sue for damages while excluding smaller platforms and certain types of services.
Long summary:
Amends Section 230 of the Communications Act to introduce a duty of care for social media platforms using recommendation-based algorithms.

Requires these platforms to exercise reasonable care in the design and operation of algorithms to prevent foreseeable bodily injury or death.

Removes liability protection under Section 230 for platforms that violate this duty of care.

Exempts certain actions from this requirement, such as chronological sorting and user-initiated searches.

Allows civil actions against platforms if injuries arise due to non-compliance, voiding predispute arbitration agreements.

Long summary:
Establishes a New York State commission to study and make recommendations on the regulation of AI, robotics, and automation.

Tasks the commission with examining existing state laws, comparative policies, liability issues, impacts on employment, confidentiality, regulatory impacts on the technology industry, and public sector AI applications.

Defines membership requirements for the thirteen-member commission, to be appointed by state government officials and university chancellors.

Authorizes the commission to conduct hearings and gather testimony to thoroughly analyze relevant AI issues.

Requires the commission to publish a final report for state leadership at least thirty days before the act's expiration.

Official name: AI Innovation and Development for Efficiency Act of 2024
Casual name: AI Innovation and Development for Efficiency Act of 2024
Short summary: Requires the National Science Foundation to support research on AI-enabled efficient technologies, focusing on smart grids, transportation, and emissions reduction. Emphasizes impact assessments and prioritizes projects at EPSCoR institutions. Mandates reporting findings and recommendations to Congress.
Long summary:

Requires the National Science Foundation to consider projects that support research on the impact of artificial intelligence on efficient technologies.

Determines that research may focus on smart grids, transportation, agriculture, waste and emissions reduction, and resource conservation, while also assessing adoption feasibility and evaluating public understanding of AI technologies.

Requires to fund project must include an impact assessment evaluating the energy consumption of the AI technologies involved. 

Requires the director must also give special consideration to research conducted at EPSCoR institutions.

Create recommendation no later than 18 months after enactment of this Act that shall work with multiple agencies.

Requires the Director to submit a report within 4 years of enactment to designated Senate and House committees on the results of the research conducted under this section.

Casual name: Preparing Election Administrators for AI Act
Short summary: Requires the Election Assistance Commission to issue voluntary guidelines addressing AI use and risks in election administration. Includes guidelines on AI benefits, cybersecurity risks, accurate information sharing, and combating election disinformation impacting public trust.
Long summary:
Cites the Act as the “Preparing Election Administrators for AI Act”.

Requires the Election Assistance Commission to submit a report with voluntary guidelines to Congress, State and local election offices, and the public within 60 days of enactment.

Includes guidelines addressing the risks and benefits of using AI in election administration.

Addresses the cybersecurity risks posed by AI technologies in elections.

Guides on managing AI-generated information to ensure the sharing of accurate election information.

Provides guidance on how to distribute and generate information from AI and prevent it from creating disinformation during elections that undermines public trust.

Official name: National New Generation AI Standards System Construction Guide
Casual name: National New Generation AI Standards System Construction Guide
Short summary: Establishes a comprehensive AI standards system emphasizing basic, security, ethical, and industry-specific standards. Targets development in areas like machine learning, natural language processing, smart vehicles, and healthcare. Prioritizes international cooperation, security, and ethical considerations by 2023.
Long summary:
Establishes a comprehensive framework for developing a national AI standards system, emphasizing the integration of ethical, security, and privacy standards.

Aims to clarify top-level design and develop key standards by 2023, focusing on data, algorithms, systems, and industry-specific applications.

Outlines an AI standards architecture, comprising eight categories: basic standards, supporting technologies, software/hardware platforms, general/niche technologies, products/services, industry applications, and security/ethics.

Emphasizes the need for international cooperation and alignment with global standards to ensure high-quality AI development.

Prioritizes the development of standards for key technologies such as machine learning, natural language processing, computer vision, and quantum computing.

Addresses AI applications across various sectors, including healthcare, transportation, finance, and smart cities, ensuring cross-industry standardization.

Focuses on security and ethics, proposing standards for AI data, algorithms, models, and application security, alongside ethical guidelines for impactful AI use.

Official name: Utah HB 464 (Social Media Amendments)
Casual name: Utah HB 464 (Social Media Amendments)
Short summary: Establishes legal recourse for Utah minors against social media companies for mental health harm from excessive use of algorithmically curated services. Requires parental consent and sets usage limits for minors. Prohibits waiving protections and specifies severability of provisions.
Long summary:
Enacts new provisions governing minors' use of algorithmically curated social media services.

Allows Utah minors or their parents to sue social media companies if minors suffer adverse mental health outcomes from excessive use of such services.

Defines "adverse mental health outcome" and "excessive use," setting presumption rules that favor establishing causation by social media design elements unless companies prove compliance with specific usage restrictions.

Requires social media companies to limit minor usage to under three hours daily, block access during night hours, require parental consent, and disable certain engagement-driven features to avoid liability.

Prohibits waivers of rights provided by these regulations, ensuring public policy enforcement and protecting private rights of action.

Conveys state's responsibility to protect minors from mental health risks associated with social media usage and mandates corrective legislative actions for safeguarding against such harms. 

Repeals existing sections related to social media platform age requirements and protections, effective May 1, 2024, with some provisions effective October 1, 2024.

Official name: Utah HB 31 (Unaccompanied Minors in Autonomous Vehicles)
Casual name: Utah HB 31 (Unaccompanied Minors in Autonomous Vehicles)
Short summary: Establishes the Autonomous Vehicles and Unaccompanied Minors Workgroup to review and recommend on-demand autonomous vehicle networks' issues, especially concerning unaccompanied minors. Requires an annual report to the Transportation Interim Committee. Repeals the section on January 1, 2023.
Long summary:
Establishes the Autonomous Vehicles and Unaccompanied Minors Workgroup in Utah.

Comprises various representatives, including government officials and industry members.

Chairs the workgroup by appointed members of the House of Representatives and the Senate.

Requires the workgroup to review issues related to on-demand autonomous vehicle networks and unaccompanied minors.

Requires a large public transit district to provide staff support.

Mandates that the workgroup present annual reports and legislative recommendations to the Transportation Interim Committee.

Sets a repeal date for this section as January 1, 2023.

Official name: New York S933 (Establishes the position of chief artificial intelligence officer)
Casual name: New York S933 (AI Officer)
Short summary: Establishes a Chief Artificial Intelligence Officer to regulate AI use in New York, developing policies, oversight, risk management, and governance standards. Creates an advisory committee to support AI policy development and ensure compliance with state and federal laws.
Long summary:
Establishes a definition for "artificial intelligence" (AI) and "automated decision-making systems" within New York's state technology law, excluding basic software from these definitions.

Creates the Office of Artificial Intelligence, headed by a Chief Artificial Intelligence Officer appointed by the governor, tasked with developing AI policies and governance, coordinating state AI activities, and providing guidance on AI usage.

Charges the office with investigating resources needed for AI adaptation, recommending discontinuation of harmful AI systems, and annually reporting on AI use in government.

Forms an Advisory Committee for State Artificial Intelligence Policy to advise the Chief AI Officer on best practices, policy, and research, with representatives appointed by state leadership.

Exempts the AI Office and Advisory Committee from some director oversight, allowing independent operation within the state technology office.

Official name: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026, Section 1086 ("Framework for reforming technology transfer and foreign disclosure policies")
Casual name: FY2026 NDAA, Section 1086 ("Framework for reforming technology transfer and foreign disclosure policies")
Short summary: Requires the Secretary of Defense to create a framework for revising technology transfer and foreign disclosure policies, accommodating advanced technologies like artificial intelligence. Instructs updates to the National Disclosure Policy and mandates annual audits of license denials.
Long summary:
Directs the Secretary of Defense to produce a framework to revise technology transfer and foreign disclosure policies, emphasizing emerging and advanced technologies like AI.

Requires guidelines to balance technology protection with information sharing.

Includes recommendations for updating the National Disclosure Policy to incorporate AI and other advanced technologies.

Requires mechanisms to streamline approval processes and enhance transparency.

Mandates the consolidation of technology security and foreign disclosure approvals.

Requires updated directives detailing responsibilities in technology transfer.

Establishes metrics for evaluating policy effectiveness and mandates annual audits of denied license applications.

Instructs regular engagement with defense industry stakeholders, including nontraditional contractors.

Requires submission of the framework and annual reports to congressional defense committees, detailing improvements and industry feedback incorporation.

Allows reports to be unclassified but may include a classified annex.

Official name: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026, Section 233 ("Limitation on use of funds for certain navy software")
Casual name: FY2026 NDAA, Section 233 ("Limitation on use of funds for certain navy software")
Short summary: Prohibits expending funds on Navy's unmanned vessel software unless the Secretary of the Navy reports program schedules, cost estimates, performance assessments, and capability delivery assessments to congressional defense committees, and the Chief of Naval Operations validates operational user needs.
Long summary:
Prohibits the use of funds for the Navy's autonomy baseline manager or common control system for unmanned surface vessel programs unless specified conditions are met.

Requires the Secretary of the Navy to submit to congressional defense committees the original and current schedule of key deliverables, cost estimates, test and experimentation reports, and a market assessment from the Defense Innovation Unit.

Requires an assessment that program capabilities meet or exceed industry standards.

Requires the Chief of Naval Operations to validate that the program meets the operational needs of the Navy to congressional defense committees.

Requires the CAIO to evaluate, oversee, and facilitate the responsible adoption of AI and machine learning to inform decisions and support programs and operations.

Designates the CAIO as the principal advisor to the Secretary of State on the ethical use of AI and advanced analytics in diplomacy.

Mandates the CAIO to possess skills in data analytics, AI, machine learning, and organizational change management.

Requires the Chief Information Officer to consult with the CAIO on scaling AI capabilities across software applications.

Defines “artificial intelligence” as per section 238(g) of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2019.

Casual name: Department of State Authorization Act, Sec. 303 ("AI-enabled influence operations task force")

Long summary:

Requires the Task Force to collaborate with private industry and academia to develop digital content provenance detection techniques.

Mandates internal coordination within the Department on AI-enabled disinformation issues.

Directs the Task Force to create a unified international approach for standards and frameworks to counter AI-enabled disinformation.

Requires the Task Force to identify necessary tools and resources for detecting AI-enabled disinformation, producing counter-messaging, expanding digital literacy, and coordinating with various stakeholders.

Involves representatives from various relevant offices in the Task Force.

Defines key terms including "artificial intelligence" and "digital content provenance."

Allocates $250 million for the development, production, and integration of wave-powered unmanned underwater vehicles.

Earmark $250 million for advancing the artificial intelligence ecosystem, with an emphasis on defense applications.

Official name: S2367 AI Accountability and Personal Data Protection Act 2025
Casual name: S2367 AI Accountability and Personal Data Protection Act 2025
Short summary: Establishes liability for using individuals' data without express prior consent, including AI training. Permits private legal actions for violations. Invalidates predispute arbitration agreements for such claims. Requires transparent disclosure of third-party data use. Sets a federal minimum standard without preempting stronger state laws.
Long summary:
Establishes a federal tort for any individual or entity that appropriates, uses, collects, processes, sells, or otherwise exploits an individual's data without express, prior consent.

Defines key terms such as “artificial intelligence,” “generative artificial intelligence system,” and “covered data.”

Allows individuals to bring civil actions against violators and recover compensatory and punitive damages, injunctive relief, and attorney’s fees.

Requires explicit disclosure and consent for data use by third parties, invalidating consent obtained through coercion or bundled with general terms.

Excludes application of predispute arbitration agreements, ensuring individuals can pursue judicial recourse.

Applies a minimum standard for data protection, allowing states to enforce more stringent protections.

Mandates that courts, not arbitrators, decide the applicability of the Act to disputes, preventing reliance on arbitration clauses.

Ensures specific third-party data usage disclosures to individuals, invalidating non-specific or passive consent.

Requires the development of multilingual resources promoting AI literacy.

Directs the dissemination of these materials, possibly through a public website and multimedia campaigns.

Requires the Commission to develop a national strategy to address opportunities and challenges in AI literacy, ensuring continued U.S. global AI leadership.

Instructs the submission of this strategy to Congress and mandates periodic reviews and updates.

Ensures coordination of Federal Government efforts for strategy implementation.

Defines the composition of the Commission, chaired by the Director of the Office of Science and Technology Policy, including representatives with AI expertise from multiple government departments and sectors.

Official name: HR7064 AI in Health Care Efficiency and Study Act 2025
Casual name: HR7064 AI in Health Care Efficiency and Study Act 2025

Directs the study to include evaluation of AI in reducing administrative burdens, improving data interoperability, and enhancing cybersecurity measures against threats like ransomware.

Instructs the Secretary to consult with various stakeholders including NIST, NIH, developers, and healthcare providers during the study.

Mandates a report, due 6 months after the study, detailing findings, existing AI tool assessments, recommendations for future AI-related research, and policy options to Congress.

Ensures any AI deployment supports administrative efficiency and strong patient privacy protections.

Instructs the appropriate entities to assist small businesses in evaluating AI in their operations.

Provides information, guidance, and training on using AI, including best practices and applications for data protection, cybersecurity, regulatory compliance, and improving customer trust.

Requires outreach to small businesses to promote the use of AI.

Defines 'artificial intelligence' according to the meaning in the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020.

Official name: San Francisco Generative AI Guidelines
Casual name: San Francisco Generative AI Guidelines
Short summary: The San Francisco Generative AI guidelines basically establish citywide requirements for the responsible use of generative AI by San Francisco personnel. It also mandates human oversight, fact-checking, and transparency disclosures under Chapter 22J. Furthermore, it prohibits deepfakes or AI-driven decision-making without expert review. It also restricts the use of public AI tools as it requires documentation and an inventory of enterprise systems. It also imposes governance, auditing, and compliance duties to protect privacy, equity, and public trust.
Long summary:
Establish mandatory guardrails for generative AI (GenAI) use by City personnel, applying to all employees, contractors, consultants, volunteers, and vendors working on behalf of the City of San Francisco. This means that it requires human accountability for all AI-generated content. 

Furthermore, it mandates transparency and disclosure for public-facing or sensitive AI use under Chapter 22J. In short, it requires documentation of GenAI systems in the City’s inventory, direct notice to impacted individuals when AI substantially contributes to work product. 

It also limits which AI tools can be used and how they are used. This allows City-approved enterprise tools for certain tasks. It also strongly discourages public or consumer AI tools. This requires prior approval for non-approved systems. 

It also bans high-risk or deceptive uses of AI, including creating deepfakes, impersonating real people, fabricating public input, hiding AI use, or allowing AI to make final decisions that affect people’s rights, services, safety, or legal matters without expert human review.

Casual name: FY2026 NDAA, Section 1048 ("Authorization of Eastern Regional Range Complex for multi-domain operations and robotic autonomous systems training, testing, and experimentation")

Conduct training, experimentation, and testing of robotic autonomous systems, and develop tactics and procedures for unmanned systems.

Evaluate emerging technologies and systems in contested cyber and electromagnetic environments.

Authorize consultation with the FCC and NTIA for spectrum access to support operations.

Official name: Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024, Sec. 758 ("Implementation of Technology for Classification and Declassification")
Casual name: Intelligence Authorization Act FY 2024, Sec. 758 ("Technology for Classification and Declassification")

Requires developers and deployers to conduct pre-deployment evaluations and annual impact assessments with independent audits to identify potential harms or biases from AI systems.

Casual name: HR 6461 READ AI Models Act 2025

Authorizes reimbursable agreements and collaboration with other Federal agencies to enhance research effectiveness.

States that OpenAI will include the publication of a system card in every new AI system, which informs users of key factors impacting system behavior.

States that OpenAI has initiated a reporting mechanism for responsible disclosure of dangerous capabilities among AI labs, focusing on national security-related risks.

Details OpenAI's emphasis post-deployment monitoring for misuse, security controls to protect intellectual property and data, and the development progress provenance techniques to identify AI-generated content.

States that OpenAI implemented data input controls and provides mechanisms for users to opt-out of their data being used for AI training.

Casual name: Advancing Governance, Innovation, and Risk Management for Agency Use of Artificial Intelligence

Long summary:

Requires agencies to develop AI strategies to responsibly adopt AI, including generative AI, and to facilitate sharing and reuse of AI models, code, and data.

Obligates agencies to annually inventory AI use cases, identifying those impacting rights and safety, and to report on associated risks and mitigation strategies. Encourages removing barriers to AI innovation related to IT infrastructure, data, and workforce while ensuring compliance with existing federal policies and risk management practices.

Ensures transparency and public trust through periodic reporting on AI oversight activities, with unclassified information made publicly available where possible.

Casual name: Indiana Senate Bill 2024-150 (AI and Cybersecurity)
Short summary: Establishes an Artificial Intelligence Task Force to study AI use and impact, requiring state agencies to inventory all artificial intelligence technologies in use, being developed or considered by the agency.
Long summary:
Establishes an Artificial Intelligence Task Force to study AI technologies used by Indiana state agencies, assessing their benefits, risks, and impacts on privacy, civil rights, and legal protections.

Requires the Task Force to produce annual reports with findings and recommendations for policies or legislation to govern AI use by state agencies.

Mandates state agencies compile and submit inventories of AI technologies in use or development, detailing vendors, intended use, data security measures, benefits, risks, and financial implications.

Official name: West Virginia HB 5690 (Artificial Intelligence Task Force)
Casual name: West Virginia HB 5690 (AI Task Force)
Short summary: Establishes the West Virginia Task Force on Artificial Intelligence to recommend AI definitions, policies, legislation, and best practices. Requires submission of a report by July 1, 2025, and terminates the Task Force upon report submission or on July 1, 2025.
Long summary:
Establishes the West Virginia Task Force on Artificial Intelligence within the Office of the Governor. 

Specifies membership including representatives from government, industry, education, and health sectors, appointed by various authorities. 

Charges the Task Force with responsibilities such as recommending AI definitions for legislation, identifying relevant state agencies for AI policy oversight, and developing best practices for public sector AI use. 

Mandates recommendations on AI's impact on employment, protecting individual rights and data, and addressing AI use in education. 

Requires the Task Force to assess current AI use in state agencies and consider extending its mandate to keep pace with AI advancements. 

Obligates submission of a comprehensive report by July 1, 2025, after which the Task Force terminates. 

Requires initial appointments within 90 days and quarterly meetings, with administrative support provided by the Office of Technology.

Official name: California Assembly Bill 2876 (2024)
Casual name: California AB 2876 (Pupil instruction: media literacy: artificial intelligence literacy: curriculum frameworks: instructional materials) (2024)
Short summary: Require the California Instructional Quality Commission to incorporate AI literacy in curriculum frameworks for mathematics, science, and history-social science and consider AI literacy in its criteria for evaluating instructional materials when they are next adopted by the state board after January 1, 2025.
Long summary:
Defines "AI literacy" as the knowledge, skills, and attitudes related to how artificial intelligence works, including its principles, concepts, applications, limitations, implications, and ethical considerations.

Mandates the commission to consider incorporating AI literacy content into the mathematics, science, and history-social science curriculum frameworks when those frameworks are next revised after January 1, 2025.

Requires the commission to consider including AI literacy in the criteria for evaluating mathematics, science, and history-social science instructional materials adopted by the state board after January 1, 2025.

Official name: Colorado House Bill 24-1468
Casual name: Colorado HB 1468 (Artificial Intelligence Impact Task Force)
Short summary: Creates the Artificial Intelligence Impact Task Force to develop policy recommendations against AI system risks and algorithmic discrimination affecting consumers and workers. Requires diverse membership and adherence to transparency standards. Mandates a report by February 2025 to the legislature and governor; task force sunsets in 2027.
Long summary:
Establishes the Artificial Intelligence Impact Task Force in Colorado to develop policy recommendations for protecting consumers and workers from harms posed by AI systems and automated decision systems.

Defines key terms, including "artificial intelligence system," "automated decision system," and "algorithmic discrimination."

Requires the task force to consider transparency, disclosure, and protection measures against algorithmic discrimination, and to recommend best practices for the ethical and equitable use of AI.

Mandates the task force to include diverse representation and expertise in AI and related fields, with a focus on communities that have been historically impacted by algorithmic discrimination.

Obligates the task force to convene by September 1, 2024, and submit a report of findings and recommendations to the legislature and governor by February 1, 2025.

Official name: Florida House Bill 919
Casual name: Florida HB 919 (AI Use in Political Advertising)
Short summary: Requires political ads using generative AI to include a disclaimer. Specifies disclaimer format based on media type. Imposes first-degree misdemeanor for non-compliance. Authorizes complaints to the Florida Elections Commission with expedited hearings. Effective July 1, 2024.
Long summary:
Establishes requirements for disclaimers on political advertisements using generative artificial intelligence in Florida.

Defines "generative artificial intelligence" as a system emulating input data to create synthetic content.

Requires advertisements with AI-generated content depicting actions that did not occur to include a prominent disclaimer stating "Created in whole or in part with the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI)."

Specifies format requirements for disclaimers across various media, including print, television, internet, and audio.

Imposes first-degree misdemeanor penalties for failure to include required disclaimers, in addition to other civil penalties.

Authorizes any person to file complaints with the Florida Elections Commission for violations of this requirement.

Mandates expedited hearings for such complaints.

Sets an effective date of July 1, 2024.

Official name: California Senate Bill 942 (2024)
Casual name: California AI Transparency Act (2024)
Short summary: Enacts the California AI Transparency Act, requiring AI providers with over 1 million users to offer free AI detection tools and include clear disclosures in AI-generated content. Establishes enforcement through civil penalties and mandates preservation of disclosure features in licensed products.
Long summary:
Enacts the California AI Transparency Act, requiring covered providers of generative AI systems with significant user bases to offer free AI detection tools that allow users to assess whether image, video, or audio content was created or altered by the provider’s system.

Requires AI-generated content to include both manifest and latent disclosures, identifying it as AI-generated, with details about the provider and system.

Requires ongoing evaluation of AI-detection tools while prohibiting the collection or retention of personal information from detection tool users, except in specific opt-in scenarios.

Mandates disclosure capabilities to be clear and permanent, and demands that licenses for GenAI systems include obligations for content disclosures.

Imposes civil penalties of $5,000 per violation for non-compliance, with each day constituting a separate violation.

Excludes specific entertainment products from applicability and sets the operative date as January 1, 2026.

Official name: Virginia Senate Bill 487
Casual name: Virginia SB 487 (Use of Artificial Intelligence by Public Bodies)
Short summary: Requires JCOTS to analyze AI use by public bodies, focusing on procurement, implementation, and discrimination prevention. Instructs JCOTS to assess creating a Commission on AI to advise on related issues. Mandates JCOTS's report submission to legislative committees by December 1, 2024.
Long summary:
Mandates the Joint Commission on Technology and Science (JCOTS) to conduct an analysis of artificial intelligence use by public bodies in Virginia.

Requires JCOTS analysis to include examination public bodies' policies & procedures on AI procurement, implementation, and assessment of AI systems. 

Requires JCOTS analysis to also ensure public bodies continually review the impact of AI systems to avoid discrimination and unlawful outcomes against an individual or a group.

Mandates consideration of establishing a Commission on Artificial Intelligence to advise the General Assembly on AI-related issues.

Requires JCOTS to evaluate the composition and duties of this commission based on specified criteria.

Obligates JCOTS to report findings and recommendations to relevant House and Senate committees by December 1, 2024.

Official name: Iowa Senate Bill 2435
Casual name: Iowa S 2435 (Appropriations to the Education System), Division III, Section 6. ("GENERAL FUND APPROPRIATIONS")
Short summary: Allocates $2.8 million to Iowa State University for expanding AI, cybersecurity, computer science, and related technology programs to address workforce needs and foster innovation in digital agriculture, manufacturing, and biosciences.
Long summary:
Allocate $2.8 million to Iowa State University of Science and Technology to address workforce needs in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) by expanding degree and certificate programs in artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, computer science, and related fields.

Promote innovation in areas such as digital agriculture, manufacturing, water quality, vaccine delivery technologies, and biosciences with the allocated funds.

Ensure that the state board of regents and the institutions of higher learning governed by them do not reduce budgeted funds for their police departments for the fiscal year 2024-2025.

Require the state board of regents to submit a quarterly financial report to the general assembly, including details on five-year graduation rates for the regents universities in the report for the quarter ending December 31, 2024.

Official name: AI Fraud Deterrence Act
Casual name: AI Fraud Deterrence Act
Short summary: Increases penalties for financial crimes like mail fraud, wire fraud, bank fraud, and money laundering when committed with the assistance of artificial intelligence, including higher fines (up to $2 million) and longer prison sentences (up to 30 years), and define "artificial intelligence" as per the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020.
Long summary:
Amends penalties for financial crimes committed with the assistance of artificial intelligence, increasing fines to $1,000,000 and imprisonment terms.

Mandates fines for AI-assisted money laundering to be not more than $1,000,000 or thrice the value of the funds involved, with imprisonment terms up to 20 years.

Defines "artificial intelligence" according to the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020 definition.

Codifies increased penalties and definitions within the United States Code to deter AI-assisted financial crimes.

Official name: Maryland House Bill 622
Casual name: Maryland HB 622 (Industry 4.0 Technology Grant Program)
Short summary: Establishes a grant program for small and medium-sized manufacturers to adopt Industry 4.0 technologies, including AI. Allocates grants competitively, requiring matching funds. Creates a special fund for grants. Mandates annual budget appropriations to support the program until 2028.
Long summary:
Establishes the Industry 4.0 Technology Grant Program in Maryland's Department of Commerce to support small and medium-sized manufacturers in implementing advanced technologies, including artificial intelligence, to improve productivity and competitiveness.

Creates a special, nonlapsing Industry 4.0 Technology Grant Fund to provide financial support, with grants ranging from $25,000 to $500,000, requiring matching funds based on company size.

Reserves 20% of funds for manufacturers with 50 or fewer employees, allowing unused reserves to be reallocated to larger companies.

Requires grant recipients to report on fund usage within one year and mandates potential repayment if conditions are unmet.

Mandates the Governor to allocate $1,000,000 annually from 2024 to 2028 to the Fund.

Directs the Secretary to establish regulations for program implementation and commence the Act on October 1, 2023.

Official name: Modernizing Data Practices to Improve Government Act
Casual name: Modernizing Data Practices to Improve Government Act
Short summary: Defines artificial intelligence using existing legislation and includes AI in data governance. Requires the Chief Data Officer Council to identify AI opportunities and enhance data practices. Mandates biennial reports on AI use and data governance improvements in agencies.
Long summary:
Amends title 44 of the United States Code to define "artificial intelligence" and "data governance."

Requires Chief Data Officers to focus on data management and governance, including AI-related data standards.

Mandates the Chief Data Officer Council to enhance data governance, evaluate new technologies, and ensure AI use improves government operations.

Directs the Council to report on data governance progress and provide recommendations for AI and emerging technology adoption, including data transparency and privacy.

Obliges the Director to issue guidance on implementing Council recommendations and maintain a public inventory of Chief Data Officers.

Sets reporting requirements for the Comptroller General on the Council's effectiveness and challenges.

Establishes a sunset clause, rendering the section ineffective after December 14, 2031.

Prohibits the allocation of additional funds to implement the Act.

Official name: California Senate Bill 1120 (2024)
Casual name: California SB 1120 (Health care coverage: utilization review) (2024)
Short summary: Requires health care service plans and disability insurers using AI for utilization review to ensure compliance with clinical criteria, non-discrimination, transparency, and auditability. Prohibits AI from replacing provider decision-making or denying services based on medical necessity.
Long summary:
Requires health plans and disability insurers that use AI for utilization review or work with an entity that uses AI for utilization review to ensure that the AI is lawful; nondiscriminatory; based on clinical information; open to review; responsibly uses patient data; does not supplant health care provider decisionmaking; and does not cause harm to the enrollee.

Prohibits health plans and disability insurers that use AI for utilization review from denying, delaying, or modifying health care services based on medical necessity and mandates that only licensed health care professionals make determinations of medical necessity by evaluating clinical issues on a case-by-case basis; clarifies that state departments may issue guidance to help implement federal rules regarding AI in healthcare; and requires that health plans have a medical director review and report on the health care service plan's compliance with requirements

Casual name: Connecticut SB 1103 (AI Automated Decision Making)
Short summary: Requires state agencies to inventory and annually assess AI systems for discrimination risks, and mandates the development of AI governance policies by February 2024. Prohibits AI implementation without impact assessments and establishes a working group to recommend AI best practices and future legislation.
Long summary:
Mandates the Department of Administrative Services to inventory AI systems used by state agencies and make this information publicly available, identifying the system's vendor, capabilities, use, and impact assessment before implementation. 

Directs the Office of Policy and Management to establish AI policies and procedures for state agencies by February 1, 2024, governing procurement and implementation to avoid discrimination.

Requires ongoing assessments of AI systems to prevent unlawful discrimination or disparate impacts, in accordance with established procedures, and prohibits state agencies from implementing AI systems without such impact assessments.

Obligates the Judicial Department to inventory its AI systems, adopt AI governance policies, and continuously monitor system use to prevent discrimination.

Prohibits state contracts with businesses unless they require compliance with applicable AI statutory requirements.

Creates a working group to recommend ethical AI use in government, assess federal AI guidelines, and propose potential legislation modeled after the OSTP AI Bill of Rights, reporting findings by February 1, 2024.

Official name: Washington Senate Bill 5838 (2024)
Casual name: Washington S 5838 (Artificial Intelligence Task Force)
Short summary: Establishes a task force to assess AI use and trends, recommending guidelines and legislation. Requires examination of AI's impact on safety, privacy, and rights. Mandates reports by 2026. Defines AI-related terms. Task force expires June 30, 2027.
Long summary:
Establishes a task force in Washington State to assess current AI uses and trends and recommend guidelines and potential legislation for AI systems.

Composes the task force of an executive committee with appointed members from legislative bodies, the attorney general's office, technology experts, industry representatives, and community advocates.

Charges the task force with examining AI development and use, focusing on safety, privacy, and civil rights, and submitting recommendations to the legislature.

Mandates a literature review on AI public policy issues, analysis of existing legal protections, and proposals for ethical AI guidelines and high-risk AI use identification.

Tasks the office of the attorney general with administering the task force, retaining consultants, and supporting subcommittee formation.

Requires the task force to deliver reports to the governor and legislature, with a final report due by July 1, 2026.

Expires the task force on June 30, 2027.

Official name: Alabama House Bill 172
Casual name: Alabama HB 172 (Use of Materially Deceptive Media in Elections)
Short summary: Criminalizes distributing AI-generated materially deceptive media to influence elections. Exempts media with clear disclaimers. Permits injunctive relief by affected parties. Provides exceptions for certain media outlets and satire. Effective October 1, 2024, with penalties for second offenses.
Long summary:
Prohibits the distribution of materially deceptive media, produced by AI, within 90 days before an election if intended to harm a candidate's reputation or influence voting patterns.

Defines "materially deceptive media" as AI-generated content falsely depicting individuals in actions or speech they did not partake in.

Allows exceptions if disclaimers clearly state the media's manipulation and provide source citations for edited content.

Classifies violations as Class A misdemeanors, with repeat offenses within five years as Class D felonies.

Permits the Attorney General, depicted individuals, candidates, and voter-representing entities to seek permanent injunctive relief against violators.

Excludes distributors without knowledge of deception or intent to harm from violations, including media entities distributing content as part of legitimate news coverage.

Protects satire and parody, provided they don't rely on AI for impersonation.

Effective October 1, 2024.

Official name: Nebraska L 1284 (Teacher Incentive Programs), Sec. 2.
Casual name: Nebraska L 1284 (Teacher Incentive Programs), Sec. 2.
Short summary: Creates the Dyslexia Research Grant Program for Nebraska businesses researching AI-based writing assistance for dyslexia. Limits total grants to $500,000 from the Education Future Fund. Requires compliance; misuse triggers legal action to recover funds. Allows State Board rulemaking.
Long summary:
Create the Dyslexia Research Grant Program, administered by the State Department of Education, to support research on AI-based writing assistance for individuals with dyslexia.

Allow privately owned businesses in Nebraska researching AI writing tools for dyslexia to apply for grants, using a prescribed form.

Limit the total grant awards to $500,000, intended to be funded by the Education Future Fund.

Require all grant funds to be used specifically for researching AI tools that use aggregate writing analytics to help develop literacy plans for dyslexic students.

Mandate notification of the Attorney General if grant funds are misused, prompting a civil action to recover funds, which are then credited back to the Education Future Fund.

Authorize the State Board of Education to adopt rules and regulations to implement the program.

Official name: Improving Diagnosis in Medicine Act of 2024
Casual name: Improving Diagnosis in Medicine Act of 2024
Short summary: Establishes a research program to improve diagnostic safety and quality, including integrating AI-enabled tools. Requires expert panel consultation for data needs, involving the Chief AI Officer. Forms an interagency council to enhance research, policy, and collaboration in diagnosis improvement.
Long summary:
Amends the Public Health Service Act to establish a comprehensive research program on diagnostic safety and quality, focusing on reducing diagnostic errors and integrating AI tools.

Directs funding for new and existing research centers and mandates stakeholder engagement to enhance diagnostic quality and safety.

Requires the convening of an expert panel, including the Chief Artificial Intelligence Officer, to recommend data types and sources for research improvement.

Establishes an Interagency Council on Improving Diagnosis in Health Care, including members from AI-related departments, to enhance diagnosis quality and identify research gaps.

Mandates the creation of a strategic federal plan to improve diagnosis, with updates and progress reports submitted biennially to Congress.

Authorizes appropriations for these initiatives from 2025 to 2029, ensuring sustained financial support for improving diagnostic practices and integrating AI solutions.

Official name: Idaho House Bill 575
Casual name: Idaho HB 575 (Disclosing Explicit Synthetic Media)
Short summary: Criminalizes disclosing or threatening to disclose explicit synthetic media without consent if it causes distress, is intended to harass, or is used for blackmail. Defines terms, provides penalties, and exemptions. Excludes certain services from liability unless they aid disclosure of explicit synthetic material.
Long summary:
Establishes the crime of disclosing or threatening to disclose explicit synthetic media without consent, intending to cause distress or obtain valuables, punishable as a misdemeanor or felony for repeat offenders.

Defines "explicit synthetic media" as AI-altered images or videos depicting sexual conduct involving identifiable individuals without their engagement.

Exempts disclosures for lawful purposes, such as criminal investigations, public interest reporting, scientific research, or legal proceedings.

Excludes liability for interactive computer services and telecommunications providers for third-party content, unless they intentionally aid disclosures.

Declares provisions severable, ensuring unaffected sections remain valid if parts are invalidated.

Declares an emergency and sets the effective date for July 1, 2024.

Official name: Maryland House Bill 1128
Casual name: Maryland  H 1128  (Talent Innovation Program and Fund )
Short summary: Establishes the Talent Innovation Program to enhance AI job training using innovative financing. Creates a nonlapsing Talent Innovation Fund to support the program, including AI sector initiatives. Allows fund investments and requires annual reporting to government officials starting in 2025.
Long summary:
Establishes the Talent Innovation Program in the Maryland Department of Labor to increase access to high-quality job training, with a focus on industries such as artificial intelligence.

Creates the Talent Innovation Fund as a special, nonlapsing fund to support the program, including job training and talent financing mechanisms.

Requires the program to conduct pilots, research, and stakeholder engagement to develop sustainable talent financing approaches.

Mandates an initial pilot program focused on the cybersecurity sector to expand regional cyber ranges for job training.

Authorizes the Department to provide grants and funding to various entities and individuals for training and support services.

Directs the State Treasurer to invest the fund's money, with interest earnings credited to the fund.

Compels the Department to adopt regulations and report annually on program activities and fund utilization to state leadership.

Official name: Idaho House Bill 2472
Casual name: Idaho HB 2472 (Managed Care Reform and Patient Rights Act), Sec. 30
Short summary: Requires utilization review programs using algorithmic processes to ensure clinical peers make adverse determinations, comply with accreditation standards, and include policies for algorithm verification. Establishes registration every two years with proof of compliance. Sets appeal procedures for adverse determinations.
Long summary:
Amends the Managed Care Reform and Patient Rights Act to require utilization review programs using algorithmic automated processes to ensure that only clinical peers make adverse determinations based on medical necessity.

Mandates these programs to register with the Department of Insurance every two years and provide proof of compliance with Health Utilization Management Standards or equivalent standards.

Requires licensed physicians with relevant board certifications to establish criteria for these automated processes and verify their accuracy.

Obliges health care plans to have appeals procedures, allowing appeals to be filed orally or in writing, with decisions rendered within specified timeframes.

Ensures confidentiality of patient-specific information obtained during utilization reviews, restricting access to authorized individuals.

Permits adverse determination appeals to an external independent review, with potential further appeals to the Department if found arbitrary or capricious.

Authorizes the Department to issue corrective actions or cease and desist orders for non-compliance.

Official name: West Virginia House Bill 3214
Casual name: West Virginia H 3214 (Road Optimization Assessment Data Pilot Program)
Short summary: Creates the "Road Optimization and Assessment Data Road Pilot Program" using AI and ML for road condition assessment. Requires data collection via GPS, laser systems, and video imagery in Monongalia and Preston Counties. Aims for predictive road maintenance over three years.
Long summary:
Creates the "Road Optimization and Assessment Data Road Pilot Program" to study alternative methods for assessing and financing road maintenance. 

Mandates the use of Machine Learning (ML) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) to evaluate road conditions in Monongalia and Preston Counties.

Requires the Commissioner of Highways to promulgate rules for legislative approval concerning data collection and road assessment.

Instructs the Division of Highways employees to drive all roads in the pilot counties for data capture.

Utilizes GPS, geotagged positioning, and laser measuring systems to assess road geometry and conditions.

Employs video documentation and reflectometer systems for comprehensive road condition analysis.

Requires biannual data capture and processing over three years to track road condition changes and provide predictive maintenance analysis.

Official name: California Assembly Bill 1831 (2024)
Casual name: California AB 1831 (Child Pornography Crimes)
Short summary: Prohibits the creation, distribution, possession, and exhibition of AI-generated child sexual assault material (CSAM) in California and imposes severe penalties.
Long summary:
Clarifies that child sexual assault material (CSAM) generated by artificial intelligence (AI) is obscene and prohibits the creation, distribution, and possession of this material in California.

Defines AI as a machine-based system that can infer from inputs how to generate outputs that influence environments.

Punishes the distribution or possession of AI-generated CSAM depicting minors under 18 engaging in sexual conduct with imprisonment and fines and classifies this conduct as a felony in certain cases 

Exempts law enforcement; medical, scientific, educational activities; lawful conduct between spouses; and legally emancipated children under 18 from these provisions.

Specifies enhanced penalties for possessing certain material and for repeat offenders

Specifies enhanced penalties for using government-owned computers, computer networks, or property for CSAM-related offenses.

Requires revenue from fines to support sexual assault investigator training and services for human trafficking victims.

Becomes operative only if Senate Bill 1381 is enacted by January 1, 2025.

Official name: California AB 2355 (2024), Section 8
Casual name: California AB 2355 (AI in political advertisements), Sec 8
Short summary: Requires political advertisements generated or altered by AI to disclose “Ad generated or substantially altered using artificial intelligence.” Permits enforcement actions for non-compliance. Defines AI-related terms and specifies disclosure methods. Exempts service providers' rights under Section 230.
Long summary:
Requires committees creating or distributing qualified political advertisements to include a disclosure stating, “Ad generated or substantially altered using artificial intelligence,” in a clear and conspicuous manner.

Mandates that the disclosure be displayed or spoken as specified in existing sections of the Government Code.

Excludes alteration or negation of rights under Section 230 of Title 47 of the U.S. Code for interactive service providers.

Authorizes the Commission to seek injunctive relief or pursue administrative or civil remedies if committees fail to comply with disclosure requirements.

Defines "artificial intelligence" and specifies conditions under which media is considered "generated or substantially altered using artificial intelligence.”

Clarifies that immaterial alterations, such as cosmetic adjustments or resizing, do not qualify as being substantially altered by artificial intelligence.

Specifies that non-compliance does not constitute a misdemeanor.

Official name: Executive Order on Advancing United States Leadership in Artificial Intelligence Infrastructure (EO 14141)
Casual name: Executive Order on Advancing United States Leadership in Artificial Intelligence Infrastructure (EO 14141)
Short summary: Requires federal agencies to identify, solicit proposals for, and lease federal lands suitable for AI infrastructure and related clean energy projects. Requires the Secretary of State to develop a plan to coordinate AI infrastructure development with U.S. allies and partners, including workforce development.
Long summary:
Requires federal agencies to identify, solicit proposals for, and lease federal lands suitable for AI data centers and related clean energy projects, with the aim of full-capacity operation by the end of 2027.

Emphasizes high labor standards and community collaboration, among other factors, in the selection of sites for projects to account for community health, public safety, and ecological risks and harms.

Mandates cybersecurity, AI model evaluation, supply-chain protection, and other requirements for AI infrastructure developed pursuant to the executive order.  

Directs the Secretary of Energy to facilitate grid interconnection for AI infrastructure developed pursuant to the executive order. 

Calls for an expedited permitting processing for federal sites hosting AI infrastructure and related clean energy projects.  

Directs relevant agencies to take additional enumerated measures to expedite permitting and power procurement for AI infrastructure nationwide.

Requires the Secretary of State to develop a plan for robust engagement with allies on global AI infrastructure development, which includes exchanging best practices for workforce development and ensuring security and resilience in international supply chains.
