Grants competitive grants and fellowships for organizations advancing risk assessment through AI. Adds AI and machine learning to the list of research areas that the Director of the National Science Foundation can award grants to. Makes awards available for supporting basic research to advance critical minerals mining strategies that involve AI. Requires the development and testing of models to inform implementation of government-wide data infrastructure for statistical activities. Requires a study on U.S. higher education's AI research capacity and an annual update to key technology focus areas.
Long summary:
Instructs the Director of the National Science Foundation (Director) to develop a report on the need and feasibility as well as construct plans to implement a program to recruit and train the next generation of AI professionals in US government. Mandates that the report include statistical data on the federal AI workforce, assessments of current and future demand for AI expertise across the federal government and the ability of higher education institutions to prepare students to meet this demand, and an evaluation of the need for and feasibility of establishing a scholarship-for-service program for AI professionals in US government, as well as the possibility of leveraging existing programs such as the Federal Cyber Scholarship-for-Service Program. 

Authorizes the Director and other appropriate agency heads to establish a Federal AI scholarship-for-service program to recruit and train AI professionals to achieve the missions of US government. Requires the Director, in coordination with other agency heads, to establish criteria such as excellence in AI education and the ability to attract diverse students to designate qualified institutions of higher education that shall be eligible to participate in the program. Requires the program to provide scholarships through qualified higher education institutions to students pursuing fields of study related to AI, provide scholarship recipients with temporary appointments related to work on AI in the federal government, prioritize placement of scholarship recipients in executive agencies, identify opportunities to promote multidisciplinary programs of study, support capacity building for educational institutions to enable them to train the next-generation AI workforce, create courses in technology ethics for scholarship recipients, and award fellowships to masters and doctoral students who are pursuing degrees or research in AI and related fields. Instructs scholarship amounts to cover a student’s tuition and fees for not more than 3 years with an additional stipend, and obligates scholarship recipients to work for a period of time equivalent to the length of the scholarship in the AI mission of the US government entity or affiliated entity.

Instructs the Director to establish competitive awards to institutions to advance knowledge of risk assessment including the utilization of AI in our ability to understand and predict extreme events and natural hazards, create engineered system solutions and develop instrumentation for innovation in resilient infrastructure, and advance research on multidisciplinary wildfire science and behaviors related to increasing resilience.

Amends Section 506(a) of the America COMPETES Reauthorization Act of 2010 by adding AI and machine learning to the list of research areas that fall under information technologies for manufacturing that the Director can award grants to.

Instructs the Director to make competitive awards to institutions to support basic research to advance critical minerals mining strategies to make better use of domestic resources and eliminate national reliance on minerals subject to supply chain disruptions, including the application of AI for geological exploration of critical minerals and the application of machine learning for detection and sorting of critical minerals.

Requires the Director to conduct or support the development of a study on AI research capacity at US institutions of higher education. Requires the study to, at minimum, address which universities are putting out significant peer-reviewed AI research based on quantity and number of citations, which factors of these universities such as computing power enable their research, promising practices at these universities for advancing diversity, equity, and inclusion in AI research programs, geographic diversity of universities that have AI research-enabling factors, and how universities that are not currently top producers of AI research could improve, including potential pilot programs that the federal government could develop or support to help universities produce AI research.

Instructs the Director, in consultation with the Director of the Office of Management and Budget and the interagency committee established under the National AI Initiative Act of 2020, to develop and test models to inform the implementation of a government-wide data linkage and access infrastructure for statistical activities.

Requires the Director to identify, and annually review and update a list of not more than 10 key technology focus areas, which includes AI, machine learning, autonomy, and related advances.

Official name: 21 CFR § 864.3750 ("Adjunctive hemodynamic indicator with decision point")
Casual name: 21 CFR § 864.3750 ("Adjunctive hemodynamic indicator with decision point")
Collections: U.S. regulations, executive orders, and agency policies
Short summary: Subjects the adjunctive hemodynamic indicator with decision point -- a device that monitors medical conditions relating to blood flow -- to special regulatory controls, including mandating a risk assessment and the reporting of clinical data proving the devices's efficacy.
Long summary:
Classifies the adjunctive hemodynamic indicator with decision point -- a device that monitors medical conditions relating to blood flow -- into the Food & Drug Administration's class II, requiring special controls. That set of controls:

Requires a full description of the technical parameters of the device's software and sensors.

Requires a risk assessment for the device.

Requires mechanisms designed to mitigate the impact of user error or failure of any subsystem components (signal detection and analysis, data display, and storage) on the accuracy of the device's output.

Requires statistical documentation, based on robust clinical data, of the device's efficacy. The accuracy of the device's algorithm must be tested using an independent dataset. 

Requires a usability assessment to demonstrate that the risk of misinterpretation of the status indicator is appropriately mitigated.

Requires detailed product labeling.

Casual name: 21 CFR § 870.2785 ("Software for optical camera-based measurement of pulse rate, heart rate, breathing rate, and/or respiratory rate")
Collections: U.S. regulations, executive orders, and agency policies
Short summary: Classifies software for optical camera-based measurement of pulse rate, heart rate, breathing rate, and/or respiratory rate into the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's class II, requiring special controls. Those controls require comprehensive hazard analysis and risk assessment; clinical testing data demonstrating the software's efficacy; a usability assessment; and detailed product labeling.
Long summary:
Classifies the Oxehealth Vital Signs device -- which uses software to enable camera-based measurement of pulse rate, heart rate, breathing rate, and/or respiratory rate -- into the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's class II, requiring special controls. The set of special controls:

Requires a full characterization of the technical parameters of the device's software, as well as documentation of a cybersecurity vulnerability and management process to assure software functionality.

Requires the results of verification and validation testing based on a comprehensive hazard analysis and risk assessment of the software and associated device, to include a description of all mitigations for user error or failure of any subsystem components (including signal detection, signal analysis, data display, and storage) on output accuracy.

Requires clinical data demonstrating the software and device's efficacy, including comparing the device's output with a clinically accurate patient-contacting relevant comparator device in an accurate and reproducible manner.

Requires a human factors and usability engineering assessment that evaluates the risk of improper measurement.

Requires detailed product labeling, to include instructions for using the device and interpreting its output; warnings of factors that may impede proper functionality; and a description of the measurements the device takes.

Long summary:
Classifies the Cognoa ASD Diagnosis Aid, a machine-learning software program and device used in the diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder, into the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's class II regulatory category requiring special controls. The mandated special controls are as follows:

Requires clinical performance testing to demonstrate that the device performs as intended under anticipated conditions of use, including an evaluation of sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value using a reference method of diagnosis and assessment of patient behavioral symptomology.

Requires software verification, validation, and hazard analysis to be provided for the device. Software documentation must include a detailed, technical description of the algorithm(s) used to generate device output(s), and a cybersecurity assessment of the impact of threats and vulnerabilities on device functionality and user(s).

Requires a usability assessment that must demonstrate that the intended user(s) can safely and correctly use the device.

Requires detailed product labeling that includes instructions for the device's use and a summary of any clinical testing done to demonstrate the device's functionality.

Long summary:
Requires disclosure of inputs, outputs, components, and limitations of image analysis algorithms used in medical image analyzers.

Requires performance testing that demonstrates the algorithms meaningfully improve the detection of abnormalities during patient radiographs.

Requires appropriate software documentation including device hazard analysis, software specs, traceability analysis, pass/fail criteria, and cybersecurity.

Requires a detailed summary of the methodology behind the performance testing.

Casual name: 21 CFR § 870.2345 ("Electrocardiograph software for over-the-counter use")
Collections: U.S. regulations, executive orders, and agency policies
Short summary: Labels over-the-counter use of electrocardiograph software devices as Class II (special controls), which requires manufactures to conduct hazard analysis of detection algorithms in the devices.
Long summary:
Labels over-the-counter use of electrocardiograph software devices as Class II (special controls), which requires manufactures to verify, validate, and conduct hazard analysis of detection algorithms in the devices.

Mandates manufactures to produce clinical performance testing results that shows the performance characteristics of the detection algorithm by sensitivity and either specificity or positive predictive value.

Requires manufacturers who fail to conduct non-clinical performance testing to validate detection algorithm performance using a previously adjudicated data set.

Requires human factors and usability testing to demonstrate that the user can correctly interpret the device output and understand when to seek medical care.

Official name: Limited Applicability of Consumer Financial Protection Act's “Time or Space” Exception With Respect to Digital Marketing Providers
Casual name: Limited Applicability of Consumer Financial Protection Act's “Time or Space” Exception With Respect to Digital Marketing Providers
Collections: U.S. regulations, executive orders, and agency policies
Short summary: Clarifies Section 1002 of the Consumer Financial Protection Act of 2010's definition of "service provider" to include digital marketing providers that use algorithmic models or other analytics to commingle the targeting and delivery of advertisements to consumers.
Long summary:
Clarifies Section 1002 of the Consumer Financial Protection Act of 2010's definition of "service provider" to include digital marketing providers that use algorithmic models or other analytics to commingle the targeting and delivery of advertisements to consumers, rendering those providers subject to the Act's prohibition on unfair, deceptive, or abusive acts or practices.

Outlines the ways in which digital marketers provide additional services beyond "time or space" and are materially involved in the development of content strategy -- often through the use of targeting and delivering algorithms -- thus qualifying them as "service providers" under the law.

Outlines specific circumstances in which digital marketers are and are not considered service providers under the CFPA; they qualify as service providers when using algorithms and data to target and deliver advertisements with certain characteristics, or when using algorithms and business-specific data to determine when to display specific advertisements to specific consumers.

Official name: Illinois HB53 2021
Casual name: AI Video Interview Discrimination Act
Short summary: Requires employers that rely solely on AI to analyze video interviews to report the demographic information of candidates who are and are not interviewed in person or hired so the state can identify if there is a racial bias in using AI.
Long summary:
Requires employers that rely solely on AI to analyze video interviews to collect information on the race and ethnicity of candidates who are and are not consequently interviewed in person or hired and to report this information annually to the Illinois Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity.

Requires the Department to analyze the data reported and report annually to the Governor and General Assembly on whether the data discloses a racial bias in using AI.

Short summary: Requires employers who use AI to analyze video interviews of applicants in Illinois to notify and receive consent from the applicant, and explain the AI evaluation process.
Long summary:
Requires employers who use AI to analyze video interviews of applicants in Illinois to notify and receive consent from the applicant before the interview and provide information explaining how the AI system works and what characteristics it uses to evaluate applicants.

Requires employers to refrain from sharing applicant videos except what’s necessary to evaluate the applicant and delete videos, including any copies shared with other actors, upon applicant request within 30 days.

Casual name: Hawaii AI Advisory Committee Resolution
Short summary: Establishes an AI advisory committee in Hawaii to investigate how to implement, develop, and regulate AI in the state. Requires the committee to survey AI applications in other governments, methods for encouraging AI R&D in Hawaii, and potential dangers of, and regulatory systems for, integrating AI into state operations.
Long summary:
Establishes an AI advisory committee in Hawaii to investigate how to implement, develop, and regulate AI in the state; the committee will be composed of government, academic, and industry stakeholders.

Requires the committee to evaluate and make recommendations on AI applications in other governments, competitive advantages to be gained by integrating AI into Hawaii’s economy, methods for encouraging AI R&D in universities and private sector, the potential danger of integrating AI into state operations, and potential regulatory systems for AI. 

Requires the committee to submit a report of findings and proposed legislation to the Legislature before its convening in 2020.

Official name: Literacy in Future Technologies Artificial Intelligence Act
Casual name: LIFT AI Act
Short summary: Establishes awards for developing K-12 AI literacy curricula. Supports research and professional development to enhance AI literacy. Defines AI literacy as the ability to use and interpret AI effectively and ethically.
Long summary:
Establishes the "LIFT AI Act" to advance AI literacy in K–12 education.

Empowers the Director of the National Science Foundation to award competitive grants to higher education institutions or nonprofits for developing AI literacy curricula and evaluation methods.

Endorses AI literacy education to prepare a skilled workforce and maintain U.S. leadership in AI.

Recognizes the importance of AI literacy in mitigating ethical challenges and adapting to rapidly evolving AI technologies.

Supports the development of curricula focussed on AI competency, AI literacy evaluation tools, and professional development courses in AI literacy for educators.

Encourages incorporating AI literacy in existing curricula, emphasizing responsible AI use.

Official name: AI Ads Act
Casual name: AI Ads Act
Short summary: Amends the Federal Election Campaign Act to include AI-generated content in prohibitions against fraudulent misrepresentation and solicitation. Expands the scope to cover any person misrepresenting candidates, parties, or committees for any purpose, not just candidates themselves.
Long summary:
Amends the Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971 to include fraudulent misrepresentation through content generated with artificial intelligence (AI) under its prohibitions.

Clarifies that fraudulent misrepresentation of campaign authority or solicitation of funds includes the use of AI-generated content.

Extends the prohibition against fraudulent misrepresentation beyond candidates to any person misrepresenting candidates, political parties, or committees for any purpose.

Broadens the scope of prohibited fraudulent solicitation to encompass any candidate, political party, or fictitious political organization, not just those directly involving a candidate or party employee.

Expands the provisions to cover AI-generated content used in misrepresentation or solicitation within political campaigns, ensuring comprehensive regulation of AI's role in electoral fraud.

Official name: S.4306, Five AIs Act 2024
Casual name: Five AIs Act 2024
Short summary: Establishes the "Five AIs Strategic Artificial Intelligence Working Group" to coordinate AI initiatives among Five Eyes countries. Tasks include enhancing AI interoperability, testing systems, managing data, leveraging commercial AI technologies, and sharing results with allies. Controls export of technical data.
Long summary:
Establishes the "Five AIs Strategic Artificial Intelligence Working Group" within 90 days to coordinate AI initiatives among the Five Eyes countries (Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the UK, and the US).

Requires the Secretary of Defense and Director of National Intelligence to lead and designate a head for the Working Group.

Mandates the Working Group to develop strategies for AI interoperability, ethical frameworks, and innovation among the Five Eyes countries.

Instructs testing and evaluation of AI systems for intelligence sharing and battlespace awareness.

Emphasizes leveraging commercial AI technologies and managing data-informed AI systems.

Requires submission of a plan within 60 days and biannual reports on the Working Group's activities.

Specifies control of knowledge and technical data by individual countries under their export laws.

Allows termination of the Working Group on September 30, 2028, with possible extension for national security interests.

Official name: Iowa (2019) SB 302 (Automated Driving System Motor Vehicles)
Casual name: Iowa (2019) SB 302 (Automated Driving System Motor Vehicles)
Short summary: Permits driverless vehicles on Iowa highways if compliant with safety laws and manufacturer certification. Requires insurance for autonomous vehicles and mandates accident reporting. Allows on-demand driverless vehicle networks. Centralizes regulation authority, prohibiting local restrictions or taxes on automated vehicles.
Long summary:
Defines key terms like "automated driving system" and "driverless-capable vehicle" relevant to motor vehicles operated by autonomous systems.

Allows the operation of driverless-capable vehicles on public highways without a human driver present, provided they meet safety and compliance standards.

Requires system-equipped vehicles to operate within designated operational domains and comply with state traffic and safety laws unless exempted.

Mandates financial liability coverage for system-equipped vehicles before they can operate on public highways.

Stipulates that automated vehicles involved in accidents must remain at the scene and report to law enforcement, holding vehicle owners accountable for compliance.

Permits the operation of on-demand driverless-capable vehicle networks for transporting persons or goods, integrating with digital transport services.

Grants exclusive governance and regulatory authority over automated systems to the state department, prohibiting additional local regulations or taxes on such systems.

Official name: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency Securing AI Task Force Act
Casual name: CISA Securing AI Task Force Act
Short summary: Establishes a CISA Task Force to coordinate AI safety and security efforts, assess initiatives, address workforce gaps, and promote secure AI adoption. Requires biannual briefings to Congress. Ceases effect five years post-enactment.
Long summary:
Establishes a Task Force within the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to coordinate efforts related to AI safety and security.

Requires coordination of Agency efforts to improve the safe and secure design, development, adoption, and deployment of AI.

Ensures Agency collaboration in interagency and nongovernment AI-related initiatives.

Mandates assessment and evaluation of Agency safety initiatives to address AI challenges.

Leverages expertise to use AI in defending against cyber threats.

Coordinates efforts to advise stakeholders on AI-related cyber risks.

Identifies AI workforce gaps and proposes solutions.

Promotes secure adoption of AI-based software.

Recommends new initiatives for AI safety and security.

Ensures AI efforts meet privacy, civil rights, and civil liberties standards.

Supports publication and accuracy of the Agency’s AI use inventory.

Mandates biannual briefings to Congress on Task Force activities.

Sunsets the Act 5 years after enactment.

Official name: No AI Audits Act
Casual name: No AI Audits Act
Short summary: Limits IRS use of AI for audits by requiring guidance as rule-making and adherence to NIST explainability principles. Requires Comptroller General to audit and report on IRS's AI use. Mandates that only IRS staff can initiate taxpayer investigations.
Long summary:
Limits the Internal Revenue Service's (IRS) use of artificial intelligence (AI) for audits or investigations.

Requires any IRS guidance on AI for audits to follow rule-making procedures under Section 553 of Title 5, U.S. Code.

Prohibits the IRS from conducting audits or investigations initiated by AI unless the AI meets explainability principles set by the National Institute of Standards and Technology.

Defines "artificial intelligence" according to the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020.

Mandates the Comptroller General to audit and report on the IRS's AI use, including a cost-benefit analysis and the impact on taxpayer rights.

Stipulates that IRS investigations or examinations must be initiated by a staff investigator, with documentation including the investigator's contact information.

Official name: Artificial Intelligence Weapon Accountability and Risk Evaluation Act of 2024
Casual name: AWARE Act of 2024
Short summary: Requires the Secretary of Defense to create a ledger of AI-enabled military systems with regular updates and requires a comprehensive risk assessment process covering dependability, cybersecurity, privacy, and bias. Requires annual assessments, annotations for exports, and public reporting to ensure transparency and accountability.
Long summary:
Mandates the Secretary of Defense to create a ledger of all uses by the Department of Defense of AI-enabled weapon, targeting, and decision support systems within three years.

Requires the ledger to be a structured, indexed database that is regularly updated.

Calls on the Secretary of Defense to develop a risk assessment process to evaluate dependability, cybersecurity, privacy, and civilian harm risk for each AI system.

Mandates annual reevaluations of each system, and when an AI model receives an update, a new system is procured, or a new weapons review is conducted.

Requires annotations in the ledger when AI systems are shared, exported, or used internationally, noting additional risks.

Obligates annual progress reports and submissions to Congress, including the ledger and risk assessment findings, to be publicly accessible

Official name: Dubai International Financial Centre Data Protection Regulations, Regulation 10 ("Personal data processed through autonomous and semi-autonomous systems")
Casual name: DIFC Data Protection Regulations, Regulation 10
Authority: Government of the United Arab Emirates
Short summary: Establishes comprehensive obligations for entities deploying or operating AI systems that process personal data. Requires clear notices, transparency, accountability, and ethics in AI design. Mandates compliance with audit and certification requirements, ensuring systems process data for human-defined purposes.
Long summary:
Requires Deployers and Operators of autonomous and semi-autonomous systems to adhere to personal data processing principles.

Mandates clear notification to users of such systems about underlying technology and data processing purposes, with detailed descriptions of system capabilities and safeguards.

Obligates the provision of evidence of compliance with audit and certification requirements, and human intervention algorithms in cases of bias or legal non-compliance.

Imposes design requirements focused on ethics, fairness, transparency, security, and accountability.

Prohibits systems from processing personal data unless in compliance with human-defined purposes and legal frameworks.

Forbids use in high-risk processing without compliance with certification requirements and appointment of an Autonomous Systems Officer.

Deems Deployers as Controllers and Operators as Processors of personal data.

Allows data subjects to challenge processing outcomes per applicable law.

Official name: Connecticut (2017) SB 260
Casual name: Connecticut SB 260 (Autonomous Vehicles)
Short summary: Establishes a pilot program for municipalities to allow testing of fully autonomous vehicles, requiring operator oversight and insurance. Prohibits testing on limited access highways. Forms a task force to study and recommend regulations for autonomous vehicles, with progress reporting mandated.
Long summary:
Establishes a pilot program for testing fully autonomous vehicles in up to four municipalities, requiring participation from autonomous vehicle testers and compliance with specific operational constraints.

Mandates that autonomous vehicle testers register vehicles, provide liability insurance, and ensure a licensed operator is present who can take manual control if needed.

Prohibits testing on limited access highways and allows the Secretary of the Office of Policy and Management to halt testing if public safety is at risk or compliance issues arise.

Creates a task force to study autonomous vehicle regulation, evaluate national and state standards, and assess the pilot program, providing reports on findings and recommendations for potential legislation.

Requires the Secretary to submit annual reports on the pilot program's progress to the General Assembly’s transportation committee.

Stipulates the task force composition, appointment deadlines, and reporting requirements, with a final report due by January 1, 2019.

Official name: California (2017) AB 1444
Casual name: California (2017) AB 1444 (Livermore Amador Valley Transit Authority)
Short summary: Authorizes the Livermore Amador Valley Transit Authority to test autonomous vehicles without drivers in Dublin, California, contingent on insurance, controlled testing, and compliance certifications. Requires safety-related data collection and local law enforcement cooperation. Prohibits testing if statewide regulations are adopted by specified deadlines.
Long summary:
Authorize the Livermore Amador Valley Transit Authority to conduct a shared autonomous vehicle (SAV) demonstration project in the City of Dublin, California, for vehicles lacking traditional controls such as a steering wheel or pedals.

Require vehicles to operate below 35 miles per hour.

Mandate obtaining insurance or self-insurance of five million dollars and approval from local authorities.

Certify compliance with federal safety standards and National Highway Traffic Safety Administration guidance, ensuring vehicles operate only in approved conditions.

Require disclosure of personal data collection to participants and establish a law enforcement interaction plan.

Oblige reporting of accidents and disengagements during testing to the Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV).

Allow the DMV to require data collection for safety evaluations.

Specify that the section becomes inoperative on May 1, 2018, and repeals on January 1, 2019.

Clarify that this project does not influence statewide autonomous vehicle regulations.

Official name: New Jersey (2019) Assembly Joint Resolution 164
Casual name: New Jersey (2019) AJR 164 (Advanced Autonomous Vehicle Task Force)
Short summary: Establishes the "New Jersey Advanced Autonomous Vehicle Task Force" to study and recommend integration laws for advanced autonomous vehicles. Requires issuing a report evaluating existing laws, suggesting pilot programs, and recommending safe integration on public roads within 180 days after its initial meeting.
Long summary:
Establishes the "New Jersey Advanced Autonomous Vehicle Task Force" to study and recommend policies for the safe integration of autonomous vehicles on state roads.

Comprises 11 members, including key state officials and public experts appointed by the Governor.

Mandates the task force to hold its initial meeting within 90 days of the law's effective date and to elect a chair from among its members.

Requires the task force to issue a report within 180 days after its first meeting, evaluating existing laws, proposing pilot programs, and suggesting legislative measures.

Entitles the task force to utilize the services of state employees and receive assistance from the New Jersey Motor Vehicle Commission, Department of Transportation, and Alan M. Voorhees Transportation Center.

Defines "advanced autonomous vehicle" as one with a driving automation level of 3, 4, or 5, per SAE J3016 standards.

Expires the act upon the report's submission.

Official name: Sensible Classification Act of 2023
Casual name: Sensible Classification Act of 2023
Short summary: Requires the Administrator of the Office of Electronic Government, in consultation with key defense, intelligence and declassification officials, to research and report on AI and machine learning solutions for efficient classification and declassification.
Long summary:
Mandates the research and recommendation of AI and machine learning solutions for efficient classification and declassification systems, to be interoperable across the Federal Government.

Requires the Administrator of the Office of Electronic Government to consult with key defense and intelligence agencies for technology implementation and submit a report on the recommended solution.

Official name: Federal AI Governance and Transparency Act
Casual name: Federal AI Governance and Transparency Act
Short summary: Establishes governance requirements for Federal AI systems to ensure actions align with laws, promote fairness, manage risks, and maintain transparency. Requires the development of AI charters and oversight, with provisions for public disclosure, privacy protection, and periodic evaluations.
Long summary:
Amends chapter 35 of title 44, United States Code, to establish Federal AI system governance requirements.

Instructs Federal actions involving AI to align with the Constitution, relevant laws, and policies, protecting civil rights and privacy.

Mandates the assessment and management of AI risks before deployment, ensuring AI outcomes remain ethical and accurate.

Requires transparency and explainability of AI systems' purpose, operations, and outcomes to maintain safety and security, and protect against vulnerabilities.

Obligates regular testing and oversight of AI applications to ensure they align with intended purposes and create mechanisms to deactivate AI systems that do not meet standards.

Instructs agencies to publicly disclose AI use to stakeholders and establish notification and appeal processes for AI-based decisions.

Establishes a Federal AI System Inventory for cataloging agency AI governance charters to be publicly available and regularly updated.

Official name: To direct the Director of the National Institutes of Health to establish a grant program to facilitate research regarding the use of generative artificial intelligence in health care, and for other purposes.
Casual name: H.R. 7381 (Health AI)
Short summary: Directs the NIH Director to establish a grant program promoting research on generative AI in healthcare. Prioritizes projects enhancing AI adoption, workforce development, reducing disparities, and improving underserved care. Supports AI applications in documentation, insurance, and customer service efficiency.
Long summary:
Establishes a grant program by the Director of the National Institutes of Health to fund research on the use of generative AI in health care.

Permits research to include enhancing note-taking, reducing administrative burdens, expediting insurance claims, improving customer service efficiency, and other health care improvements.

Prioritizes grants for entities promoting AI adoption in health care, investing in workforce development, mitigating workforce burnout, reducing health disparities, and improving care for medically underserved populations.

Defines eligible entities to include higher education institutions, nonprofit organizations, and various governmental agencies.

Defines "generative artificial intelligence" as AI producing content in response to prompts.

Official name: Tools to Address Known Exploitation by Immobilizing Technological Deepfakes on Websites and Networks Act
Casual name: TAKE IT DOWN Act
Short summary:
Amends the Communications Act to criminalize nonconsensual intimate deepfakes and requires platforms to remove deepfakes within 48 hours.

Grants the Federal Trade Commission enforcement authority over this act.
Long summary:
Amends the Communications Act to criminalize the non-consensual production and dissemination of pornography, especially when intended to cause harm or when involving minors.

Requires covered platforms to establish a takedown process for such depictions, and mandates them to remove the content within 48 hours upon valid request.

Levels criminal punishments, including imprisonment, on violators of this law.

Grants enforcement authority to the Federal Trade Commission.

Defines key terms relevant to the instrument, including "covered platform," "deepfake," and "intimate visual depiction."

Casual name: Safe and Secure Innovation for Frontier AI Act (SB 1047)

Short summary: Requires developers of frontier AI models to implement comprehensive safety and security protocols and detailed risk assessments. Requires annual audits, mandates incident reporting within 72 hours, creates a regulatory board and introduces plans for a public cloud computing cluster called CalCompute.
Long summary:
Requires developers of frontier AI models to implement comprehensive safety and security protocols, including cybersecurity protections, full shutdown capabilities, and detailed risk assessments.

Mandates annual independent audits and public disclosure of redacted audit reports and obligates developers to report AI safety incidents to the Attorney General within 72 hours.

Establishes policies for entities operating computer clusters to assess whether customers intend to use the clusters for training covered models.

Creates the Board of Frontier Models to update AI model thresholds and auditing requirements, ensuring alignment with technological advancements and best practices.

Imposes penalties for non-compliance, including civil penalties, injunctive relief, and punitive damages.

Introduces CalCompute, a public cloud computing cluster to support AI research and innovation, with a framework to be developed by a consortium.

Official name: Provisions on the Administration of Deep Synthesis Internet Information Services
Casual name: Provisions on the Administration of Deep Synthesis Internet Information Services
Short summary: Subjects deep synthesis technology in China to a variety of regulations, including restrictions on false or otherwise unwanted content, sending notification to individuals if their biometric information is being edited, and labelling deep synthesis content. Mandates security assessments and implementation of security measures.
Long summary:
Prohibits generative AI ("deep synthesis") systems in China from producing a variety of forms of unwanted content, including false information or content that harms lawful rights, national security and "social order."

Requires deep synthesis systems to verify the true identity of each of their users.

Requires deep synthesis developers to assess the security of their AI systems, including by assessing the systems' cybersecurity attributes and their ability to abide by relevant regulations.

Requires deep synthesis systems to notify any individuals whose biometric information is edited in the production of AI-generated content.

Requires the labelling or watermarking  of realistic deep synthesis content that could potentially mislead or confuse the public.

Requires deep synthesis developers to submit filings with the relevant authorities, and requires regulators to carry out inspections of deep synthesis systems.

Official name: STAND with Taiwan Act of 2023
Casual name: STAND with Taiwan Act
Short summary: Imposes sanctions on China if its military invades Taiwan, including blocking property, prohibiting trades, and investment restrictions. Targets Chinese officials, institutions, and entities involved in aggressive actions. Coordinates with allies for sanctions, allowing exceptions for national security or intelligence activities.
Long summary:
Mandates the imposition of sanctions on the People's Republic of China if the People’s Liberation Army initiates a military invasion of Taiwan. 

Requires sanctions against Chinese officials and entities involved in military campaigns or efforts undermining Taiwan's security and infrastructure.

Blocks property and imposes visa restrictions on identified Chinese officials and affiliates involved in military and coercive actions against Taiwan.

Prohibits U.S. financial institutions from investments that benefit Chinese government-controlled entities or priority sectors like artificial intelligence and other advanced technologies.

Bans the listing and trading of securities of Chinese entities on U.S. securities exchanges following an invasion.

Prohibits the importation of goods from China post-invasion unless exceptions for national security are made.

Grants the President authority to enforce sanctions and provides for penalties under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.

Official name: An Act concerning consumer protections in interactions with artificial intelligence systems.
Casual name: Colorado AI Act (SB 205)
Collections: Editors' Picks;U.S. state and local documents
Short summary: Establishes consumer protections and imposes disclosure, evaluation, and performance obligations on developers and deployers of high-risk AI systems that may generate algorithmic discrimination in making consequential decisions (related to employment, housing, health benefits, etc.).
Long summary:
Requires developers of high-risk AI systems to disclose foreseeable uses and risks of their systems, the inputs used in their training data, and how the systems were evaluated for performance.

Requires developers to display these disclosures publicly on their websites in a public use case inventory.

Mandates developers to disclose to the Colorado Attorney General, within 90 days, if their systems have caused or will likely cause algorithmic discrimination.

Requires deployers of high-risk AI systems to notify consumers of how AI is used to make consequential decisions and inform them of their right to opt out of the processing of their personal data.

Requires deployers to give consumers the opportunity to correct erroneous personal data and appeal adverse consequential decisions.

Mandates deployers to make all these disclosures publicly available on their websites.

Provides exemptions to the Colorado AI Act for certain deployers of high-risk AI systems including those who employ less than 50 people and do not use thier own data to train the system.

Grants the Colorado Attorney General exclusive authority to enforce all regulations laid out by this act and engage in any additional rulemaking necessary for the implementation and enforcement of this act.

Official name: Alabama (2019) SB 47
Casual name: Alabama (2019) SB 47 (Autonomous Commercial Vehicles)
Short summary: Authorizes autonomous commercial vehicles and teleoperation systems to operate without a conventional driver present. Mandates compliance with federal and state laws, registration, certification, and liability coverage. Assigns jurisdiction to Alabama's Department of Transportation. Specifies operator responsibilities and emergency protocols.
Long summary:
Authorizes autonomous commercial vehicles and vehicles with teleoperation systems to operate without a conventional driver physically present in Alabama.

Grants jurisdiction exclusively to the Department of Transportation over these vehicles and prohibits additional requirements by local entities.

Requires automated vehicles to comply with federal motor vehicle safety standards and maintain motor vehicle liability coverage of at least $2,000,000.

Establishes that the vehicle owner or lessee is considered the operator for legal compliance and that automated driving systems are licensed operators.

Mandates accident protocols requiring vehicles remain on the scene with prompt law enforcement notification.

Requires remote drivers to hold the appropriate licenses and obey state traffic laws, subject to alcohol and drug testing in cooperation with local law enforcement.

Clarifies that this act does not alter existing liability laws for vehicle stakeholders.

Specifies that the act is effective upon the Governor’s approval or enactment into law.

Official name: Kids Online Safety Act, Title II (Filter Bubble Transparency)
Casual name: Kids Online Safety Act, Title II (Filter Bubble Transparency)
Short summary: Requires platforms using opaque algorithms to notify users about their use and data application and mandates the option to switch to input-transparent algorithms.
Long summary:
Requires online platforms using opaque algorithms to provide users with clear notice about the use of such algorithms and how user-specific data is utilized. 

Mandates platforms to allow users to easily switch between opaque algorithms and input-transparent algorithms. Prohibits differential pricing or service denial based on a user's choice to use an input-transparent algorithm.

Empowers the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) to enforce these requirements as violations of unfair or deceptive practices under the Federal Trade Commission Act. 

Ensures that trade secrets, confidential business information, or privileged data are not required to be disclosed. Preserves the ability of platforms to allow users to personalize content restrictions and interactions.

Official name: Federal Improvement in Technology Procurement Act
Casual name: FIT Procurement Act
Short summary: Requires the Federal Acquisition Institute to incorporate experiential learning into certification programs within 18 months. Mandates a cross-functional ICT acquisition training program. Encourages off-the-shelf technologies and innovative procurement techniques. Reassigns AI training responsibility to GSA. Expands Commercial Solutions Opening Authority. Increases simplified acquisition threshold to $500,000. Requires Administrator to issue past performance guidance. Establishes a working group to address Federal vendor base issues.
Long summary:
Requires the Federal Acquisition Institute to incorporate experiential learning into key acquisition certification programs within 18 months.

Mandates the development and implementation of a cross-functional ICT acquisition training program, emphasizing market research, cloud computing, artificial intelligence, and cybersecurity.

Encourages the use of commercially available off-the-shelf technologies and innovative procurement techniques like oral presentations and product demonstrations.

Reassigns the responsibility for AI training requirements from the Office of Management and Budget to the General Services Administration.

Expands the Commercial Solutions Opening Authority to include commercial services and mandates public reporting and data collection on its use.

Increases the simplified acquisition threshold from $250,000 to $500,000.

Requires the Administrator to issue guidance on using past performance from a broader range of projects to increase competition.

Establishes a working group to address the shrinking Federal vendor base and recommends actions to remove barriers to qualified vendors.

Requires all AI-generated materials to be labeled with a watermark. 

Authorizes the federal government to establish requirements and standards for watermarks.

Enables the federal government to levy penalties against entities that violate the above stipulation.

Defines key terms including AI-generating entity, AI-generated material, and covered AI-generated material, specifying criteria for materials that must be watermarked.

Official name: Future of Artificial Intelligence Innovation Act of 2024
Casual name: Future of Artificial Intelligence Innovation Act of 2024
Short summary: Establishes the "Artificial Intelligence Safety Institute" to assist sectors in AI best practices and innovation. Requires AI research and standards development and mandates an international coalition for AI standards. Directs reporting on regulatory barriers and orders prioritized AI training data and Federal AI challenges.
Long summary:
Establishes the "Artificial Intelligence Safety Institute" to assist private and public sectors in developing best practices for AI assessment, provide technical assistance, and promote AI innovation, with a director appointed by the Under Secretary of Commerce for Standards and Technology.
Requires the Institute to conduct AI research, develop standards, and create guidelines for safe AI development and deployment, including generative AI and foundation models.

Mandates the formation of an international coalition to harmonize AI standards and support bilateral and multilateral AI research collaborations. Directs the Comptroller General to report on regulatory barriers affecting AI innovation and recommend legislative or administrative actions to enhance AI development.
Orders the development of prioritized public data sets for AI training and evaluation, and the establishment of Federal grand challenges in AI to stimulate research and commercialization in key areas.

Official name: Jobs of the Future Act of 2023
Casual name: Jobs of the Future Act of 2023
Short summary:
Requires the Secretary of Labor and the NSF Director to submit interim and final reports on AI's workforce impact. 

Mandates identification of necessary data, affected industries, and vulnerable demographics. 

Requires analysis of skills and education needed to work with AI.

Demands recommendations to mitigate displacement and promote equitable AI education. 

Requires collaboration with educational institutions, industry stakeholders, and federal agencies.
Long summary:
Requires the Secretary of Labor and the Director of the National Science Foundation to submit interim and final reports on AI's impact on the U.S. workforce.

Mandates these reports to identify data necessary for analyzing AI's workforce impact, industries most affected by AI, and demographics vulnerable to job displacement.

Requires analysis of skills, expertise, and education needed to work alongside AI and methods to deliver these to the workforce.

Demands recommendations to mitigate workforce displacement, promote knowledge sharing, and ensure underserved demographics have access to necessary AI-related education.

Requires collaboration with educational institutions, industry stakeholders, and federal agencies in preparing the reports.

Official name: Closing Loopholes for the Overseas Use and Development of Artificial Intelligence Act
Casual name: CLOUD AI Act

Long summary: Grants authority to the Secretary of Commerce to prohibit US persons and subsidiaries from supporting the use of remote or cloud integrated circuits listed under Export Control Classification Number 3A090 and 4A090 of the Export Administration Regulations by entities located in the People’s Republic of China or Macau.

Establishes rights for teenagers and parents to access, correct, and delete data.

Imposes strict security measures for processing children's and teenagers' data.

Casual name: TORNADO Act
Short summary: Requires the Under Secretary of Commerce to improve NOAA's communication system for hazardous events using methods such data analysis supported by artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies.
Long summary:
Requires the Under Secretary of Commerce for Oceans and Atmosphere to improve the communication system of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) for hazardous weather and water events to prevent loss of life and property.

Mandates the establishment of a hazard risk communication office to simplify and improve communication, using the latest social, behavioral, risk, and communication science research, including AI and machine learning technologies.

Instructs the Under Secretary to create a research program to modernize risk-based hazard communication and establish a pilot program for tornado hazard communication.

Official name: Modernizing Retrospective Regulatory Review
Casual name: Modernizing Retrospective Regulatory Review
Short summary: Requires agencies to use AI in retrospective reviews of regulations. Directs the Office of Management and Budget to issue guidance on AI use for identifying obsolete or burdensome regulations. Mandates agency plans and implementation strategies for these AI-assisted reviews.
Long summary:
Requires the Director of the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) to report on the Federal Government's progress in making agency regulations available in machine-readable format within 180 days after enactment.

Mandates the OMB Director to issue guidance within 18 months on using technology, including AI, for efficient and accurate retrospective reviews of regulations.

Obliges agency heads to submit a detailed plan within two years for implementing OMB guidance on retrospective reviews, identifying regulations for review, and including necessary data and analysis.

Directs agency heads to implement the submitted plan within 180 days of submission, focusing on retrospective regulatory reviews.

Official name: Kids Online Safety Act, Sec. 13 ("Filter Bubble Transparency Requirements")
Casual name: Kids Online Safety Act, Sec. 13 ("Filter Bubble Transparency")
Short summary: Requires covered internet platforms to inform users about opaque algorithm and user data usage and provide detailed algorithm operational information. Mandates offering an input-transparent algorithm alternative and prohibits discrimination against users of this alternative.
Long summary:
Requires providers of covered internet platforms that use opaque algorithms to notify users about their use and provide detailed information about their operation, including their features, user-specific data collection, and algorithmic inputs in an easily accessible form.

Mandates platforms to offer an easily accessible input-transparent algorithm alternative and prohibits discrimination, via methods like differential pricing, against users who choose the alternative.

Empowers enforcement by the Federal Trade Commission to treat violations as unfair or deceptive acts under the Federal Trade Commission Act.

Exempts small downstream providers and non-profit organizations from certain enforcement provisions.

Official name: DATA Privacy Act

Short summary: Establishes national data privacy standards for covered entities. Requires clear privacy notices. Mandates FTC regulations within one year. Imposes data minimization requirements. Long summary:

Requires covered entities to post clear, accessible privacy notices detailing data collection, processing, storage, and disclosure practices.

Mandates the FTC to create regulations within one year for reasonable, equitable, and non-deceptive data practices, including opt-out and affirmative consent mechanisms.

Imposes data minimization requirements, limiting data collection to what is necessary for specified purposes and ensuring timely deletion.

Empowers individuals with rights to access, correct, delete, and transfer their data.

Mandates large entities to appoint privacy protection officers to oversee compliance and advocate for privacy policies.

Directs the National Science Foundation to support research on privacy-enhancing technologies.

Grants enforcement authority to the FTC and state attorneys general, with civil penalties for violations.

Allocates resources to the FTC for enforcement and compliance activities.

Official name: To establish a Joint Autonomy Office in the Department of Defense, and for other purposes.
Casual name: HR3168, 2023, Joint Autonomy Office Establishment
Short summary: Establishes the Joint Autonomy Office in the Department of Defense, responsible for coordinating and accelerating the adoption of all-domain autonomous systems for operational users, and for developing a Department-wide classification framework for autonomous capabilities.
Long summary:
Directs the Secretary of Defense to establish the Joint Autonomy Office in the Department of Defense, responsible for coordinating and accelerating the adoption of all-domain autonomous systems for operational users, including through the adoption of commercial and defense best practices

Requires the Office to implement an all-domain enterprise autonomous systems software development and testing platform across DoD's classification levels, including an all-domain data acquisition and curation process to build and manage datasets; these datasets and platforms should be released to various services and acquisition programs as they mature.

Requires the Secretary of Defense to ensure that the Office has unlimited access to existing datasets regardless of classification level, and to introduce security protocols to protect data shared with or maintained by the Office.

Requires the Director of the Office must establish a Department-wide classification framework for autonomous capabilities, considering the complexity of autonomous systems, the necessity of human supervision or control, their applicability to various warfighting domains, and costs; the Director must submit this framework along with an explanation of its criteria and requirements to Congress, with updates released no less frequently than once every two years.

Requires the Director to develop and implement plans to standardize planning, resource and integration of autonomous capabilities across the Department; this includes a report assessing the Department's current efforts which identifies acquisition, training and evaluation gaps, as well as recommendations to address these.

Casual name: AI for National Security Act

Official name: Justice in Forensic Algorithms Act of 2024
Casual name: Justice in Forensic Algorithms Act of 2024
Short summary: Requires the Director of the National Institute of Standards and Technology to establish a program to create and maintain testing standards for computational forensic software, including AI-enabled software for evidence analysis.
Long summary:
Requires the Director of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to establish a program (“Testing Standards”) to create and maintain testing standards for computational forensic software, which includes software that relies on AI-enabled automated or semiautomated computational processes to analyze or interpret evidence.

Requires Testing Standards to solicit public input, address the potential for disparate impacts on protected groups, and specify requirements for publicly available documentation by developers, validation processes by those using computational forensic software, reports provided to defendants regarding software used, and how to test software and report results. 

Requires the Director of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to establish a program (“Testing Program”) that tests computational forensic algorithms according to the testing standards, using realistic and representative sample data and adversarial examples, and publishing results. Requires software to be re-tested after significant changes. 

Requires Federal law enforcement agencies only to use computational forensic software tested by NIST’s Testing Program and only after conducting an internal validation and making results publicly available. 

Requires evidence from computational forensic software to be admissible only if it has been submitted to NIST’s Testing Program and the developers waive legal claims against the defense analyzing or testing it. Requires information about the software (e.g., source code) and results from analyses by the software to be shared with the defendant.

Short summary: Requires the Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Communications and Information to conduct a study on accountability mechanisms to provide assurances that an artificial intelligence (AI) system is trustworthy and hold public meetings to gather feedback on the disclosure of information about AI systems.

Long summary: Amends Section 230 of the Communications Act of 1934 (which prevents providers of an interactive computer service from being held legally liable for third-party content) to remove this protection for claims involving the use or provision of generative artificial intelligence.

Official name: CONSULT Act of 2023
Casual name: CONSULT Act
Short summary: Prohibits the Department of Defense from awarding contracts to any individual or entity, including those producing AI-powered products and services, that has entered into working agreements with any organization from a blacklist of national security threats.
Long summary:
Requires the Department of Defense to refrain from awarding contracts to any individual or entity, including those producing AI-powered products and services, that has worked with any organization from a blacklist of national security threats.

Authorizes the DOD to punish any contractor of the Department who has a proven conflict of interest with the DOD and fails to disclose that conflict of interest.

Official name: Artificial Intelligence Environmental Impacts Act of 2024
Casual name: Artificial Intelligence Environmental Impacts Act of 2024
Short summary: Requires the Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency to submit a report to Congress on the environmental impacts of artificial intelligence
Long summary:
Requires the Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to study  the environmental impacts of artificial intelligence, with a report on its findings submitted to Congress within two years of the Act's enactment.

Mandates that the EPA study examine the energy, water consumption, and pollution throughout the full lifecycle of AI models, hardware, and data centers, considering the effects of location, power sources, and AI model design on these environmental impacts.

Requires that the EPA study assess the positive environmental impacts associated with the use of AI, such as optimizing systems for energy efficiency or automatically monitoring environmental changes.

Directs the Director of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to work with other government officials to form a consortium comprising academic, civil society, and industry representatives to assess and report on AI's environmental impacts, including the feasibility of open-source tools for measurement and recommendations to mitigate negative environmental effects.

Instructs the Director of NIST to work with other government officials and the consortium to establish a voluntary reporting system for entities to report on their AI systems' environmental impact.

Requires the Administrator of EPA, Secretary of Energy and Director of NIST to submit a joint report on the consortium's findings and its proposed voluntary reporting system within four years of the Act's enactment.

Prohibits artificial intelligence entities from being classified as artists under this act.

Requires the establishment of the Artist Compensation Royalty Fund to help provide financial support to those whose employment was negatively impacted by AI.

Mandates service providers to collect and deposit a living wage royalty fee and a percentage of non-subscription revenue into the Fund.

Authorizes the Fund Administrator to impose penalties for violations and non-compliance by service providers.

Casual name: Government Surveillance Reform Act of 2023, Title VII (Protection of Car Data from Warrantless Searches)
Short summary: Prohibits law enforcement from accessing vehicle data without a warrant, except with operator consent or in emergencies.
Long summary:
Prohibits law enforcement from accessing vehicle data without a warrant, except with operator consent or in emergencies. 

Defines "covered vehicle data" to include all onboard and telematics data in noncommercial vehicles, excluding certain data types like automotive software and geolocation data for traffic enforcement.
Prohibits the use of any vehicle data obtained in violation of these provisions as evidence in any legal proceedings. Amends the Driver Privacy Act of 2015 to align with these new restrictions on accessing vehicle data.

Official name: Preventing Deep Fake Scams Act
Casual name: Preventing Deep Fake Scams Act
Short summary: Establishes a task force to help formulate appropriate AI regulations in the financial services industry and requires the task force to produce a report for Congress with these recommendations within one year.
Long summary:
Establishes a task force examining the fraudulent use of artificial intelligence in the financial services sector.

Instruct the task force to solicit public feedback from industry and expert stakeholders, including depository institutions, credit unions, third-party vendors, and AI experts.

Directs the task force to produce a report for Congress within one year that identifies potential risks from AI misuse, and proposes AI fraud detection measures, among other legislative recommendations.

Terminates the task force 90 days after the final report's issue.

Official name: CONSENT Act
Casual name: CONSENT Act
Short summary: Establishes a private right of action against individuals sending unsolicited explicit visual depictions. Defines “machine-manipulated media” as AI-modified. Permits recipients to sue for damages and attorney fees. Exempts third-party providers and certain senders. Allows legal guardians to sue for minors. Permits minors to use initials for privacy. Ensures civil remedies do not supersede criminal laws. Includes severability clause.
Long summary:
Establishes a private right of action against individuals who send unsolicited visual depictions of sexually explicit conduct.

Defines “machine-manipulated media” as media substantially modified using machine-learning techniques.

Permits recipients to bring civil actions for statutory damages up to $500, compensatory damages for emotional distress, attorney fees, and injunctive relief.

Exempts third-party providers, good faith medical, educational, or law enforcement senders, and lawful adult websites from liability.

Allows legal guardians to sue on behalf of minors, incompetent, or incapacitated individuals.

Permits plaintiffs who were minors at the time of the incident to use initials for privacy in court documents.

Ensures civil remedies do not modify or supersede criminal laws.

Includes a severability clause to maintain the act’s provisions if parts are deemed unconstitutional.

Official name: National Patient Safety Board Act of 2024
Casual name: National Patient Safety Board Act of 2024
Short summary: Establishes the National Patient Safety Board (NPSB) to prevent patient safety events. Empowers NPSB to monitor, study, and propose solutions. Grants authority to request changes and review reports. Mandates annual audits. Forms Patient Safety Research Division. Requires privacy and AI compliance. Prohibits use in civil cases.
Long summary:
Establishes the National Patient Safety Board (NPSB) within the Office of the Secretary of Health and Human Services to prevent and reduce patient safety events.

Empowers the NPSB to support federal agencies in monitoring patient safety, studying causes of patient safety events, and formulating preventive solutions.

Grants the NPSB authority to request changes to patient safety measures, review reports, and make them publicly available within one year of study commencement.

Mandates annual audits and reports to Congress on progress, including detailed solutions and unaddressed needs.

Forms a Patient Safety Research and Development Division to aggregate and analyze patient-level data, identifying and anticipating safety events and disparities.

Requires compliance with privacy laws and AI governance frameworks, including NIST's AI Risk Management Framework and the Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights.

Prohibits the use of NPSB reports as evidence in civil liability cases but allows their use in developing standards of care.

Official name: Artificial Intelligence and Biosecurity Risk Assessment Act
Casual name: AI Biorisk Assessment Act
Short summary: Requires the Assistant Secretary for Preparedness and Response to conduct risk assessments and implement strategic initiatives that address threats to public health posed by AI, especially using AI to develop novel pathogens and bioweapons.
Long summary:
Requires the Assistant Secretary for Preparedness and Response to conduct risk assessments and implement strategic initiatives that address whether AI can develop novel pathogens, viruses, bioweapons, or chemical weapons, including monitoring and researching the global biological catastrophic risk landscape.

Requires the Assistant Secretary for Preparedness and Response to include a summary of the risk assessment above in the National Health Security Strategy.

Official name: National AI Commission Act
Casual name: National AI Commission Act
Short summary: Establishes the National AI Commission, an independent and bi-partisan commission in the legislative branch responsible for reviewing and recommending measures to mitigate AI risks and protect US leadership in AI development
Long summary:
Establishes the National AI Commission, an independent and bi-partisan commission in the legislative branch responsible for reviewing and recommending measures for the US to mitigate the risks and possible harms of AI, and to ensure US leadership in AI innovation and development.

Directs the National AI Commission to review the Federal Government's existing approach to AI oversight and regulation, including the existing distribution of oversight and regulatory authorities across various agencies, and to recommend governmental structures that may be needed to regulate powerful general-purpose AI systems.

Instruct the National AI Commission to submit an interim report to Congress and the President within six months, a final report with its findings and recommendations for a binding regulatory framework no later than six months after the interim report, and a follow-up report within one year of the final report's submission.

Requires the National AI Commission to comprise twenty commissioners appointed by the President and by Congressional leadership, with ten appointed by each party and co-chaired by a Democratic appointee and a Republican appointee.

Official name: National Critical Capabilities Defense Act of 2023
Casual name: National Critical Capabilities Defense Act
Short summary: Defines "national critical capability sector" as including artificial intelligence and defines "covered activities" as being related to "national critical capability sectors". Establishes the "Committee on National Critical Capabilities" to review U.S. investments abroad threatening national security.
Long summary:
Defines "national critical capabilities sector" as sectors, including artificial intelligence, subject to regulation described in the bill.

Establishes the "Committee on National Critical Capabilities" to review U.S. investments in foreign countries that may threaten national security.

Requires U.S. persons to notify the Committee of covered activities in critical sectors, including artificial intelligence, at least 90 days before initiation.

Instructs the Committee to review and potentially mitigate risks posed by such activities, with authority to prohibit or regulate investments.

Defines "covered activities" broadly to include acquisitions, joint ventures, and other engagements with foreign entities in critical sectors.

Identifies countries of concern, including China, Russia, and North Korea, where such investments are scrutinized more closely.

Grants the Committee authority to enforce compliance, including imposing civil penalties up to $250,000 or twice the amount of the covered activity.

Official name: AI Leadership Training Act
Casual name: AI Leadership Training Act
Short summary: Establishes an AI leadership training program for executive agencies. Requires annual training on AI capabilities, risks, and ethics. Mandates topics cover AI basics, risks, and constitutional issues. Obligates updates biennially. Demands participation metrics. Permits Congressional oversight. Sets a 10-year sunset clause.
Long summary:
Establishes an AI leadership training program for management officials, supervisors, and other designated employees in executive agencies, to be developed and implemented within 18 months.

Requires annual training to cover AI capabilities, risks, safety, ethics, Federal Government requirements, and best practices related to AI procurement, use, testing, evaluation, and auditing.

Mandates program topics include AI basics, benefits, risks, data significance, AI system failures, continuous refinement, risk mitigation, organizational considerations, and constitutional risks related to AI use.

Obligates updates to the program every two years to incorporate new AI information and ensure compliance with training requirements.

Demands metrics to measure participation and feedback for program improvements.

Permits Congress to request detailed information about the program materials and responsible personnel.

Encourages interaction with experts from various sectors as part of the training.

Sets a sunset clause for the program 10 years after enactment.

Official name: Digital Defense Content Provenance Act of 2023
Casual name: Digital Defense Content Provenance Act
Short summary: Requires the DMA Director to establish a DINFOS course on digital content provenance within one year. Mandates coverage of forgery challenges and authentication standards. Obligates a pilot program with an interim report by January 1, 2026, ending January 1, 2027. Defines key terms.
Long summary:
Requires the Director of the Defense Media Activity (DMA) to establish a course of education at the Defense Information School (DINFOS) on digital content provenance within one year of enactment.

Mandates the course to cover digital content provenance, challenges posed by digital content forgery, and the use of industry open technical standards for authenticating digital content.

Obligates the Director to start a pilot program within one year to assess the implementation of industry standards for digital content provenance for official Department media.

Sets termination date for the pilot program on January 1, 2027, with an interim report due by January 1, 2026, to assess effectiveness and feasibility.

Defines key terms including "digital content forgery" and "digital content provenance" to ensure clarity in implementation.

Official name: Promoting Resilient Supply Chains Act of 2023
Casual name: Promoting Resilient Supply Chains Act
Short summary: Requires the Assistant Secretary of Commerce to promote U.S. leadership in AI and strengthen supply chains. Mandates a resiliency program. Requires coordination with agencies. Promotes domestic manufacturing. Supports best practices. Mandates regular reporting on AI supply chains.
Long summary:
Requires the Assistant Secretary of Commerce to promote U.S. leadership in emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI), and strengthen critical supply chains and national security.

Mandates the establishment of a critical supply chain resiliency and crisis response program within the Department of Commerce, which includes mapping and monitoring AI supply chains.

Requires coordination with other agencies, industry, and international partners to identify vulnerabilities and prepare for supply chain shocks affecting AI technologies.

Promotes the growth of domestic manufacturing capacities for AI and other emerging technologies and encourages the relocation of manufacturing facilities to the U.S. or allied countries.

Supports the development and dissemination of best practices for supply chain resilience, including the use of blockchain and other technologies to authenticate and trace critical goods.

Mandates regular reporting on the state of AI and other emerging technology supply chains, including assessments of vulnerabilities and recommendations for enhancing resilience.

Official name: Disincentivizing Internet Service Censorship of Online Users and Restrictions on Speech and Expression Act
Casual name: DISCOURSE Act
Short summary: Amends Section 230 to limit liability protections for dominant service providers. Deems providers as content creators if they manage content or use targeted algorithms with a discernible viewpoint. Excludes protections for actions against religious material. Mandates public disclosure of content management practices. Reclassifies immunity as an affirmative defense.
Long summary:
Amends Section 230 of the Communications Act of 1934 to limit liability protections for dominant interactive computer service providers based on their content management practices.

Deems providers as content creators if they engage in content moderation or use targeted algorithmic amplification that expresses, promotes, or suppresses a discernible viewpoint.

Excludes liability protections for actions against religious material that burden the exercise of religion.

Mandates public disclosure of content management mechanisms and practices by providers to enable informed consumer choices and entrepreneurial activities.

Reclassifies immunity under Section 230 as an affirmative defense, requiring providers or users to prove they are not information content providers in legal actions.

Official name: Protect Victims of Digital Exploitation and Manipulation Act of 2024
Casual name: Protect Victims of Digital Exploitation and Manipulation Act of 2024
Short summary: Prohibits producing or distributing digital forgeries of intimate visuals without consent, with penalties up to 5 years imprisonment or fines. Exempts good faith distributions for specific purposes. Excludes service providers unless reckless. Defines digital forgery. Establishes extraterritorial jurisdiction. Ensures severability.
Long summary:
Prohibits the production or distribution of digital forgeries of intimate visual depictions of identifiable individuals without their consent, under penalty of fines or imprisonment up to 5 years.

Exempts distributions made in good faith to law enforcement, during legal proceedings, for medical purposes, or in reporting/investigating unlawful content or conduct.

Excludes communications service providers from liability unless they knowingly or recklessly distribute such content.

Defines "digital forgery" as intimate visual depictions created or altered using software, machine learning, AI, or other computer-generated means to appear authentic.

Establishes extraterritorial jurisdiction if the offender or victim is a U.S. national.

Ensures severability of the Act’s provisions if any part is found unconstitutional.

Requires social media companies to disclose content moderation data, including the total number of flagged items, actioned items, user engagement, and how artificial intelligence is used to support content moderation efforts.

Allows Attorney General's office to bring a civil penalty of $5,000,000 per violation per day against social media companies who fail to meet these requirements

Short summary: Identify categories of technologies and prohibit certain activities in sectors related to AI development that that poses acute threats to US national security.
Long summary:
Requires the President to identify, list, and annually update categories of technologies and products in the AI sector that pose acute threats to U.S. national security if acquired by adversaries.

Requires the President to prescribe regulations prohibiting U.S. persons from engaging in covered activities involving listed technologies and products in the AI development sector.

Directs the President to submit annual congressional reports on notifications of covered activities and assessing the need for regulatory amendments.

Encourages multilateral engagement to align with allied countries on similar mechanisms for prohibitions and notifications on technologies in the AI sector.

Authorizes $25 million for implementation and allows direct hiring to administer the entire Act.

Casual name: Emerging Innovative Border Technologies Act
Short summary: Requires the Secretary of Homeland Security to develop a plan for identifying, integrating, and deploying advanced technologies, including AI, to enhance border security. Involves privacy impact assessments, CBP Innovation Teams, and collaboration with private and public sectors.
Long summary:
